What kind of place is Bensalem Township?

Bensalem is a township of about 62,800 people at the southern tip of Bucks County, tucked against the Northeast section of Philadelphia. The Census Bureau puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 62,783, and the 2020 census counted 62,707, which made it the most populous municipality in Bucks County.

Despite the word township, Bensalem has had a mayor and a five-member council since voters chose that form in 1987. It has no incorporated boroughs inside its lines. Villages such as Andalusia, Cornwells Heights, Eddington, Oakford and Trevose are communities within the one township, and each shows up in mailing addresses and listings.

How did Bensalem get its name and its shape?

The name comes from the Manor of Bensalem, the estate of an early settler who combined the Hebrew word for peace with a nod to William Penn. The township was defined by a Bucks County jury in 1692 and carries its present name from a 1701 record, which makes it nearly as old as Pennsylvania itself.

Bensalem covers 21.0 square miles, of which 1.0 is water. Neshaminy Creek marks the eastern edge and Poquessing Creek the western edge, and the Delaware River runs along the southeast border across from Burlington County, New Jersey. The Fall Line, which separates the Atlantic Coastal Plain from the Piedmont, passes through the township near Neshaminy Mall. Population rose from 11,365 in 1950 to 52,368 in 1980, and it has stayed between 56,000 and 63,000 since 1990.

Which roads and rail lines serve Bensalem sellers and buyers?

The township maintains 144.61 of its 195.30 miles of public road. PennDOT looks after 45.89 miles and the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission 4.80.

  • Interstate 95, US 1, US 13 (Bristol Pike), PA 63, PA 132 and PA 513 all cross the township.
  • The Turnpike's Bensalem interchange, exit 351, sits on US 1 in Trevose, and exit 352 at Street Road is E-ZPass only.
  • SEPTA's Trenton Line stops at Cornwells Heights and Eddington, and its West Trenton Line stops at Trevose and Neshaminy Falls.
  • Cornwells Heights also has Amtrak Keystone Service and Northeast Regional trains and a park-and-ride lot reached from I-95 and PA 63.
  • Philadelphia International Airport is about 25 miles away.

What do Census figures show about Bensalem homes?

Bensalem leans toward homeownership, with 62.3 percent of homes owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024 and a median home value of $364,400. About one resident in five was born outside the United States, and 27.2 percent of residents age five and over speak a language other than English at home.

What must a Bensalem seller file before closing?

Bensalem requires a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit whenever a dwelling changes hands. The Building and Planning Department's application form describes it as the permit to occupy a single or multi-family dwelling or condominium through new ownership or new use, and it carries a $100 fee.

  • File the application one month before the settlement date. The form is signed, and a signed copy is required before the permit issues.
  • Attach an electrical panel certificate from one of the approved electrical underwriters named on the form.
  • Attach a maintenance certificate from a registered contractor saying the heating system is in good working condition.
  • Attach a chimney, flue and vent inspection at NFPA 211 Level II, usually done with a camera.
  • Pay in cash, check or money order. The township does not accept credit cards or electronic payments.

The certifications may be obtained up to one year before settlement. Staff search the property's history for open permits, complaints and liens, and unresolved items delay the certificate, so clearing them falls to the seller. Questions go to the Building and Planning Department at 2400 Byberry Road, phone 215-633-3644, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. See the township's resale application.

How does Bucks County assess a Bensalem house?

The Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals, at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown, keeps the assessment rolls for Bensalem. Its office number is 215-348-6219, and the board meets at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesday of each month.

The county's page gave August 3, 2026 as the deadline for annual appeals that year, and any change from an annual appeal takes effect in the 2027 tax year. That date has passed; the next annual deadline will appear on the same page. The same page lists March 1, 2027 as the homestead and farmstead deadline for the tax year starting July 1, 2027.

It also explains Act 29: a new owner must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying a property. Bensalem's sewer service comes from the Bucks County Water and Sewer Authority and its water from Aqua Pennsylvania, since the township sold both systems in 1999, so utility transfers at closing go through those companies. PECO supplies electricity and natural gas.

How does Bensalem's weather affect a house?

Bensalem has a humid subtropical climate. Since 1981 the air temperature has peaked at 103.0 degrees on July 22, 2011, and bottomed out at minus 8.8 on January 22, 1984. July is the wettest month, and thunderstorms peak then.

The wettest single day since 1981 delivered 6.70 inches of rain, on August 27, 2011. The township sits in plant hardiness zone 7a. Houses near Poquessing Creek, Neshaminy Creek or the Delaware are worth checking for drainage and basement moisture, and a buyer can ask the township's engineering and building staff about the flood zone for a specific parcel.

How do schools and employers affect Bensalem buyers?

The Bensalem Township School District runs six elementary schools, two middle schools and Bensalem High School, with a nine-member school board. Holy Ghost Preparatory School is a private Catholic high school in the township, and Catholic elementary schools include St. Charles Borromeo in Cornwells Heights and Saint Ephrem.

  • Rita's Franchise Company has headquarters in Trevose, and Philly Pretzel Factory has headquarters in Bensalem.
  • Healthcare Services Group is headquartered here, as is the United States base for Ibanez guitars and Tama drums.
  • Parx Casino and Racing, which opened as Keystone Racetrack in 1974, and the Penn Community Bank Amphitheater bring regional visitors.
  • Wat Mongkoltepmunee on Knights Road, a Buddhist temple, is a landmark in the township.

What are the options for selling a house fast in Bensalem?

A Bensalem owner can list the house, sell directly, or take a cash offer. A listing exposes the house to the most buyers, while a cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting from the schedule.

All three routes depend on the same township paperwork. Because the use and occupancy application asks for a settlement date and certificates from outside contractors, order the electrical, heating and chimney inspections as soon as a buyer is lined up, and keep the one month filing window in mind when you pick a closing date.

More questions about Bensalem, PA

Does Bensalem require a certificate when a house is sold?

Yes. The township issues a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit for a change in ownership, based on electrical, heating and chimney certificates and a $100 application fee.

How far ahead should I apply for the Bensalem resale permit?

About one month before the settlement date. The township asks for the signed application and all three certifications at that point, and the township accepts only cash, check or money order.

Who inspects the chimney for a Bensalem sale?

A chimney sweep company of your choice, with an NFPA 211 Level II inspection noted on the certification. The township also states that it will not accept certifications from two named companies.

Where do I send a Bucks County assessment appeal?

To the Board of Assessment Appeals at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown. The 2026 annual deadline was August 3, 2026, and the board posts each year's date on its page.

What do new owners of Bensalem property file with the county?

Under Act 29, a new owner submits contact information to the Board of Assessment within 30 days of the purchase, according to the Bucks County page.

Cash Home Buyers in Pennsylvania

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Abington, PA sale

Abington at a glance

  • Abington is in Montgomery County.
Selling in Abington?
We buy Abington houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What do I have to do before closing on a house in Abington?

Abington Township requires an affidavit at or before settlement on any single-family, two-family or multifamily dwelling. The seller swears that the house shows a clear street address, has smoke detectors and has at least one carbon monoxide detector. Under the township's Resolution 92-008, a deed is not accepted for registration unless this certification comes with it.

The rules in Ordinance 1894 are specific, and a buyer's agent will check them.

  • Address numerals at least three inches high on the street side of the structure, visible from the center of the street
  • A smoke detector on each level and in each bedroom or sleeping area
  • A carbon monoxide detector no more than 40 feet from every sleeping area
  • Detectors that are UL rated and approved

Breaking the ordinance is a summary offense that can bring a fine of $1,000 at most, up to 30 days in jail, or both, and every day of a continuing violation is charged separately. The affidavit form is on the township's document center. Smoke and CO alarms cost little, and installing them before listing removes a closing delay.

Does Abington require a use and occupancy permit to sell a home?

No. The township's permit page states that Abington does not have a use and occupancy permit for residential properties. Use and occupancy review applies to commercial properties, new businesses and business transfers, and includes a Fire Marshal inspection.

That makes a typical Abington house sale lighter on municipal paperwork than in towns that demand a resale inspection. The detector affidavit is the main township requirement. Any building work you did without a permit is a separate question. Ask the Code Enforcement Division before listing if you finished a basement, built a deck or added a bathroom.

What are the real estate and transfer taxes in Abington?

Abington's 2026 tax sheet lists a real estate tax split among the township, the Abington School District, a school referendum levy and Montgomery County with its community college. On a house assessed at $150,000 the sheet shows a total of $7,994 a year. The school district portion, at 39.8992 mills, is $5,970 of that.

2026 tax example for a $150,000 assessment, from the Abington Township tax sheet
LevyAnnual amount
Abington Township$926
Abington School District$5,970
School district referendum$206
Montgomery County$819
Community college$73
Total$7,994

The same sheet lists a township realty transfer tax of 1 percent, collected by Montgomery County, on top of the state's 1 percent. Ask your closing agent whether the school district adds a share on your deed. Pennsylvania's Department of Revenue exempts some transfers, such as property passing by will or intestate succession.

Abington does not assess property. The Montgomery County Board of Assessments does, and the last countywide reassessment was in 1998. The township bill, which also covers sewer and refuse, is mailed in the first week of February for a January to December year. The school bill follows in the first week of July and runs July to June.

What is Abington Township like for a seller?

Abington is a first-class township in Montgomery County, incorporated in 1704 and described by the township as a first-ring suburb of Philadelphia. It covers about 15.5 square miles. The township names Willow Grove, Roslyn, Crestmont, Glenside, Rydal, North Hills and Meadowbrook among its neighborhoods.

Easton Road, Huntington Pike (PA 232) and Old York Road (PA 611) run through the township, and I-276 and PA 309 are minutes away. Seven SEPTA stations on three regional rail lines serve it: North Hills on the Doylestown line; Crestmont, Roslyn and Ardsley on the Warminster line; and Meadowbrook, Rydal and Noble on the West Trenton line. The township says the ride to Center City takes less than half an hour.

Most of the township has public water from Aqua Pennsylvania and public sewer maintained by the township. It runs more than 25 parks covering over 375 acres, and its fire protection comes from an all-volunteer department with five stations. The Abington School District is a separate body from the township government.

What do the numbers say about Abington housing?

The Census Bureau's mid 2025 estimate for the township is 58,656 people, compared with 55,310 in 2010. Density comes to roughly 3,769 people per square mile.

  • Owners live in 77.3 percent of occupied homes
  • A typical owned home is valued at $391,800
  • Rent in the middle of the market is $1,493
  • 22,391 households, averaging 2.56 people
  • Household income in the middle is $103,645
  • 51.1 percent of adults over 25 hold a bachelor's degree or more
  • Workers spend 28.7 minutes getting to their jobs on average

These come from Census QuickFacts for Abington township and cover 2020 to 2024. The same table shows 92.5 percent of residents in the house they lived in a year before, so turnover is low and a listing with defects or title questions takes more effort to place.

Which sale routes suit an Abington house?

Sellers here generally choose among three routes. An agent listing reaches the widest pool of buyers, and it also means staging, showings and waiting on a buyer's financing and inspection. Selling without an agent saves the commission but leaves the paperwork, from the detector affidavit to the deed, in your hands.

A direct cash sale skips showings and repairs. It suits an inherited house, a tenant-occupied property, a house with code or maintenance issues, or a seller who needs a firm closing date. A cash buyer's price reflects the work the house needs, so weigh it against what a repaired and listed house would net once fees, repairs and months of carrying costs come out.

Whichever route you pick, the same Abington steps apply: the detector certification, the tax figures above and a recorded deed at the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds.

How do I handle an inherited or tenant-occupied Abington house?

With an inherited house, settle first who can sign for the estate, because title must be in order before a deed can be recorded. Title passing through an estate carries no state transfer tax, though the later sale does.

With a tenant in place, read the lease before you list. Showings and possession dates depend on its terms and on Pennsylvania landlord and tenant law. Buyers who plan to keep the tenant will ask for the lease and rent history, and the detector rules cover rentals sold in the township too.

For questions about the township tax sheet, call the Abington tax office at 267-536-1024 on weekdays between 8 am and 4 pm. Owners of a primary residence can apply for a homestead exclusion through the Montgomery County Board of Assessments, and applications must arrive by March 1 to reduce the school tax bill.

More questions about Abington, PA

Does Abington require a smoke and carbon monoxide certification when I sell?

Yes. Ordinance 1894 requires smoke detectors on each level and in each bedroom, plus a carbon monoxide detector within 40 feet of every sleeping area, with a seller's affidavit at or before settlement.

Is there a residential use and occupancy permit in Abington?

No. The township says it has no use and occupancy permit for residential properties. That review applies to commercial buildings and business transfers.

What is Abington's transfer tax?

The township's 2026 tax sheet lists a 1 percent real estate transfer tax, collected by Montgomery County. The state adds its own 1 percent. Ask the closing agent whether any other local share applies.

Who assesses property in Abington Township?

The Montgomery County Board of Assessments, not the township. The township says the last countywide reassessment was in 1998, and interim bills reflect changes such as additions or demolitions.

When must I apply for the homestead exclusion?

Applications must be in the Board of Assessments' hands by March 1 to cut the school tax bill. Approved owners are not asked to refile annually, but a move or a change of title means applying again.

Lancaster at a glance

  • Lancaster is in Lancaster County.
Selling in Lancaster?
We buy Lancaster houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does selling a house in Lancaster, PA work?

Whether you hire a broker, post a sign yourself or take a cash offer, the same city and county paperwork applies. The city issues its own payoff figures, the recorder collects transfer tax, and a countywide reassessment is something buyers will raise.

Lancaster is a small, dense city. About 58,366 people lived in Lancaster by the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate. They share barely 7.2 square miles of land, around 8,000 per square mile. Much of the housing is rowhomes on narrow lots, so a sale often turns on the condition of one building.

A cash sale can move faster, since no lender appraisal holds up the closing. It does not remove the city steps below. Someone still has to order the property certification, record the deed and pay the transfer tax.

What kind of city is Lancaster for a home seller?

Lancaster is the county seat and one of the oldest inland cities in the country. It began as Hickory Town, was laid out in 1734, became a borough in 1742 and a city in 1818, and served as the state capital from 1799 to 1812. That age shows up in the housing stock, where nineteenth century brick and early twentieth century rowhouses sit beside factory conversions.

The city sits in the Piedmont region just north of the Conestoga River. Its neighborhoods include the Historic East Side, Chestnut Hill, Cabbage Hill, the West End, Prospect Heights, Musser Park, Mussertown, Woodward Hill and the Gallery Row arts district. Central Market, built in 1889, anchors the downtown core, and Park City Center is the largest enclosed shopping center in south central Pennsylvania.

Jobs come mostly from health care, government, education and retail. Lancaster General Hospital was the largest city employer in the 2018 financial report, with 9,406 employees, followed by the county government and the School District of Lancaster. Franklin & Marshall College and several other schools add rental demand near the center of town.

  • Public schools: the School District of Lancaster, with McCaskey and McCaskey East as the high school campuses.
  • Weather: about 42 inches of precipitation a year, and 72 inches of snow in the winter of 2009 to 2010, which is the record. Older roofs and basements take the strain.

What do the Census numbers say about Lancaster homes?

They describe a city with more renters than owners and home values far below the Philadelphia suburbs. Less than half of occupied homes have their owner living in them, which means many sales involve tenants.

Lancaster city in the Census Bureau's five-year survey covering 2020 through 2024
MeasureLancaster city
Residents, mid-2025 estimate58,366
Occupied households21,971
Share of homes lived in by owners48.6%
Middle home value among owners$219,500
Middle monthly rent$1,240
Middle household income$63,690
Stayed in the same home for a year81.3%

The gap between a $219,500 middle home value and $1,240 middle rent is why investors buy in the city. A seller with a rental can expect offers that price in the rent roll and the cost of the next licensing inspection.

Which City of Lancaster rules can affect a sale?

The ones that matter most are rental licensing, the vacant property registry and the lead safety rules for older rentals. They are run by the Bureau of Property Maintenance and Housing Inspections at 120 North Duke Street.

  • Rental licenses and inspections. The city runs a residential rental program under its Chapter 238 and inspects every licensed rental at least once every six years, with at least three weeks of notice. For a tenant-occupied house, request the license status and open inspection items from the city before replying to any bid.
  • Lead safety. Rentals and child care facilities built before 1978 must meet lead safety requirements every two to four years under rules that took effect in January 2023. The city plans to cover roughly 12,000 older rentals over a four year cycle.
  • Vacant or abandoned houses. An owner must register a vacant building within 10 days. The semiannual fee is $200, with extra charges for buildings vacant two years or longer, and a house actively marketed for sale is outside the definition of vacant. If a registered property is sold, the new owner has 10 days to update the registration and inherits unpaid fees.
  • Short term rentals. The city allows them only in listed zoning districts, with a Certificate of Zoning Compliance, a rental license and an inspection first. A buyer planning an Airbnb use should confirm the district before paying for the house.

The vacant property rule counts a house in mortgage default or under a pending sheriff sale as abandoned, and those properties face monthly inspections. A seller behind on the mortgage should know that before listing.

What does the 2027 Lancaster County reassessment mean for sellers?

It means every parcel in the county, including each house in Lancaster, received a new assessed value for the 2027 tax year. The county mailed the notices on June 15, 2026, and the deadline to appeal a reassessment value was August 3, 2026, so that window has closed. Annual appeals after that point must be filed by August 1 of a given year to take effect for the following tax year.

The old values were based on market conditions from 2018. The new ones draw on arm's length sales from 2022 through 2024, adjusted by neighborhood. For a Lancaster seller this matters in two ways. A buyer may notice a higher assessed value than the one on the old bill. The county points out that every taxing body must lower its millage so that the reassessment alone does not bring in more revenue.

  • County and municipal millage for 2027 gets set around the close of December 2026.
  • School district millage for the 2027 to 2028 school year is set in June 2027, and the reassessment does not change 2026 to 2027 school taxes.
  • The assessment office is at 150 North Queen Street, Suite 310, and property records can be searched free on the county reassessment site.

Have the new assessed value ready when you talk to a buyer. A parcel that jumped will raise questions about the tax bill, and the answer is that the rates reset before 2027 bills go out.

What paperwork does the city require before closing in Lancaster?

The settlement company must send the city a Request for Property Certification with payment, and for a house inside city limits a smoke detector certification has to be completed before the city will release information. The city asks for two full business days to return the figures once the request is complete.

The 2025 version of the city form listed an $18 tax certification, a $5 trash final, a $17 water final and a $40 combined final. It also asks for the meter reading, the new owner's details and the settlement date, and it tells the title agent to escrow estimates if the city does not answer in time. The form flags delinquent city taxes, property violations, police alarm charges, housing licenses and liens.

  1. Order the property certification early, since the smoke detector step comes first.
  2. Have the buyer open a water account using the city application.
  3. Check for delinquent county taxes with the Lancaster County Tax Claim office, which the city form lists at 717-299-8232.
  4. The form also has a line for Downtown Investment District (DID) charges, with a separate DID office number.

What does a Lancaster sale cost at the recorder's office?

The state's cut is 1 percent of the property value. The county recorder gathers it at the same time as any local transfer tax. Buyer and seller are both liable for it. State exemptions cover certain family transfers and property passing by inheritance.

The title agent can quote the exact combined rate for a Lancaster deed, since the local portion depends on the taxing bodies involved. Who pays it is negotiated in the sales contract.

With an as-is purchase, check the contract line by line for who covers transfer tax and the city finals.

Which Lancaster houses suit a cash offer?

It makes sense when speed, condition or tenants matter more than the last dollar of price. A rowhouse with deferred repairs, a rental with an open inspection report, or a vacant inherited house are cases where a cash buyer can simplify the sale.

Compare any offer to a realistic list price less repairs, agent commission, transfer tax, city finals and months of carrying cost. To see what a direct buyer would pay for your Lancaster house, request a quote from Cash Home Buyers and weigh it against the net sheet.

More questions about Lancaster, PA

Do I need a smoke detector certification to sell a house in Lancaster city?

Yes for a house inside city limits. The city's property certification request states that a completed smoke detector certification is required before the city provides settlement information. Have it done before the title company orders the finals.

Can I still appeal my Lancaster County reassessment?

The reassessment appeal deadline for the 2027 tax year was August 3, 2026, so that window has closed. Annual appeals can still be filed each year by August 1 for the following tax year, and an appeal can lower or raise the value.

What happens to a vacant house in Lancaster while I try to sell it?

A vacant house that is not actively marketed must be registered with the city within 10 days and carries a semiannual fee. Properties in mortgage default count as abandoned and face monthly inspections. Check the registry rules with the housing bureau at 717-291-4781 before the house sits empty.

Does a tenant have to leave before I sell a Lancaster rental?

No. Tenants do not have to move out for a rental to sell, because the buyer steps into the lease. The unit still needs a current city rental license, and any open inspection items should be cleared or priced into the sale.

Who collects the transfer tax when a Lancaster house sells?

The Lancaster County recorder takes payment at the moment the deed is filed. The state's piece is 1 percent of the value, with local taxes stacked on top. The title company will show the exact figures on the settlement statement.

What is the fastest way to sell a house in Lower Paxton Township?

A cash sale is the fastest route in Lower Paxton Township, and the main gating item is the sewer settlement form that your closing agent has to send the township authority. Listing with an agent gives more exposure, but it adds showings, buyer financing and appraisal steps that a cash buyer skips.

Lower Paxton is the most populous municipality in Dauphin County, with 53,501 residents at the 2020 census and an estimate of 55,564 for July 1, 2025. It lies about 9 miles northeast of Harrisburg, with Interstates 81 and 83 both inside the township. Sellers who ask for speed here are usually dealing with an inherited house, a relocation, a rental they no longer want to manage, or deferred maintenance.

  • Choose your closing date first, then work backward on payoffs and utility balances.
  • Ask your closing agent to submit the township sewer transfer form early.
  • Confirm in writing who pays the 2 percent combined transfer tax.

What should sellers know about Lower Paxton Township itself?

The township covers 28.1 square miles in south central Dauphin County. Susquehanna Township is on its west, Middle Paxton on its north, West Hanover and South Hanover on its east, and Swatara on its south. Beaver Creek forms the eastern border, and Blue Mountain, the southernmost ridge of the Ridge and Valley Appalachians in the region, sits along the northern edge. Four unincorporated communities are counted as census designated places: Linglestown in the northeast with 6,334 residents, Paxtonia in the center with 5,412, Colonial Park in the west and southwest with 13,229, and a small piece of Progress in the far west.

The name comes from Paxtang, spelled Peshtank in the original Native American language and understood to mean standing water. Dauphin County was split from Lancaster County in 1785, and what remained of the old Paxtang Township after a 1767 division was renamed Lower Paxton. Harrisburg was formed as a borough in 1791 and Swatara Township followed in 1799. Population jumped from 6,546 in 1950 to 17,618 in 1960 and 26,517 in 1970, which explains why so many neighborhoods date from the postwar suburban boom.

Two interstates meet here. Interstate 83 runs through the west with Exit 50 at US 22 and Jonestown Road and Exit 48 at Union Deposit Road, and I-81 crosses the center from west to east, with Exit 72 between Linglestown and Paxtonia. Children attend the Central Dauphin School District.

What do Census figures show about Lower Paxton homes?

About two thirds of housing is owner occupied, at 66.5 percent, so roughly a third of housing is not owner occupied. The median value of an owner-occupied home was $284,700 over 2020 to 2024, median gross rent was $1,417, and the township had 22,025 households. Median household income was $91,789 in 2024 dollars, 38.8 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and mean travel time to work was 21.4 minutes. Some 86.0 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

A median value under $300,000 means transfer taxes and closing costs are smaller in dollars than in the Philadelphia suburbs, but they still add up. At the median value, the combined 2 percent transfer tax is $5,694. A landlord selling a rental pays the same percentage, so settle the split before you sign.

What happens to sewer and stormwater accounts when I sell?

Lower Paxton's sewer authority requires settlement agents to request balances on a specific form before a sale or refinance, and it can take up to five business days for the form to be reviewed and returned. Start this the day the contract is signed.

  • The completed Sewer and Stormwater Services Transfer Form goes to the authority's settlements email address or by fax.
  • A new sewer account carries a $15 processing fee collected at settlement.
  • The authority bills in arrears each January, April, July and October, so ask your settlement agent to prorate a mid-quarter sale. Its billing page lists a flat residential sewer rate and a single family stormwater fee on the same quarterly bill.
  • Delinquent accounts can go to a collection law firm, and unpaid charges become a lien that follows the property.

If your account is on automatic withdrawal, call the Sewer and Utilities Department at 717-657-5617 so the draft stops after the sale. Bills stay in the owner's name, which matters when you own a rental and a tenant normally pays the household bills.

How do Lower Paxton property taxes work?

Real estate is taxed by the township, Dauphin County and the Central Dauphin School District, and the school district is by far the largest bill at 18.2934 mills for 2025 to 2026. The township says its assessments rest on a January 2002 base, adjusted for new construction and appeals, so the figure on your bill can differ a great deal from market value. Earned income tax is 2 percent, with 1.5 percent to the school district and 0.5 percent to the township, and the local services tax is $52 for people who work in the township.

Unpaid taxes pass to the Dauphin County Tax Claim Bureau after December 31. Interim bills follow new construction, pools and additions, so a seller who finished a basement or built a deck may owe an interim bill even after the regular one.

How do I appeal a Dauphin County assessment?

Dauphin County accepts annual appeals after June 1 and no later than 4:30 p.m. on August 1, and a late filing is rejected even if it was mailed on time. An appeal from a new or revised assessment must arrive within 40 days of the notice. The filing fee must come with the form and is not refunded, and all delinquent taxes on the parcel must be current before the Board will accept or hear it.

The Board of Assessment Appeals sits in the Administration Building at 2 South 2nd Street, Harrisburg, and takes filings by mail or in person on weekdays. The aggrieved party must appear at the hearing, and anyone representing an owner must be a Pennsylvania attorney who brings a power of attorney.

What closing costs should a Lower Paxton seller expect?

The state realty transfer tax is 1 percent, the township levies one half of one percent by ordinance, and the Central Dauphin School District levies one half of one percent. Together that is 2 percent of the sale price, collected at settlement by the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds. Both parties are jointly liable under state law, so allocate it in the contract. Exempt transfers include certain moves between close family members and property that passes by will or intestacy.

Add pro-rated real estate tax, sewer and trash charges, any agent commissions, and payoff of any mortgage or lien. Ask the township codes office whether any sale-related inspection or certificate applies to your address.

More questions about Lower Paxton, PA

How much is the transfer tax in Lower Paxton Township?

The total is 2 percent of the sale price: 1 percent to Pennsylvania, one half percent to the township and one half percent to the Central Dauphin School District. The county Recorder of Deeds collects it at settlement.

Does the Lower Paxton sewer authority need anything before closing?

Yes. The settlement agent must send the Sewer and Stormwater Services Transfer Form and allow up to five business days for balances, and the authority charges a $15 new account fee at settlement.

What is the Dauphin County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 at 4:30 p.m., with filing allowed after June 1. A new or revised assessment can be appealed within 40 days of its notice.

Who collects real estate tax in Lower Paxton Township?

An elected tax collector handles real estate tax payments for the township, county and school district. Unpaid taxes go to the Dauphin County Tax Claim Bureau after December 31.

Which interstates serve Lower Paxton Township?

Interstate 83 runs through the west and Interstate 81 runs across the center. I-83 has Exits 50 and 48 in the township, and I-81 has Exit 72 between Linglestown and Paxtonia.

How does selling a house in Bristol work?

Bristol in Bucks County is most often Bristol Township, the large municipality of about 54,000 residents that includes Levittown neighborhoods, Croydon and Bath. A sale there runs through the agreement of sale, a township change of occupancy approval on resale, settlement and a deed recorded with the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds. Bristol Borough is a separate municipality with its own rules, so confirm which one your address falls in. Your tax bill names the municipality and school district, and the Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals can confirm the parcel's location.

The township's Building and Planning Department is at 2501 Bath Road and answers questions at 215-785-3680. Most of what follows comes from the township's 2026 fee schedule and permit pages, plus Bucks County's assessment office and the Census Bureau.

What should a seller know about Bristol Township's layout and history?

Bristol Township covers 15.84 square miles of land and another 1.27 of water, and its housing mixes postwar subdivisions with older villages near the river. It was formed in 1692 as Buckingham Township and renamed Bristol in 1702. The Delaware Canal arrived in 1831, and the township stayed largely agricultural until the 1950s, when William Levitt began building Levittown in 1952, partly inside its borders.

Named places inside the township include Bath, Croydon, Edgely, Midway, Newportville, Pine Grove and part of Levittown, with Fairless Hills also counted in its neighborhoods. Mill Creek, Neshaminy Creek and Queen Anne Creek run through it. The township ranked as the 13th largest municipality in Pennsylvania in the 2020 census, and the springs at Bath once drew wealthy Philadelphians. The Phineas Pemberton House, begun in 1687, is on the National Register of Historic Places, and the War Dog Memorial stands in front of the municipal building. Public schools belong to the Bristol Township School District, whose main high school is Harry S. Truman High School.

Which roads and transit connect Bristol Township?

Bristol Township sits at the junction of Interstate 95, the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Interstate 295. Bristol Pike carries US 13 through the township, and Veterans Highway carries PA 413 toward the Burlington-Bristol Bridge.

  • Public roads: 203.47 miles in 2022, with 172.22 miles township-maintained, 27.45 miles under PennDOT and 3.80 miles under the Turnpike Commission.
  • Bus: SEPTA Suburban routes 127, 128 and 129.
  • Rail: SEPTA's Trenton Line stops at Croydon station in the township.

Commutes average 27.4 minutes, and 92.2 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, so few households move in a given year.

What do the Census numbers say about Bristol Township homes?

Most Bristol Township homes are owner occupied. The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates are below.

  • Owner-occupied rate: 72.4 percent of housing units.
  • Median value of an owner-occupied home: $315,500.
  • Median gross rent: $1,245.
  • Households: 20,908, with a median income of $79,101.

The population was 54,291 in the 2020 census and an estimated 54,063 in July 2025, a dip of half a percent. The climate is humid subtropical, and the wettest day since 1981 delivered 6.42 inches of rain on August 27, 2011, so check basements and sump pumps before showings.

What does the township charge for resale and related fees?

The Resolution 2026-25 fee schedule sets a $100 charge for a residential change of occupancy on resale, and a second inspection costs $40 if one is needed. The table lists the fees most sellers meet.

Source: Bristol Township 2026 fee schedule (Resolution 2026-25). Order the tax and sewer certifications before settlement is scheduled.

How do transfer tax and property tax work in Bristol Township?

The township's fee schedule lists a real estate transfer tax of 1 percent of the purchase price, split 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the Bristol Township School District. Add the state's 1 percent and the total on a sale is 2 percent, and the grantor and grantee are jointly liable under state law.

Township millage for 2026 lists these funds: general 16.58 mills, debt 2.45, capital improvement 1.5, fire protection 3, recreation 0.9 and rescue squad 0.55. That adds to 24.98 mills before the school and county rates. A buyer must send contact information to the Bucks County Board of Assessment within 30 days of buying, under Act 29. The board's 2026 annual appeal deadline was August 3, 2026, with a $75 filing fee per parcel, and any change takes effect in the 2027 tax year. Ask the board each year for the next date.

How does the Bristol Township permit process run?

The township's permit page describes six steps from application to a Certificate of Approval, and a finished project closes the file for the next owner. Applications go through the township's online self-service portal or at the municipal building.

  • Submit the application, and staff check that forms and fees are complete.
  • Township professionals review the plans against state and local construction codes and zoning.
  • The application is approved or denied; a denial can be corrected or taken to the appeals board.
  • Once the permit is paid for and issued, it must be posted where the public can see it, and approved plans stay on site.
  • Inspections happen in two phases, rough and final, and you call 48 hours ahead to schedule each one.
  • A Certificate of Approval issues when all work complies.

If an inspector finds unapproved work, the township demands compliance, and a stop work order follows when compliance is not found. Sellers who have open permits should finish the final inspection before listing.

What permits and open work should a Bristol seller check?

Unpermitted work is the common obstacle, because the township doubles permit fees when it finds work done without a permit and may add court fines. Permits are needed for additions, fences, renovations, decks, pools, demolitions and electrical, plumbing and HVAC equipment.

All contractors working in the township must be registered, and registrations are renewed annually from January through December. The township also asks everyone who lives or works there to complete a municipal and school income tax registration through Keystone Collection. Before you list, confirm that finals were signed off on past projects. The fee schedule also lists an annual rental fee of $100 for a single-family dwelling and an occupied rental fine of $320, so landlords selling a tenant-occupied house should check their rental status first.

More questions about Bristol, PA

Do I need a use and occupancy inspection to sell a house in Bristol Township?

The township's 2026 fee schedule lists a $100 residential change of occupancy charge on resale and $40 for a second inspection if one is needed. Call 215-785-3680 to confirm the steps for your address.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Bristol Township sale?

The contract sets who pays, but state law makes seller and buyer jointly liable. The total is 2 percent: 1 percent to Pennsylvania, 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the school district.

What certifications does the township issue at sale?

Tax and sewer certifications. A four-year tax certification costs $35, or $50 rushed, and a sewer certification costs $50. Order them before settlement is scheduled.

Is Bristol Township the same as Bristol Borough?

No. They are separate municipalities in Bucks County with separate rules and officials. The figures on this page describe the township.

Can I appeal my Bristol Township assessment after selling?

Appeals are filed by the aggrieved party of record, and the Bucks County board's 2026 annual deadline was August 3, 2026. Changes from an annual appeal take effect in the 2027 tax year.

  • Millcreek is in Erie County.
Selling in Millcreek?

Get My Cash Offer →

What kind of place is Millcreek Township, Pennsylvania?

Millcreek Township fills the lakefront and suburban ground west and south of the city of Erie, and the Presque Isle peninsula joins the mainland inside its western edge. Its 2020 count of 54,070 makes it the biggest township in western Pennsylvania and 14th among all municipalities statewide.

Total area is 32.79 square miles, and elevation rises from 572 feet at Lake Erie to 1,170 feet near Belleview Heights. Most land is given over to retail, services, light industry, schools and residential streets. Only about 1 percent is zoned for agriculture, so a house here is almost always a suburban lot with public roads and utilities.

Parks and open space that shape neighborhoods include:

  • Presque Isle State Park, whose entrance sits in the township
  • Zuck Park and the Erie Golf Course
  • Asbury Woods Nature Center and Recreation Center
  • Waldameer and Water World, an amusement park near the Presque Isle entrance

How did Millcreek grow into the largest township in the region?

Millcreek was one of the original 16 townships of Erie County. Settlers moved inland from the bayfront and formed hamlets such as Federal Hill, Kearsarge, Marvintown and Weigelville, and the city of Erie later annexed pieces of the township as it expanded. Tavern keepers opened inns about every mile once Ridge Road, now part of U.S. 20, was extended west through the area in 1805. The Nicholson Tavern, put up by Isabella Nicholson and her sons in 1836, is still owned by the family and is a listed historic site.

The big jump came after World War II. Population was 16,776 in 1950, 28,239 in 1960 and 36,946 in 1970, then it levelled off near 54,000. A July 2025 estimate of 52,680 sits about 2.6 percent under the 2020 base. Because the postwar boom built so much of the housing, a typical Millcreek house carries a roof, furnace and wiring that are decades old.

The township is also home to Erie International Airport, Millcreek Mall and the LECOM Health system, three large employers and destinations that anchor demand for housing close to them.

How do Millcreek housing and income figures look?

Roughly two of every three Millcreek homes are owner-occupied, and the median value is $230,600. Every row below is taken from the Census Bureau's Millcreek township profile.

With 23.1 percent of residents past 65, long-owned homes and estates make up part of what comes to market, and a 17.1 minute average trip to work keeps most destinations close.

Which Millcreek code enforcement rules can affect a sale?

Millcreek's Bureau of Code Enforcement applies the International Property Maintenance Code and the International Fire Code, so an unresolved violation on your parcel can hold up a closing. Complaints from neighbors or callers usually start a case.

The office handles these common problems:

  • Weeds, debris and trash piling up on the lot
  • Sidewalks that are a tripping hazard, and unshoveled snow or ice on sidewalks
  • Electrical, building and fire violations
  • Pest infestations and abandoned vehicles on private property
  • Illegal burning, demolition permits and condemnations

A notice of violation gives you 20 days to appeal the inspector's decision. If you ignore it, the inspector returns for a second look and can file a non-traffic summary citation with the local magistrate, who then schedules a hearing for the owner of record. Vacant houses follow the same path, and when compliance never comes the township can move to clean and secure the building or raze it. If your house is empty or run down, clear these items or write down what remains before you sign a contract.

Can a Millcreek house be rented short term?

Yes, but only in certain zones and only after registering with the township. Millcreek calls Airbnb or VRBO style stays Limited Lodging, defined as renting to the same guest for at least two and no more than 30 consecutive nights. A stay beyond 30 nights is a long-term rental and is not covered.

Limited Lodging is allowed in the MU-1 Neighborhood Mixed Use, MU-2 Corridor Mixed Use and PI Presque Isle Gateway districts, plus two Limited Lodging Overlay areas near the lake. One overlay runs from the west line of the Hartt Estates Subdivision along Montpelier Avenue, south to West Lake Road and north to Lake Erie. The other starts at the east line of Calvary Cemetery and runs to West 11th Street, the Corridor Mixed Use 2 boundary and the Presque Isle district.

Each property in an approved area registers with the Code Enforcement Office. A buyer who wants a lakeside house for guest stays should first ask the Zoning Office, 814-833-2935, whether the parcel lies inside one of those areas.

How do Millcreek assessments and appeals work through Erie County?

Erie County, not the township, sets your assessed value. Its Board of Assessment Appeals takes the annual appeal form between January 1 and August 1 and holds hearings from July to October. Filing costs $50 for a parcel, with $10 more for each added parcel in the same property.

Points taken from the county's appeal form:

  • An owner may speak at the hearing, or a Pennsylvania attorney may; a company owner must use an attorney.
  • Name up to three comparables, either recent sales or active listings.
  • Send two copies of your evidence ten days ahead, and any appraisal should be effective within six months of the appeal.
  • An appeal reopens the valuation, and the figure can fall, hold or rise.

Erie County's assessment office also offers forms for the homestead exclusion, owner changes, Clean and Green land and catastrophic loss, and it publishes a millage chart each year. Find Millcreek Township and its school district on that chart for the rates behind a bill.

What happens at closing, and what must a Millcreek seller disclose?

Deeds for Millcreek houses are recorded at the Erie County Recorder of Deeds in the courthouse on West Sixth Street, which also collects the state and local transfer tax and the county's recording fees. Deeds between spouses, parents and children, or siblings can be exempt. The county's tax sale page quotes 2 percent as its standard transfer cost, so ask the Recorder for the local split on an ordinary Millcreek sale.

State law, Title 68 Chapter 73, has you fill out a disclosure statement and hand over a signed copy before any agreement of transfer is signed. Its subjects include the roof, basement, drainage and flood risk indicators. An executor or other fiduciary selling for an estate is excused from it, which applies to inherited Millcreek homes.

Act 74 of 2026 adds a written flood insurance warning to the seller package once the Insurance Department puts up its flood page, which is relevant for parcels near the lake.

What if property taxes on a Millcreek house are behind?

The county's annual upset sale covers parcels with taxes two or more years behind, and it runs as an online auction. A winning bid does not end the owner's rights until the bidder pays in full, so the owner can still clear the debt first and keep the house. After full payment, nothing can be redeemed.

Parcels that do not sell go to a judicial sale and then a repository list, and the owner cannot bid on a parcel in either group. The buyer inherits liens and judgments and receives a quit claim deed. A sale that happens before this point usually keeps more of your equity. The Tax Claim Bureau can give a payoff and tell you where your parcel stands.

What are the main ways to sell a house in Millcreek?

Which route fits depends on repairs, timing and any code problems at the property.

  • Agent listing: a fit when the house shows well and you can wait for showings, a buyer's inspection and loan approval.
  • Owner sale: skips the agent but puts pricing, the disclosure form and negotiation on you.
  • Cash sale as is: used for estate homes, houses with open Millcreek code notices, tenant-occupied properties and places needing work, generally at less than a repaired house would bring.

Start by pulling the Erie County parcel record, confirming no township notice is open and completing the state disclosure statement.

More questions about Millcreek, PA

Is Millcreek a city or a township?

Millcreek is a township in Erie County. The city of Erie annexed pieces of it over the years, but the township keeps its own zoning, code enforcement and police.

Can a Millcreek house with open code violations still be sold?

Yes. A notice of violation leaves 20 days to appeal, and ignored notices can reach the local magistrate as a summary citation. Disclose the notice to buyers and ask the Code Enforcement office what closes the file.

When does Erie County accept assessment appeals for Millcreek homes?

The appeal form is accepted January 1 through August 1 and hearings run July through October. Filing costs $50 a parcel, and an appeal can raise the value as well as lower it.

Must Millcreek sellers hand buyers a disclosure statement?

Usually yes. Pennsylvania requires a signed property disclosure statement before an agreement of transfer is signed, except for fiduciaries selling on behalf of an estate.

Can I run my Millcreek house as an Airbnb before selling?

Only inside the zones where the township permits Limited Lodging, meaning guest stays of 2 to 30 nights. Those are the MU-1, MU-2 and Presque Isle Gateway districts and two overlay areas, and registration with Code Enforcement is required.

Who is selling homes in Haverford Township, PA?

Haverford Township is a settled, high-value inner suburb on Philadelphia's western edge, and owners live in most of its homes. The 2025 Census estimate is 50,997 people, and 92.9 percent of them were in the same house a year before the survey.

The 2020 to 2024 survey shows 87.4 percent of homes owner-occupied, a typical value of $466,400 and rent near $1,766. Households earned a median $131,674, 64.4 percent of adults have a four-year degree, and 19.2 percent of residents are past 65. Long-held homes and older owners explain why so many Haverford sales follow a downsize, an inheritance or a house that has outlived its last update.

When a house needs a roof, kitchen or electrical work, the cost of making it market-ready is large at these price levels. Many owners set that against an as-is sale.

Where is Haverford Township and what are its neighborhoods?

Haverford Township fills the northeast corner of Delaware County, a 10-square-mile area that is all land. William Penn laid it out as part of the Welsh Tract, the first families arrived in 1682, and the township was incorporated in 1911. It is a first-class township run by a Board of Commissioners divided into wards.

Neighboring municipalities are Lower Merion Township to the northeast, the City of Philadelphia to the east, Upper Darby and Springfield townships to the south, Marple Township to the west and Radnor Township to the northwest. Cobbs Creek and Darby Creek mark parts of its boundary, and Naylors Run and Meadowbrook Run cross it.

  • Planned suburbs along the rail lines include Llanerch (1897) and Brookline (1909). Most of the large housing tracts date from after World War II, including Chatham Park.
  • Neighborhood names include Beechwood, Oakmont, Manoa, Westgate Hills, Paddock Farms, Merwood and Bon Air.
  • Parts of the Haverford, Ardmore, Wynnewood and Bryn Mawr communities lie inside the township.
  • Many of the post-war tracts share the Havertown postal address.

Name the neighborhood on your listing or offer request, because buyers search by it.

How do roads and SEPTA shape a Haverford house sale?

Good transit is one of the township's selling points. SEPTA's Norristown High Speed Line stops at seven stations inside the township, more than in any other township along the route: Township Line Road, Penfield, Beechwood-Brookline, Wynnewood Road, Ardmore Junction, Ardmore Avenue and Haverford. Suburban bus routes 103, 104, 105, 110, 112, 115, 120, 123 and 126 also serve the township and connect to the 69th Street Transportation Center.

As of 2018 the township had 158.26 miles of public roads, of which 123.78 miles are township-maintained and 34.48 miles belong to PennDOT. The I-476 Blue Route runs along the western edge, U.S. 1 follows Township Line Road, U.S. 30 crosses the northern tip on Lancaster Avenue, and Route 3 follows West Chester Pike. The mean commute for residents is 27.0 minutes.

Which schools and parks come with a Haverford address?

Public school students attend the School District of Haverford Township, which runs Chatham Park, Chestnutwold, Coopertown, Lynnewood and Manoa elementary schools for kindergarten through fifth grade, Haverford Middle School for sixth through eighth and Haverford High School for ninth through twelfth. Haverford College, an undergraduate liberal arts school founded by Welsh Quakers, is also in the area.

Golf shapes the local identity. Merion Golf Club hosted the U.S. Open in 1934, 1950, 1971, 1981 and 2013, and Llanerch Country Club hosted the 1958 PGA Championship. Neither affects your closing, but buyers often mention them when they describe why they want the area.

What does the township require when a Haverford house is a rental?

The Building and Codes Department licenses rentals every year and inspects them before a tenant moves in. Each time occupancy changes, the unit must be inspected again, so a buyer taking over a rented Haverford house should expect that step.

  • No more than three unrelated people may live in a rental house.
  • An owner-occupied unit may have only one roomer or boarder.
  • Student housing is allowed only as a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board.
  • Renting is a business activity for the township's Business Privilege Tax, so a landlord also files a business tax return.

The license application needs a list of occupants and a copy of the signed lease. If you are selling a rental, hand the buyer your current license and inspection records.

Which township permits should a Haverford seller check?

Contractors working in the township must hold a township license, and the department will not accept a permit application without a signed contract, proof of insurance with workers compensation and the cost estimate. Residential additions also need a plot plan with building coverage and impervious surface figures.

Online applications are accepted for plumbing, generator, mechanical, electrical, roofing and siding, fences, sheds, rental housing licenses and contractor licenses. If an earlier owner skipped a permit for a deck or addition, ask the department what its records show before you list.

Trees are regulated too. A permit is required to plant, prune, remove or spray a public shade tree, and owners must keep private branches 12 feet above public walks and 14 feet above streets.

The department also lists a contact for use and occupancy (U&O) inspections. Find out whether one applies to your sale, and what it costs, before you fix a closing date.

How are transfer tax and recording handled in Delaware County?

A deed for a Haverford Township property is filed with the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds. The state sets a 1 percent transfer tax on the property's value, and the recorder collects a local share that is split among school districts and municipalities.

Inherited property is exempt when it passes to heirs, which matters if you received the house and now plan to sell. The revenue department's Delaware County valuation factor is 1.83 for deeds accepted during the year that began July 1, 2026. Your title company can tell you the combined percentage and who pays which part.

How can I sell a Haverford Township house?

Owners here tend to pick one of three routes.

  • An agent listing can fetch the strongest price for a well-kept house, with showings and repair requests along the way.
  • Selling yourself avoids a commission and puts pricing and paperwork on your desk.
  • A cash offer takes the house in its present state, useful when you are clearing an estate or the property needs major work.

At Haverford price levels the gap between an as-is offer and a renovated sale can be wide, so work out what you keep on each path.

More questions about Haverford, PA

Must a Haverford rental be inspected before sale?

The township inspects before a tenant moves in and again whenever occupancy changes, at $50 per unit. Keep your latest rental license and inspection record ready, and expect the buyer to plan for the next inspection.

Is an inherited Haverford house taxed on transfer?

State rules exempt property inherited with or without a will. Your later sale to a buyer is a new transfer and carries the state 1 percent plus any local share.

How many unrelated people can share a Haverford rental?

The township's rental license rules cap a rental house at three unrelated residents. Student housing needs a special exception from the Zoning Hearing Board.

Is a permit needed to take down a tree before selling in Haverford?

Township code requires a permit to plant, prune, remove or spray a public shade tree, meaning one on public property or a street. Trees on private land follow different rules, so call the Building and Codes Department if unsure.

Which school district serves Haverford Township addresses?

The School District of Haverford Township does. It runs five elementary schools, one middle school and one high school, so name the elementary zone when you describe the house.

Who sells houses in Harrisburg, PA, and why?

Harrisburg is a state capital where most homes are rented, prices are modest and many sellers are landlords or heirs. Census figures show 50,522 people in the 2025 estimate and 22,137 households in the 2020 to 2024 survey.

Just 36.6 percent of occupied homes are lived in by their owners. A typical owned home is worth $124,200, rent runs $1,062, and a household earns a median $48,099, with 30.5 percent of residents below the poverty line. About one adult in four, 25.9 percent, holds a bachelor's degree.

These figures shape a sale. Investors who price a house by its rent roll are common buyers, and lenders can be wary of a property that needs work. A vacant or tenant-occupied Harrisburg house may suit a buyer who takes it as it stands.

What is the layout of Harrisburg?

Harrisburg sits on the east bank of the Susquehanna River and is the seat of Dauphin County and the capital of Pennsylvania. Its footprint is 8.1 square miles of land plus 3.3 of water, which makes it the third smallest U.S. state capital by land area.

  • Paxton Creek empties into the Susquehanna inside the city, and the river forms the line between Dauphin and Cumberland counties.
  • Downtown holds the State Capitol complex, and there are more than a dozen neighborhoods and historic districts around it.
  • Six municipal historic districts, several national historic districts and architectural conservation overlays guide new work in older blocks.

Be careful with addresses. Several nearby townships, including Lower Paxton and Middle Paxton, use Harrisburg as their mailing name even though they sit outside city limits and follow their own codes. Check whether your parcel is inside the city before you read any rule below.

What does the local economy mean for a Harrisburg house sale?

Government jobs keep the Harrisburg market steady even when prices are low. The Region Economic Development Corporation lists the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania as the area's largest employer at 21,885 people, followed by the federal government with about 18,000. Health care, Giant Food Stores, the Hershey companies and TE Connectivity round out the top ten regional employers.

The city's history explains its housing stock. The Pennsylvania Canal and then the Pennsylvania Railroad made Harrisburg one of the more industrial cities in the Northeast in the 1800s, and the population fell by nearly half between 1950 and 2000. Many blocks therefore hold older rowhouses and brick twins that need updates. The annual Pennsylvania Farm Show, held in Harrisburg each January since 1917, brings visitors every winter.

Which roads and transit connect Harrisburg homes to the region?

Interstate 83 runs through the middle of the city and meets Interstate 81 to the north. Interstate 76, the Pennsylvania Turnpike, passes south of town, and Interstate 283 links the turnpike and I-83 southeast of the city. U.S. 22 crosses the northern part of the city, and Route 230 follows Cameron Street.

Harrisburg International Airport sits southeast of the city in Middletown and serves about 1.2 million travelers a year. Capital Area Transit runs local bus service, and the city also has rail and intercity bus connections. Workers in the city spend an average of 20.1 minutes getting to their jobs.

What permits and codes apply to repairs in Harrisburg?

The city's Bureau of Codes handles building permits, trade licenses, rental registration and property complaints, and you can reach it at 717-255-6553. Harrisburg follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, with the 2021 international code editions in force from January 1, 2026.

  • Permits are required for roofing, fences, sheds, decks, replacement windows and doors, any structural work, new furnaces and any work above $1,000.
  • Residential permit applications must be decided within 15 business days, or 5 days if stamped by a licensed design professional. Historic Review Board review adds time.
  • A building permit expires after 6 months if work is not continuous.
  • Electricians and plumbers must hold a city license, and every contractor needs a city business privilege license.
  • The Bureau Health Officer enforces lead-based paint hazard rules for residential structures.

If you did work in the past without a permit, call the Bureau before you list. That way you know what is open on the property before a buyer asks.

What must a buyer do with a Harrisburg rental or condemned house?

A buyer of a Harrisburg rental or condemned house takes on city deadlines from the day of recording. The Bureau of Codes says a non-condemned rental must be registered within 10 days of purchase, and a condemned property needs permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase.

The program under Ordinance 1-2017 also requires an inspection at least once every five years, taxes and utilities to be current before a unit can be rented, and a local managing agent when the owner lives more than 50 miles away. The annual landlord license is separate and runs through the Bureau of Licensing, Taxation and Central Support at 717-255-6513.

If you sell a tenant-occupied house, tell the buyer which of these items are paid up.

How does transfer tax work when you sell in Dauphin County?

In Dauphin County the Recorder of Deeds takes the deed and collects the transfer tax. The commonwealth charges 1 percent of the property's value, and a local share goes to school districts and municipalities. The Department of Revenue holds grantor and grantee jointly liable, so have your title company show the split on the closing statement.

Heirs who receive a house through a will, or with none, owe no transfer tax on that inheritance. Their own later sale is a fresh transfer. The Dauphin County valuation factor published by the revenue department is 2.61 for deeds accepted in the year that began July 1, 2026.

The recorder's fee calculators add that a deed for token consideration between tax-exempt parties carries no transfer tax, and checks go to the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

Which way should I sell a Harrisburg house?

Harrisburg sellers generally pick from three paths.

  • A listing suits a house in decent shape and an owner who can wait for a buyer with loan approval.
  • Going without an agent trims the listing fee, though showings, forms and bargaining fall to you.
  • A cash offer fits a vacant, damaged, inherited or rented property, with the closing date up to you.

Weigh what you would keep after repairs, carrying costs and fees on each path, not the offer alone.

More questions about Harrisburg, PA

Can a Harrisburg house be sold with tenants in place?

Yes. The buyer steps into the lease, and one who keeps renting must register the unit with the Bureau of Codes within 10 days of purchase. Hand over your lease, deposit details and proof that rental fees are paid.

Can I sell a condemned Harrisburg house?

Yes. The Bureau of Codes says the new owner must secure permits to lift the condemnation within 30 days of purchase, so buyers who can handle repairs are the usual fit.

Is transfer tax due when I inherit a Harrisburg house?

No. State revenue rules treat inheritance transfers, with or without a will, as exempt. Your later sale to a buyer carries the 1 percent state tax plus the local share.

Where do I ask about permits on a Harrisburg house?

The Bureau of Codes, at 717-255-6553, handles permits and inspections. The city lists roofing, windows, decks, sheds and any job above $1,000 among the work that needs one.

Is my Harrisburg mailing address inside the city?

Not always. Lower Paxton, Middle Paxton and other nearby townships carry a Harrisburg mailing name but are separate municipalities with their own codes. Your tax bill or the county parcel record shows which municipality bills you.

Middletown at a glance

  • Middletown is in Bucks County.
Selling in Middletown?
We buy Middletown houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What should I know before selling a house in Middletown Township?

Middletown Township in Bucks County requires a Level 2 chimney inspection on every home that is sold, and Levittown sections add a heater compartment wall inspection. That fire marshal rule is the main local step, followed by a 2 percent transfer tax paid at recording.

The township has 46,040 residents, according to the 2020 census, spread across about 19 square miles in the Philadelphia metropolitan area. It surrounds the boroughs of Langhorne, Langhorne Manor, Penndel and Hulmeville, which is why many addresses read Langhorne even though they sit in the township. Do not confuse it with other Pennsylvania townships that share the Middletown name; this page covers the Bucks County one only.

Sellers can list, sell without an agent or accept a cash purchase. The township rules below apply whichever route you choose.

How did Levittown shape Middletown Township?

The township was formally established in 1692 and stayed farmland for most of its history. In 1930 it had only 2,095 residents, and in 1950 it had 4,987. Then William Levitt began his second Levittown, which reached into four municipalities including Middletown, and the 1960 census counted 26,936 people, a 440 percent jump.

That history explains the housing mix you will find on a listing search:

  • Levittown sections in the south, built in the 1950s, with hundreds of similar homes per development.
  • Parkland, where houses date from every decade of the 20th century and the 21st.
  • Newer townhouses and condominiums around the Oxford Valley Mall, along with assisted living and 55-plus housing.
  • A few older farm properties; Edgemont, Harewood and Beechwood carry National Register listings.

The township later preserved hundreds of acres, now Core Creek Park with Lake Luxembourg, and saved Styer's Orchards from a plan for 632 homes in the late 1990s. Sesame Place and part of Cairn University are also inside the township.

What inspection does Middletown Township require when a house sells?

Every home sold in the township needs a Level 2 chimney inspection, and the Fire and Emergency Management office keeps a copy. The rule follows NFPA 211, which calls for the inspection any time a property is sold or transferred.

The inspection covers any appliance that vents combustion gases, including oil-fired and gas-fired heaters with a metal B-vent chimney, fireplaces, wood stoves and pellet stoves. A certified CSIA chimney sweep must do it, and the township website keeps a courtesy list of local sweeps. The requirement does not apply to a home heated and cooled only by electric devices or one with a vent-less fireplace, and plastic PVC exhaust pipe does not need a Level 2 inspection.

How much are property taxes in Middletown Township?

The 2026 combined millage in Middletown Township is 252.2674 mills, according to the Bucks County millage list effective July 1, 2026. Three taxing bodies make up that number: the county at 29.65 mills, the Neshaminy School District at 198.0124 mills and the township at 24.605 mills.

The township's own 24.605 mills break down into a general fund of 7.025, a debt service fund of 5.115, fire protection of 4.75, parks and recreation of 3.25 and fire apparatus of 2.5, plus smaller street light, ambulance, road machinery and hydrant levies. One mill equals a dollar of tax on each thousand dollars of assessment. The Bucks County Board of Assessment sets each property's assessed value.

Because Neshaminy carries most of the load, the school district millage drives the difference between Middletown and nearby municipalities in other districts. For comparison, the same county list shows Falls Township at 250.763 total mills and Lower Makefield at 265.786.

What is the transfer tax on a Middletown sale?

The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds describes a 2 percent transfer tax on property sales in Pennsylvania, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. Payment is made at recording, and the value that is taxed can differ from the sales price.

Neither state nor local government says who pays, and in most agreements the buyer and seller divide it. The new owner is responsible if the amount paid turns out to be wrong. Starting in January 2026, the recorder's office stopped accepting personal checks for the tax. Payment options are cash in the office, cashier's check, money order or credit card, so tell your title company early.

  • Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings can be exempt.
  • A one-time transfer between former spouses is allowed.
  • A $1 deed or a transfer with no tax paid needs a statement of value so state investigators can check the real worth.

The recorder's office can be reached at 215-348-6209 for exemption questions.

When can I appeal a Bucks County assessment?

The 2026 annual appeal deadline was August 3, and it has passed. Any change from that cycle takes effect for the 2027 tax year.

The Board of Assessment Appeals sits at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown and can be reached at 215-348-6219. It meets at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesdays of each month. Appeal forms and rules for both residential and commercial properties are posted on the county site.

Two other county items apply to sellers and buyers. The homestead and farmstead exclusion application is due March 1 for the tax year beginning the following July 1, and a new owner must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying, under Act 29.

What affects a Middletown Township house's value and appeal?

Location along the Philadelphia and Trenton corridor, school assignments and weather exposure all shape buyer interest. Interstate 295 runs through the east side of the township, and U.S. Route 1 crosses the middle. Pennsylvania routes 213, 413, 332 and 513 also touch it. The township reports 189.70 miles of public roads, of which the township maintains 139.07 miles.

SEPTA's West Trenton Regional Rail line stops at Woodbourne station in the township, and Langhorne station is just across the line in Langhorne Manor. SEPTA also runs City Bus route 14 and suburban routes 127, 128, 129 and 130 through the area.

Neshaminy School District serves the township. Albert Schweitzer, Herbert Hoover, Pearl S. Buck, Tawanka and Walter Miller elementary schools cover kindergarten through fourth grade, Carl Sandburg and Maple Point middle schools take grades five through eight, and Neshaminy High School serves grades nine through twelve.

NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals for the Neshaminy Falls station show 50.7 inches of rain and melted snow per year plus 19.9 inches of snowfall, and July is the wettest month. The township record wet day was 6.60 inches on August 27, 2011, so basements and drainage are a fair question for any buyer inspection.

Is a listing or a cash sale the better fit in Middletown?

A cash sale suits a property with deferred repairs, while a listing suits one a lender will finance as it stands. Either way, the chimney inspection comes first, and a failed inspection can change what you can ask.

  • Book a CSIA chimney sweep before you list and send the report to the fire marshal.
  • If the house is in Levittown, ask the fire office what the heater compartment wall inspection involves.
  • Compare offers after the 2 percent transfer tax, your mortgage payoff and the school and township tax proration.

More questions about Middletown, PA

Does Middletown Township require a chimney inspection when I sell?

Yes. A Level 2 chimney inspection by a certified CSIA sweep is required for homes with combustion appliances, and a copy goes to Fire and Emergency Management. Levittown homes also need a heater compartment wall inspection.

What is the transfer tax in Middletown Township?

The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds lists 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. The tax is paid at the time of recording.

Which school district serves Middletown Township?

Neshaminy School District. Five elementary schools, two middle schools and Neshaminy High School serve the township.

What is the total property tax rate in Middletown Township?

The county's July 1, 2026 list shows 252.2674 mills combined: 29.65 for the county, 198.0124 for Neshaminy School District and 24.605 for the township.

Can I still file a Bucks County assessment appeal for 2026?

No. The 2026 annual appeal deadline was August 3, 2026, and it has passed. Call the Board of Assessment at 215-348-6219 to ask about the next annual cycle.
