What should York, PA sellers know before listing?

York is a compact city of 5.3 square miles in York County, and its Bureau of Permits and Inspections decides several things a seller needs before closing, including tenant licenses and a possible certificate of compliance. The paperwork runs through an online permit system, and the office takes appointments only.

The Census Bureau estimates 45,342 residents for July 2025, up 1.2 percent from the 2020 base. Its 2020 to 2024 survey shows 43.7 percent of homes lived in by their owners, a middle value of $119,700 and typical rent of $1,014 a month across 17,893 households. Median household income is $48,420, and 21.1 percent of residents are in poverty.

York was founded in 1741, became a borough in 1787 and a city in 1887. The Continental Congress met in the courthouse from September 1777 to June 1778 and adopted the Articles of Confederation there. Colonial-era buildings and large Gothic churches still stand around town.

Which York City documents does a house sale or rental need?

York City Bureau of Permits and Inspections document types, as described on the Bureau's permits page
DocumentWhen it applies
Tenant occupied licenseTenant-occupied residential and institutional buildings, which are inspected before licensing
Certificate of ComplianceA structure changing ownership or tenancy without a change in use classification
Certificate of OccupancyNew construction, major renovations, reoccupying condemned structures, changes in occupancy
Electrical turn on permitNeeded before the utility restores service, with a DR number from Met-Ed

The permits page says a Certificate of Compliance applies to any structure that changes ownership, while its FAQ describes it for existing commercial buildings. Call the Bureau at 717-849-2256 to confirm what a house sale requires. The office is at 101 S. George St., and the page states that it cannot take walk-in customers, so appointments are made by phone.

Permits have also moved to the 2021 Uniform Construction Code for applications filed from January 1, 2026.

Before any inspection, collect the deed, any prior certificates, receipts for permitted work and the names of every tenant. York City says permit applications must be filed before work begins, so have those records ready.

What does a tenant occupied license mean if I am selling a rental in York?

Owners of rental houses in York carry a license that depends on an inspection, and the city says no checklist exists. Inspectors apply the City of York Property Maintenance Code, which is posted on the city website, so landlords read the code itself to prepare.

  • Reinspections and the Consolidated Board of Appeals go through the tenant occupied administrative desk.
  • Typical complaints in the city include weeds over 10 inches, uncollected trash, pest problems, leaks, sewer backups and mold.
  • Neighborhood Improvement Ordinance tickets can be appealed, but the appeal form has to be mailed or hand-delivered, not emailed.
  • Property owners are responsible for the sidewalk and trees in front of the house.

A buyer who purchases rentals as is will usually want the current license and any open citations in hand before settlement. Clear those, or disclose them in writing, ahead of the contract.

How is a deed recorded and taxed in York County?

York County's Recorder of Deeds says the realty transfer tax is 2 percent in total, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to local governments. Documents go first to the county Assessment Office, which certifies the parcel number, and then to the Recorder for recording and fees.

  • You can record in person, by mail, or through Simplifile or Ingeo, with a stamped return envelope and payment for the fees.
  • One check may cover everything, or you can write three, and the county accepts either.
  • A Statement of Value is required when you claim an exemption or pay a different amount than the deed states. It adds $2 to the recording fee.
  • A deed from a father to a son and similar family transfers are tax exempt if the deed states the relationship.
  • Recorded documents come back after about four to eight weeks, depending on workload.

The state notes both buyer and seller are liable for the tax, and the sales contract decides who pays. Ask the Recorder for the share that applies to a York City address.

Which schools and neighborhoods influence York home values?

York sits inside the York City School District, one of 15 public districts across the York area, and charter options include Lincoln Charter School and Helen Thackston Charter School. York Catholic High School and Holy Trinity Catholic School are among the private options. York College of Pennsylvania, Penn State York and the Harrisburg Area Community College York campus add student renters and staff.

The Arch Street area holds WellSpan Park, home of the York Revolution since 2007, and the old Pennsylvania Railroad station now sits on the York County Heritage Rail Trail across from the stadium. The York County Judicial Center and new apartment lofts anchored later redevelopment downtown. Spring Garden and West Manchester townships border the city, and several of the area's large employers are based in them.

How do local employers and roads affect York sellers?

York has deep manufacturing roots. The area is home to a Harley-Davidson plant, Voith Hydro, BAE Systems, York International and a Starbucks roasting facility, and Dentsply Sirona and Glatfelter moved their headquarters out in 2019 and 2020. WellSpan York Hospital, a regional trauma center, and UPMC Memorial Hospital serve the city.

US 30 and Interstate 83 cross the area, Rabbit Transit runs bus routes in the city and suburbs, and a Greyhound and Trailways depot offers intercity service. The nearest commercial airports are BWI and Harrisburg International, with Lancaster's Amtrak service about 24 miles east. The Census gives a mean commute of 23.1 minutes for York workers, so sellers can market access to both Harrisburg and Baltimore.

Does York's weather or flood history matter when I sell?

The city has hot, humid summers and moderately cold winters. Rain and snow add up to about 41 inches a year, falling on roughly 127 days. Hurricane Agnes set the state's 24-hour precipitation record of 13.5 inches at the York weather station on June 22, 1972, so buyers do ask about basements.

Plan to show a dry basement and sound gutters, and keep records of sump pump work or waterproofing. An as-is purchaser prices roof and foundation questions differently from a buyer who needs a loan, so say plainly what you know.

Gather permit records for past work too. Electrical, plumbing, mechanical and demolition work in York City goes through the Bureau's online system, and sheds, decks and interior remodels need permits as well.

More questions about York, PA

Do I need a certificate to sell my York house?

Possibly. York City says a structure changing ownership or tenancy without a change in use needs a Certificate of Compliance, though an FAQ on the same site ties it to commercial buildings. Call 717-849-2256 to confirm for your address.

How much does York County charge in transfer tax?

It is 2 percent in total, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to local governments, according to the county Recorder of Deeds. The sales contract decides whether buyer or seller pays.

Can I transfer a York house to a family member tax free?

Yes, when the deed states the family relationship, such as a transfer from a father to a son. The county advises checking with an attorney, and a Statement of Value is needed if you claim any other exemption.

How do I get a permit or license from York City?

Most applications are filed online through the city's OpenGov system. The Bureau of Permits and Inspections, at 101 S. George St., also takes appointments by phone at 717-849-2256.

How long until York County returns my recorded deed?

It takes about four to eight weeks after recording, depending on workload, because each document is scanned, proofed, indexed and verified. Include a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

What should I know before selling a house in Manheim Township?

Manheim Township is a Lancaster County municipality of 43,977 people where the biggest issue for sellers is the countywide reassessment that takes effect for the 2027 tax year. A certificate of use and occupancy and a 2 percent transfer tax round out the local rules.

This page covers Manheim Township, which sits directly north of Lancaster city. Lancaster County also has a separate borough named Manheim, so check the municipality on your tax bill before relying on any local rule. The township has no ZIP code of its own, so owners carry a Lititz, Lancaster or Leola mailing address depending on where the house sits.

A retail listing, a sale by owner and a direct cash purchase are all open to a seller, and the paperwork below applies to each.

Where does Manheim Township sit in Lancaster County?

The township covers about 24 square miles and ranks as the second largest municipality in Lancaster County, behind the city itself. It was established in 1729, and its southern boundary meets the Lancaster city limits.

The township's communities include Neffsville, Dillerville and Landis Valley. Population counts show how steadily it has grown:

  • 9,289 residents in 1950.
  • 21,539 in 1970.
  • 33,697 in 2000.
  • 43,977 in 2020.

The 2000 census put the median age at 43, with 21 percent of residents 65 or older.

How does the Manheim Township School District affect a sale?

The school district is coterminous with the township, so a home inside the township boundary is in the district and a home outside it is not. That clean match makes the address check simple for a buyer.

The district runs Manheim Township High School, a virtual high school, Manheim Township Middle School, Landis Run Intermediate School and six elementary schools: Brecht, Bucher, Neff, Nitrauer, Reidenbaugh and Schaeffer. Buyers with children usually ask which elementary school serves a street, and the district office can confirm that from an address.

The township itself does not bill or collect property taxes. Lancaster County assesses the property, while the elected tax collector and the school district collect the bills.

What is the 2027 Lancaster County reassessment?

Lancaster County reassessed every parcel at current market value, and the new values apply to the 2027 tax year. The previous assessments were based on 2018 values, and the county says the new notices should land near what a property would sell for today. Notices were mailed on June 15, 2026.

The county used valid arm's-length residential sales from 2022 through 2024, adjusted for acreage, square footage, porches, garages and bathrooms. State law requires each taxing body to adjust its millage so it does not collect more revenue only because values moved, but the tax on an individual house can still rise or fall. County and municipal millage for 2027 is set near the end of December 2026, and school millage for the 2027-2028 year is set in June 2027. The reassessment does not change 2026-27 school taxes.

The reassessment appeal deadline was August 3, 2026, the first business day after August 1, and it has passed. The county says the next opportunity for an annual appeal is 2028. Ask the Property Assessment Office at 717-299-8381 what applies to a house that sold or changed after the notices went out.

Does Manheim Township require an inspection to sell?

No. The township states that it does not require an inspection before settlement. A certificate of use and occupancy can still be requested by the parties to the deal, and the zoning ordinance has required one for every structure since 1944.

If you need a copy, contact the Code Compliance Department with the property address, the home type (single-family, townhouse or duplex) and whether any part of the basement is finished. Staff check the records and send a copy if one is on file. If none exists, the owner or an agent applies in person at the township office, pays a $50 residential filing fee and books an inspection with a code official.

What does the realty transfer tax cost in Manheim Township?

The township Treasurer's Office FAQ puts the realty transfer tax at 2 percent of the value transferred. The Commonwealth receives 1 percent, and the township and school district share the other 1 percent.

The Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds, at 50 North Duke Street, takes payment as part of recording the deed. The state notes that both buyer and seller are liable for it, and the sale contract decides how it is split. Certain family transfers and property passed by inheritance are exempt from the state portion, so ask the recorder before assuming a deed is taxable.

Real estate tax bills combine the county and township taxes and go out by March 1. If a lender pays your taxes from escrow, send the lender a copy of the bill.

What rules apply if I am selling a rental in Manheim Township?

Manheim Township has licensed rental properties since 2022, and an annual license costs $50 per building. Each rental unit is inspected at least once every five years, and one- and two-unit buildings have every unit inspected.

  • Owners living more than 25 miles from the township must name a responsible local agent.
  • Inspection fees run from $40 for one unit to $250 for buildings with 51 or more units.
  • The code compliance office handles applications, renewals and de-registration.

A landlord who sells should ask the code office how to de-register or transfer the license, and should hand the buyer the latest inspection results.

Which route suits a Manheim Township seller?

The right route depends on the house's condition and your moving date. Putting it on the market reaches more buyers but brings showings and inspection haggling, while a direct cash sale can be timed around your move.

  • Request your certificate of use and occupancy early so a missing certificate does not delay the closing.
  • Look up your 2027 reassessed value on the county property search site and compare it with the price you are weighing.
  • Subtract the 2 percent transfer tax share you agree to, plus any mortgage payoff, to estimate net proceeds.

If a buyer asks for repairs, compare the cost against a quote for selling as-is.

More questions about Manheim, PA

Is Manheim Township the same as the borough of Manheim?

No. Manheim Township is a separate municipality that borders Lancaster city and has its own school district and township government. Lancaster County also has a borough named Manheim.

Does Manheim Township require a certificate of use and occupancy when I sell?

Not as a condition of settlement. The township does not inspect before closing, but buyers or lenders may ask for a copy. If none is on file, the residential filing fee is $50 and an inspection is scheduled.

What do buyers and sellers owe in transfer tax in Manheim Township?

The combined rate is 2 percent of the value transferred. The state gets 1 percent, and the township and school district share the other 1 percent. The Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds collects it.

When did the Lancaster County reassessment take effect?

The new values apply to the 2027 tax year. Notices were mailed June 15, 2026, and the appeal deadline of August 3, 2026 has passed. The next annual appeal opportunity is 2028.

Who sends the property tax bill in Manheim Township?

The elected tax collector and the school district collect the bills. Lancaster County sets the assessment, and the township does not bill or collect property taxes itself.

Wilkes-Barre at a glance

  • Wilkes-Barre is in Luzerne County.
Selling in Wilkes-Barre?
We buy Wilkes-Barre houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What sets a Wilkes-Barre sale apart from nearby towns?

Wilkes-Barre serves as Luzerne County's seat and lies on a floodplain beside the Susquehanna River. A sale there carries a few local costs that sellers in nearby towns do not pay, starting with the city's higher transfer tax.

The city took shape around anthracite. It was founded in 1769, earned the nickname "The Diamond City" for its coal output, and peaked at more than 86,000 residents in 1930. After World War II industry declined, and the 1959 Knox Mine disaster ended much of the region's mining. The Census Bureau now estimates 44,523 residents, a rise of 0.4 percent since April 2020.

The housing numbers explain why many owners look for a quick, as-is sale. Census survey figures covering 2020 to 2024 put the middle of the owner-occupied value range at $117,200, about 51 percent owner occupancy, rent that runs $946 at the median, and 16,644 households. The median household income is $48,515.

How much transfer tax do sellers pay in Wilkes-Barre?

A deed for a Wilkes-Barre property carries 3.5 percent in total transfer tax, which is well above the 2 percent charged in most Luzerne County municipalities. The county recorder will not accept a deed until payment is made, and the county says most sales agreements split it between buyer and seller.

Total realty transfer tax by location, from the Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule effective July 1, 2026

On a $100,000 sale, 3.5 percent comes to $3,500 against $2,000 at the standard rate. A split contract puts $1,750 on each side, so build that into your net before you compare offers. The state's own page says both grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable for the tax.

Which fees come with recording a Wilkes-Barre deed?

Luzerne County's schedule effective July 1, 2026 sets a deed's base fee at $87.75, covering up to four pages, four names and one parcel number. Extra pages cost $2.00 each, extra names $0.50 each and extra parcel numbers $0.50 each.

  • Deeds go to the Recorder's office at 200 North River Street. Recording runs from 9:00 A.M. until 4:20 P.M., and the lines are 570-825-1641 and 570-825-1642.
  • Every deed needs a signed, certified address for the buyer, and parcel numbers must be certified through the county Assessor's Office, which charges its own fee.
  • A Statement of Value goes in as an original plus one copy whenever the deed does not pay full tax or claims an exemption. It counts as a page at $2.00.
  • Deeds between husband and wife, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, and siblings are generally exempt, and the deed must say why.

The Recorder's staff cannot give legal or tax advice or run title searches, so the closing agent or an attorney handles those pieces.

Do floods and old mines affect a Wilkes-Barre house sale?

They can, and buyers ask about both. Tropical Storm Agnes in 1972 pushed the Susquehanna to nearly 41 feet, about four feet above the old levees, and flooded downtown under nine feet of water. The city then built a levee system rising 41 feet, finished in January 2003 at roughly $250 million. In September 2011 the river crested at a record 42.66 feet, and the levees held in Wilkes-Barre while nearby boroughs flooded.

Mine subsidence is the quieter issue. Pennsylvania's Department of Environmental Protection says standard homeowner policies usually leave out damage from collapsed underground coal and clay mines, and it sells separate coverage. It lists residential coverage of $150,000 at $41.25 a year. Its online risk map shows whether an address sits over mine workings.

If you are selling, check the map for your street and tell your buyer what you find. The DEP also notes that a seller can cancel a policy at closing and that new owners must apply for their own.

Which Wilkes-Barre neighborhoods and schools matter to buyers?

The city has more than a dozen neighborhoods. Central City is the original 16-block downtown near the river, and it holds most of the high-rises and Public Square. North End is known for its architecture, and Parsons and Miners Mills have a quieter, more suburban feel at the northeastern edge. East End, Heights and Mayflower were developed in the 1900s, and Mayflower offers some of the best views of downtown from its high streets. South Wilkes-Barre, Goose Island, Rolling Mill Hill and the Iron Triangle lie southwest of the center.

The Wilkes-Barre Area School District runs one high school, Wilkes-Barre Area High School, which opened in 2020 and replaced three older secondary schools. Holy Redeemer High School is the Catholic option. King's College and Wilkes University are in the city, and Osterhout Free Library has three branches.

What carrying costs push Wilkes-Barre owners to sell quickly?

Holding an empty or inherited home in Wilkes-Barre means paying taxes, insurance and utilities while the property sits. The latest Census five-year survey reports median monthly owner costs of $1,272 with a mortgage and $559 without one, and 23.1 percent of residents live in poverty, so an extra house is a real strain for many families.

  • A house that sits empty still draws a tax bill and a utility bill each month.
  • The city's Susquehanna floodplain location may raise insurance questions, so keep flood and mine subsidence paperwork together for the buyer.
  • Estates need proof of authority before anyone can sign a deed, and a family transfer may be exempt from tax while a sale is not.
  • Tenants in place mean inspections and notices, so line up access dates in the contract.

A direct as-is sale removes showings and repair negotiations, but compare it against a listing using your own net figure after the 3.5 percent city transfer tax and recording fees.

How do commuting and local employers shape demand?

Interstate 81 passes near the city, and the Northeast Extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-476) is close by. The Cross Valley Expressway carries PA 309 through the north of the city, and Interstate 80 lies about 10 miles south. Luzerne County Transportation Authority runs local buses, and Martz Trailways links downtown to Scranton, New York City and Philadelphia.

GUARD Insurance Group ranks among the large employers, and downtown holds regional offices for several banks and insurers. Census data for 2020 to 2024 put the mean commute at 20.7 minutes, and 58.4 percent of people aged 16 and older are in the civilian labor force. Hospitals and clinics lead the local economy: the Census counts about $2.2 billion in 2022 receipts across healthcare and social services, the biggest line it reports for the city.

What should I ask the city before listing a Wilkes-Barre property?

Call the Wilkes-Barre City code enforcement office and ask whether your property type needs a certificate of occupancy, a rental license or a buyer notice before closing. Rules for rentals and for occupied buildings differ from owner-occupied homes, and the office can say what an inspection will cover and how long it takes.

Bring the parcel number, the names on the deed and, for an estate, the letters or court papers that show who may sign. If liens or back taxes exist, request payoff figures early. An as-is purchaser can often work around those items. The seller still has to hand over a deed the Recorder will accept.

More questions about Wilkes-Barre, PA

How high is the Wilkes-Barre transfer tax?

It is 3.5 percent in total for a property inside Wilkes-Barre City, compared with 2 percent in most Luzerne County municipalities. The county says the buyer and seller usually split it, and the deed cannot be recorded until it is paid.

Who records the deed after a Wilkes-Barre sale?

The Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds at 200 North River Street records it, usually through your closing agent or title company. The base fee for a deed is $87.75 under the July 2026 schedule.

Is mine subsidence a concern for Wilkes-Barre homes?

It can be, because the region was heavily mined for anthracite. Check the state Department of Environmental Protection's online risk map for your address, and note that standard homeowner policies usually exclude this damage.

Must I fix a Wilkes-Barre house first?

Yes, an as-is buyer accepts the property with its flaws. City occupancy or rental rules may still apply, so call the code enforcement office before choosing a settlement day.

Are family transfers taxed in Luzerne County?

Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are generally exempt. The deed has to state the relationship, and a Statement of Value is needed when a non-family exemption is claimed.

What is Altoona like for someone selling a house?

Altoona is a railroad city of about 42,300 people in Blair County, built on hillsides in the Allegheny Mountains at 1,161 feet. The Census Bureau estimates 42,347 residents for July 1, 2025, down 3.6 percent from the 2020 estimates base, and the city covers 9.79 square miles.

The Census median value of owner-occupied homes for 2020 to 2024 is $119,900, against $332,700 for the United States as a whole. The city's population peaked in the 1930 census at 82,054 and has fallen in every count since, to 43,963 in 2020.

How did the railroad shape Altoona's houses and streets?

The Pennsylvania Railroad founded Altoona in 1849 as a shop and maintenance site. The borough was incorporated in 1854 and the city in 1868, and at its peak the Altoona Works employed about 15,000 people across 122 buildings. Horseshoe Curve, west of town, remains a National Historic Landmark. In late September 1862 the city hosted the War Governors' Conference of 13 Union state governors.

The housing followed the work. Many older districts mix rowhouses with single homes, built to house workers and managers. The manager houses are narrow and tall, resemble Victorian or Edwardian mansions, and have often been converted to double or triple family apartments. Street names are numbers: Streets run northwest to southeast, and Avenues run northeast to southwest.

Which Altoona neighborhoods should a seller know?

The city's sections and neighborhood names are worth knowing before you describe a house.

  • Downtown and Center City: the Downtown Altoona Historic District, with multistory brick buildings from around 1900 and the Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament at 13th Street and 13th Avenue.
  • Main sections: Logantown, Fairview, Juniata, Wehnwood, Calvert Hills, the 5th and 6th Wards, Westmont, Eldorado, East End, Dutch Hill, Pleasant Valley, Hileman Heights, Mansion Park, Llyswen, Garden Heights and Highland Park.
  • Named neighborhoods: Little Italy, Gospel Hill, Toy Town, Columbia Park, Knickerbockers and Curtin.
  • Floodplain and zoning: the city website carries a floodplain information page and a zoning and GIS map for checking a parcel.
  • Lakemont, Greenwood, Bellmeade and Newburg: considered parts of Altoona but outside city limits, in Logan Township.

That last group matters: Logan Township surrounds the city, so the tax bill and the codes office depend on which side of the line the parcel sits.

What do Census figures say about Altoona housing?

For 2020 to 2024, 63.9 percent of Altoona homes were owner-occupied, 90.2 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and 17.9 percent were 65 or older. The 2020 census counted 20,672 housing units, 9.7 percent of them vacant, with a rental vacancy rate of 9.1 percent.

What local taxes and transfer costs apply to an Altoona sale?

The city's local tax page lists the charges that touch a home sale. Real estate transfer tax applies to anyone buying or selling property in Altoona and is collected by the Blair County Recorder of Deeds. The page shows a total of 2 percent, with 1 percent going to the state and 1 percent split between the city and the Altoona Area School District.

  • Local real estate tax is listed at 7.129 mils and is collected by H. A. Berkheimer.
  • A 1.70 percent rate applies to persons and entities engaging in business in the city, and 1.40 percent applies to non-residents who work in the city. The Blair County Tax Collection Bureau collects both.
  • Employed residents pay $5.00 annually, assessed by both the city and the Altoona Area School District.

The Blair County Assessment Office is at 423 Allegheny Street, Suite 041, Hollidaysburg, phone 814-693-3110. Ask it for the appeal form and the annual deadline, and ask your closing agent how the transfer tax will be split.

What rental inspection rules apply when the Altoona house is a rental?

Every owner of a leased or non-owner-occupied dwelling in Altoona must hold a Conditional Housing Permit, which becomes a Residential Rental Unit License after the unit passes inspection. Licenses are renewed on or before July 31 each year, and most units are inspected every three years.

  • An inspection takes 20 to 30 minutes, and the owner, tenant or a representative must be present.
  • Inspectors use the International Property Maintenance Code on the interior and exterior.
  • Owners usually get 45 days to repair violations, with extensions in 30-day steps, and life-safety hazards must be corrected immediately.
  • Heat must be supplied from October 1 to May 15, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are checked.

A landlord selling a rental should confirm the license status with the Codes and Inspections Department at 1301 12th Street, Suite 103, phone 814-949-2456. The department's page does not describe a separate inspection tied to a sale, so ask it whether one applies to your property.

How does Altoona's mountain climate affect a house?

Altoona's climate is hot in summer and moderately cold in winter, with wide temperature swings. The monthly daily average runs from 28.4 degrees in January to 72.4 in July, and the extremes range from minus 25 in 1904 to 103.

Annual precipitation averages 36.65 inches over about 136 days, and September is the wettest month. Roofs, gutters and basements see regular wear from that many wet days and the winter cold, and the old rowhouse stock shares walls and rooflines between units.

How do jobs, roads and schools affect Altoona buyers?

Health care is the leading field of employment, with UPMC Altoona, a rehabilitation hospital and the James E. Van Zandt VA Medical Center. Sheetz has its headquarters in Altoona, and Boyer, maker of the Mallo Cup, is based here. Penn State Altoona, the third largest of the university's Commonwealth campuses, has bought downtown buildings.

  • I-99 runs north to I-80 and south to the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and US 22 runs east to Harrisburg and west to Pittsburgh.
  • AMTRAN provides local buses, and Amtrak's Pennsylvanian stops once daily in each direction.
  • Altoona-Blair County Airport offers daily flights to Charlotte.
  • The Altoona Area School District serves all of the city, including Altoona Area High School for grades 9 to 12.

What are the ways to sell a house fast in Altoona?

An Altoona owner can list with an agent, sell privately, or take a cash offer. With the median home value near $120,000, the cost of repairs compared with the likely sale price is a fair first question.

For a rental, check the license and inspection status first. For a vacant house, ask the Codes and Inspections Department about any open property maintenance notice before you list. Gather the deed, the tax bills from H. A. Berkheimer and the county, and any permit records before you list.

More questions about Altoona, PA

Does Altoona have a transfer tax when I sell my house?

Yes. The city's local tax page lists a 2 percent real estate transfer tax, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent shared by the city and the school district, collected by the Blair County Recorder of Deeds.

When must Altoona landlords renew their rental license?

On or before July 31 each year. Most units are inspected every three years, and owners generally get 45 days to fix violations found.

Who collects real estate tax on an Altoona home?

H. A. Berkheimer collects the city's local real estate tax, listed at 7.129 mils. Blair County and the school district bill separately.

Is Lakemont inside the city of Altoona?

No. Lakemont, Greenwood, Bellmeade, Newburg and several other areas are treated as parts of Altoona but lie in Logan Township, outside city limits.

Where do I ask about assessment changes in Blair County?

Call the Blair County Assessment Office in Hollidaysburg at 814-693-3110. It handles appeal forms and can tell you the filing deadline for the year.

How does a home sale work in Hempfield Township?

Paperwork is lighter in Hempfield than in many Pennsylvania municipalities, since the township does not ask for a certificate of occupancy at sale. What you do need is a clear view of the septic or sewer setup, the 2 percent transfer tax and the county assessment record.

Hempfield is a township in Westmoreland County, and it is big. Spread over about 77 square miles, it ranks as the Pittsburgh metro's most populous suburb, according to Wikipedia. The Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 41,421 residents, a 0.2 percent dip from its 2020 base. The township is steady rather than growing, and sellers mostly compete with other established houses.

Whether the buyer arrives through a broker, a yard sign or a direct cash purchase, the paper trail ends at the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds in Greensburg, where the deed is filed and the transfer tax is paid.

Where is Hempfield and what is inside it?

The city of Greensburg and six boroughs sit entirely inside the township: Southwest Greensburg, South Greensburg, Youngwood, New Stanton, Arona and Adamsburg. Hempfield was incorporated on April 6, 1773, and takes its name from the hemp fields of the older Hempfield in Lancaster County.

Named communities within the township include Fort Allen, Grapeville, Hannastown, Carbon, Radebaugh, Maplewood Terrace, West Point and Luxor. Neighbors include Salem, Unity, Mount Pleasant, East Huntingdon, South Huntingdon, Sewickley and North Huntingdon townships, plus the city of Jeannette. The township is large enough that a home near Greensburg and a rural parcel miles away can have very different values.

  • Schools: the Hempfield Area School District, which also serves Adamsburg, Armbrust, Bovard, Grapeville, Hunker, Luxor, Manor, New Stanton and Youngwood.
  • Higher education: the University of Pittsburgh at Greensburg, the Youngwood campus of Westmoreland County Community College, and a Carlow University satellite campus.
  • Policing: the township relies on the Pennsylvania State Police as its sole law enforcement agency.

What shapes the Hempfield economy and home demand?

Hempfield is the retail hub for Westmoreland County and the Laurel Highlands. U.S. Route 30 passes the Westmoreland Mall and the adjoining Live! Casino Pittsburgh, and Greengate Centre is the area's largest big-box center. Light industry operates from several industrial parks, including RIDC Westmoreland, which straddles the Hempfield and East Huntingdon line.

The 2011 tornado is part of local memory. An EF2 tornado touched down on March 23, 2011 southwest of Greensburg and damaged scores of homes in the West Hempfield area and the Fort Allen neighborhood, along with Hempfield Area High School and Harrold Middle School. A buyer may ask whether a house in those areas needed storm repairs.

Age matters for demand too. More than a quarter of residents (26.9 percent) have passed 65, and owners occupy 84.7 percent of homes, so estate sales and downsizing moves are common.

How do Hempfield homes look in the Census data?

Hempfield homes are owner occupied, moderately priced and held for a long time. Over 92 percent of residents stayed put for the previous year.

Hempfield township in the Census Bureau's five-year survey covering 2020 through 2024

Few sellers here are racing a mortgage payment. The usual story is a family home held for decades, a parent's estate, or an older house whose repairs the owner is tired of managing.

What local rules apply when a Hempfield house sells?

The township's planning and code department says a certificate of occupancy is not required to sell a home. Two other checks apply depending on how the house drains.

  • On-lot septic. Contact the township's Sewage Enforcement Officer about any dye test the buyer or lender wants.
  • Public sewer. Call the Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County at 724-755-5800 for the sewer account and any test or final reading.
  • Permits. Open permits or unpermitted work should be sorted out first. The township says zoning permits take up to 15 business days and building permits up to 30.

The code office is at 1132 Woodward Drive, Suite A, and answers at 724-834-7232. The county assessment office, at 724-830-3409, can explain whether a building permit changes the assessed value. Landlord and tenant disputes go to the Pennsylvania Attorney General's consumer hotline, which the township lists at 1-800-441-2555.

Township property tax is low in dollar terms. The township levies 3 mills for general purposes and 3 mills for a dedicated fire service tax, so a $25,000 assessed value pays $150 a year to the township. School and county taxes are separate and larger. Areas inside a street light district also pay a yearly light district assessment. The township also runs a rebate program that returns part of the general township real estate tax to qualifying senior homeowners, which long-time owners of older houses may already use.

How is the transfer tax split in Hempfield?

The township's own tax page puts the full charge on a sale at 2 percent of the price. One half of that goes to the state's 1 percent, and the rest is divided evenly between the township and the Hempfield Area School District at a quarter of the total each. You pay it when the deed is recorded, and the township lists the recorder at 724-830-3518.

At the $232,100 median home value the full 2 percent comes to about $4,642, and the sales contract says who covers which share. Both parties answer to the recorder for the tax, and state rules exempt certain family transfers and property passing by inheritance.

Ask the title company to show the transfer tax line before you sign. Selling an inherited house? Ask whether the inheritance exemption covers your deed.

How do Westmoreland County assessment appeals work?

The county Tax Assessment Office handles the values that set every property tax bill in the township. Anyone can appeal a change of assessment within 40 days of the mailing of the notice. A yearly appeal has to be on file by August 1 and only changes the next tax year's bill.

Hearings run on the second Thursday of every month, starting at 9:00 in the morning, in Suite 440 of the county building at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue in Greensburg. Forms come from the county website or the assessment office itself.

If you plan to sell, check the assessed value before listing. Lenders look at the current tax amount. If you think the assessment is too high, file by the next August 1.

Which Hempfield houses suit a direct cash sale?

It tends to suit worn houses, estate properties and sellers who want to pick the closing date. It is less useful for a move-in ready home you can list quickly.

Set any cash figure against what a listing would net after commission, transfer tax, repairs and months of waiting. If you want to see a number for your Hempfield house, Cash Home Buyers can quote one, and you can set it beside your other choices.

More questions about Hempfield, PA

Is a certificate of occupancy needed for a Hempfield home sale?

No. The township's planning and code office answers this directly in its FAQ: the sale of a home does not trigger a certificate of occupancy.

Who handles a dye test for a Hempfield home sale?

It depends on the system. For a septic system, contact the township's Sewage Enforcement Officer. For public sewer, call the Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County at 724-755-5800.

Who gets the 2 percent Hempfield transfer tax?

The state receives 1 percent, the township 0.5 percent and the Hempfield Area School District 0.5 percent, for 2 percent in all. The county recorder in Greensburg collects the money when the deed goes on record.

Which school district covers Hempfield Township?

The Hempfield Area School District. It also covers Adamsburg, Armbrust, Bovard, Grapeville, Hunker, Luxor, Manor, New Stanton and Youngwood.

When must a Westmoreland County assessment appeal be filed?

August 1 for a yearly appeal, which affects the following tax year. If a change of assessment notice is mailed, the window is 40 days.

State College at a glance

  • State College is in Centre County.
Selling in State College?

How do you sell a house in State College, PA?

Three routes exist: a listing, a private sale, or a straight sale to a buyer who accepts the place in its present state. Each one finishes with a deed recorded in Centre County and the transfer tax paid. What varies is the prep work and the calendar.

State College is a home rule municipality of 4.56 square miles, and it became a borough on August 29, 1896. The Penn State campus known as University Park sits partly inside the borough and partly in neighboring College Township, and that campus shapes who owns, rents and buys here more than anything else.

What does the Census say about housing in State College?

Census estimates put the 2025 population at 40,844. The 2020 count was 40,501 and the 2010 count was 42,034, so headcount has been nearly flat for fifteen years. Those residents share 4.56 square miles, roughly 8,890 per square mile.

Owners live in only 26.1 percent of the homes, and the middle owned home was valued at $437,800 in the 2020 to 2024 survey period. Gross rent runs $1,273 a month and household income $45,424. A household averages 2.24 people, and under 6 percent of residents are children.

So much of the housing here is rented that buyers often ask first whether a house carries a rental permit or a student home license. Have those papers ready.

How much transfer tax applies to a sale inside State College Borough?

Three percent of the price, against 2 percent in most Centre County municipalities. The county's rate table shows the borough with a 1.5 percent local share on top of the state and school district shares.

Realty transfer tax shares in State College Borough, Centre County rate table
ShareState College BoroughTypical Centre County municipality
State1.00%1.00%
Local (municipality)1.50%0.50%
School district0.50%0.50%
Total3.00%2.00%
On a $437,800 sale (the Census median value)$13,134$8,756

No deed gets recorded until the tax is paid. Sales agreements commonly split it evenly, yet the new owner answers for it if the amount paid is ever questioned. At the median value an even split costs each side $6,567.

Family transfers can be exempt, and so can a deed between ex-spouses. A deed reciting token consideration, say $1, travels with a state Statement of Value for Department of Revenue review.

Do rental permits and student home licenses change how a State College sale works?

They can, because they decide what a buyer may do with the property after closing. The borough hands rental permit administration to Centre Region Code Administration, a body that also covers Patton, Ferguson, College, Half Moon and Harris townships and Bellefonte Borough.

  • Rental Housing Permit: required for any unit lived in by someone other than the owner or the owner's immediate family. The unit must meet the International Property Maintenance Code and the Fire Prevention Code, and an imminent hazard can lead to a vacate order within 10 days and a suspended permit if it is not fixed within 90 days.
  • Student Home License: applies to one-family homes, one-family homes with an accessory apartment, and two-family dwellings occupied by more than one unrelated student. The borough adopted Ordinance 2029 for this in November 2013. An existing license can move to a new owner with an approved transfer application and a $25 fee.
  • New student homes: a first license costs $1,000, with a $50 zoning permit for the change of use and a $25 rental permit application fee. In the R-1, R-2 and R-3 zoning districts a new student home also has to meet spacing rules from existing ones, which is why an already licensed house is worth more to an investor.
  • Short-term rentals: the borough license costs $450 and lasts one year. It requires a rental housing permit, proof the applicant lives there at least eight months a year, off-street parking matching the bedrooms rented, and at least $100,000 of liability insurance.

Student home licenses renew every year, and the 2026 renewal deadline was October 15. Write to studenthomes@statecollegepa.us to confirm a license is current before you tell a buyer it transfers.

How does the valley setting affect a State College house?

At about 1,154 feet in a mountain-ringed valley, the borough feels its weather in basements, roofs and heating bills. January averages 27.2 degrees and July 72.2, a humid continental pattern. Yearly precipitation is 41.53 inches, snowfall 43.8 inches, and snow usually falls between October and April.

The valley floor is prone to frequent rain, snow and flooding. Inspectors here tend to check sump pumps, foundation moisture, gutters and furnace age, so hand over any repair or roof records early.

What will buyers ask about schools, getting around and utilities?

Schools come first. The State College Area School District runs eight elementary schools, two middle schools and one high school for 6,712 students. Three elementary schools sit inside the borough: Coral Street, Radio Park and Easterly Parkway. Mount Nittany Middle School serves most of the borough except College Heights, and the whole district feeds State College Area High School.

  • Roads and transit: U.S. Route 322 Business and Pennsylvania Route 26 run through the borough. The Centre Area Transportation Authority operates buses to College, Ferguson and Patton townships, and State College Regional Airport has daily flights to Charlotte, Chicago, Philadelphia and Washington.
  • Commute: workers average a 15.5 minute trip to the job, the shortest of the four Pennsylvania places the Census compares here.
  • Utilities: West Penn Power supplies electricity, Columbia Gas of Pennsylvania supplies natural gas, the State College Borough Water Authority provides water, the University Area Joint Authority handles sewer, and borough public works collects trash and recycling.
  • Employers: a 2016 list put Penn State at 27,029 employees, Mount Nittany Medical Center at 2,365 and the school district at 1,792.

Which routes sell a State College house fastest?

The quickest routes skip showings and repair haggling. A listing reaches the most people but adds inspection requests, financing contingencies and a closing date that has to suit a lender.

An investor planning a rental may close sooner, especially where a rental permit or student home license is already in place. A direct cash purchase drops the financing step and takes the property as is, with an offer that accounts for repairs. Get price, closing date and the 3 percent tax split in writing before you commit.

What should you confirm before accepting an offer?

  • Locate your deed. If it is missing, contact the Centre County Recorder of Deeds.
  • Request a payoff figure from your lender to see what remains after the mortgage clears.
  • Settle who pays the 3 percent transfer tax before you sign.
  • Confirm whether the house has a rental housing permit, student home license or short-term rental license, and disclose it.
  • Gather receipts for roof, furnace, drainage and plumbing work.
  • Check that property tax bills are current, since unpaid balances are deducted at closing.

More questions about State College, PA

Is State College's transfer tax really 3 percent?

Yes. Centre County's rate table lists State College Borough at 3.00 percent: 1.00 percent state, 1.5 percent local and 0.50 percent school district. Most other municipalities in the county total 2.00 percent. Buyers and sellers often divide it equally, but the contract decides.

Does a student home license go to the buyer?

Yes. The borough allows an existing student home license to transfer to a new owner once a transfer application is approved and a $25 fee is paid. Email studenthomes@statecollegepa.us for the current transfer application before you advertise the license as part of the sale.

Does a rented house need a rental permit to sell?

The permit is a condition of renting, so a rented house should hold a current Rental Housing Permit from Centre Region Code Administration. Selling does not create a separate permit step in the borough pages. Check the permit status first, because a lapsed permit can worry a buyer.

Who handles trash and water in State College?

Borough public works collects trash and recycling, and the State College Borough Water Authority provides water. Sewer service comes from the University Area Joint Authority. Buyers sometimes ask for these names when they set up accounts.

How can I obtain my State College deed?

Contact the Centre County Recorder of Deeds. The recorder holds the recorded deed, and the office will not accept a new deed for recording until the transfer taxes due have been paid.

Does Northampton Township require an inspection when a house sells?

No. The township's building and zoning FAQ says Northampton does not conduct an inspection or require a certificate for the resale of residential property. That makes a Northampton sale simpler on the municipal side than in towns with a resale permit, though a certificate of use and occupancy is still required to occupy a nonresidential space.

Permits still apply to projects, including replacements. The township notes that an old shed or fence may never have been approved, so replacing it needs a permit and a fresh look at current rules. Sheds of 240 square feet or less generally go behind the house, seven feet from the property line and no taller than 12 feet. Fences go in side and rear yards at up to six feet, never in easements, and corner lots and pool fences have special requirements.

The administration building is at 55 Township Road in Richboro, and the main line is 215-357-6800.

What is Northampton Township's layout and housing history?

Northampton Township is a second class township of about 26 square miles in Bucks County, roughly 12 miles northeast of Philadelphia. It became a township on December 14, 1722, and the Neshaminy Creek forms its entire northeastern edge. Its communities include Churchville, Holland, Ivyland and Richboro, and the township says Jacksonville became Ivyland, Addisville became Richboro and Rocksville became Holland.

Farmland turned into subdivisions in the second half of the twentieth century. Wikipedia lists the population at 6,006 in 1960, 35,406 in 1990 and 39,915 in 2020, which suggests much of the housing dates from those decades.

Route 332 crosses the township along Jacksonville Road, Almshouse Road and Newtown Richboro Road, while Route 232 runs north and south along Second Street Pike, Route 532 follows Buck Road and Route 213 skirts the southeast border. The township maintains about 171 of its 202 miles of public roads. Students attend the Council Rock School District, and Tyler State Park offers 1,711 acres of trails.

Does private well water affect a Northampton sale?

It can, because groundwater contamination from the former Naval Air Warfare Center in Warminster has moved into Northampton Township. The township states that the Navy has identified affected private wells and committed to some remediation, but that it believes more is needed, and it urges owners with wells to test.

Northampton Bucks County Municipal Authority supplies public water to thousands of residents and businesses, and the township page links to an authority announcement of a public water connection project for 334 homes. A seller on a private well should expect questions from buyers and lenders. Practical steps include:

  • Test the well through a laboratory from the accredited list the township posts.
  • Ask the Municipal Authority at 215-357-8515 whether public water is available at the address.
  • Keep any Navy or authority correspondence about the property with the sale documents.

What do Northampton Township property taxes include?

The 2026 township real estate rate is 35.250 mills, built from eight separate levies. The township's tax page uses a $40,000 median assessed home in its example, which produces a $1,410 township bill at that rate.

2026 Northampton Township millage breakdown (source: township tax information page)

The elected tax collector bills real estate tax from an office on Bustleton Pike in Richboro and accepts no cash, with a separate check for each bill. Earned income tax runs 1 percent and splits evenly between the township and Council Rock School District, and the local services tax is $52 a year for people who work in the township.

How do Bucks County assessment appeals work for Northampton owners?

Bucks County's Board of Assessment Appeals takes annual appeals once a year in early August, and the 2026 deadline was August 3, 2026, with any change effective for the 2027 tax year. Residential appeal forms and rules are posted on the county site, a fee applies, and the board's office is at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown.

Homeowners can also file a Homestead/Farmstead Exclusion application, and the county sets March 1 as the deadline for the tax year beginning the following July 1. The board meets on the first and third Tuesday of each month at 10 a.m.

The county also notes that Act 29 requires a new owner to send contact information to the Board of Assessment within 30 days of purchase.

What transfer taxes and recording rules apply to a Northampton sale?

Bucks County states that a sale carries a 2 percent transfer tax, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid at recording. State and local law do not say who pays, and in most agreements the buyer and seller split it, though the new owner is responsible if the amount paid is questioned.

Since January 2026 the Recorder of Deeds no longer accepts personal checks for this tax. Accepted payment is cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card. Family transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings can be exempt, and a Statement of Value (REV-183) goes in duplicate whenever the true value is not on the deed or an exemption is claimed.

If the state later finds the property worth more than stated, additional tax and interest are billed directly by the Department of Revenue.

What should a Northampton seller know about utilities, trash and transit?

Public water and sewer questions go to the Northampton Bucks County Municipal Authority, and trash and recycling are handled by the township's contractor, J. P. Mascaro and Sons, at 800-432-1616. The township posts a street listing that shows each pickup day, which is useful to hand a buyer.

Commuters have limited rail choices. The TMA Bucks Richboro-Warminster Rushbus runs peak-hour shuttles from Richboro to the SEPTA Warminster station, and passenger service on the old Fox Chase-Newtown line through Churchville and Holland ended in January 1983, with the Holland station demolished in 2000.

The township's capital project list includes Holland streetscape improvements, a Jacksonville and Almshouse Road roundabout, the Richboro sidewalk project and a Route 332 trail connection, all of which buyers may see while driving through.

Who buys homes in Northampton Township, and when is a cash sale useful?

Northampton is a high-value, stable market: QuickFacts shows $599,100 for a typical owned home, 93.8 percent of units occupied by their owners, and median household income of $158,583, with 95.4 percent of residents at the same address as the prior year. Seniors make up 22.2 percent of the population, and the average commute runs 30.5 minutes.

A cash sale becomes useful when a house needs work the owner cannot fund or when timing is tight. Situations that often lead there include:

  • An estate property with an older kitchen, roof or heating system.
  • A house with a private well that failed a test.
  • An owner relocating before a listing could reasonably sell.

Weigh the cash number against a listing's net after commissions, repairs and the 2 percent transfer tax.

More questions about Northampton, PA

Do I need a use and occupancy certificate to sell my Northampton house?

No. The township says it does not inspect or require a certificate for the resale of residential property. A certificate of use and occupancy applies to nonresidential space.

What is the Northampton Township real estate tax rate?

The 2026 township millage is 35.250 mills, made up of general purpose, fire, emergency medical, recreation, debt service, library and two road levies. County and Council Rock School District taxes are billed on top of that.

When was the Bucks County appeal deadline in 2026?

The deadline for 2026 annual appeals was August 3, 2026, and any change takes effect for the 2027 tax year. Annual appeals are due in early August each year.

How much is the realty transfer tax in Bucks County?

Bucks County lists it at 2 percent, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. It is paid at recording, and the buyer and seller usually split it.

Should I test a private well before selling in Northampton Township?

Yes, testing is a sensible step, because the township reports groundwater contamination from the former Naval Air Warfare Center in Warminster. Use a laboratory from the accredited list the township posts and ask the Municipal Authority about public water.

What do I need to sell a house in Penn Hills?

You need an Occupancy Permit and a passing dye test before the house changes hands. Penn Hills code enforcement requires the permit for every sale, purchase or deed transfer, whether or not anyone lives in the house. It is a municipal requirement, so it applies to a cash sale as much as to a listing.

The two steps have different owners. The occupancy application goes to the Code Enforcement Department at the Government Center, 102 Duff Road, and a plumber you hire handles the dye test. Starting both early keeps them from becoming the last item standing between you and the closing table.

  • Occupancy Permit: $75 for a single family dwelling and $125 for a commercial property.
  • Dye test: the plumber of your choice runs it, files the form only after the house passes, and you submit it with a $25 filing fee.
  • Septic: a house on a septic system needs an additional septic report.

How does the Penn Hills occupancy permit process work?

You file a three-part carbonless application, signed at the top and listing the new owner's information, and pay with it. The form posted on the municipal website is a sample and will not be accepted, so pick up the real one at the office. Payment can be cash, check or money order payable to the Municipality of Penn Hills, and cards are taken only at the office, where a service charge may apply.

If you mail the application, enclose a copy of a photo ID and name the person the inspector should meet at the property if that is not you. Inspections are scheduled Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., and the department's own hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. The same permit is needed for every change of tenant or occupant, which matters if you are selling a rental with a tenant in place.

Call Code Enforcement at (412) 342-1192 with questions. The municipality's FAQ also lists a building permit as a separate item for new construction or home improvements, so ask before you finish any repair work you started on your own.

What does selling in Penn Hills cost in transfer tax?

Penn Hills sellers deal with a 3% total realty transfer tax: 1.5% to the municipality, 0.5% to the Penn Hills School District and 1% to the Commonwealth. The county's table lists the first two figures and notes that its local rates leave out the state's 1%. Allegheny County collects the tax when the deed is recorded, on a separate check from the recording fees.

On a $150,000 sale the total is $4,500. The municipal share is high compared with most Allegheny County boroughs, where the local share is often one half of one percent, so Penn Hills sellers should price it in early. The sales agreement says which side pays.

Transfer tax and sale-related fees in Penn Hills (Allegheny County rate table and Penn Hills Code Enforcement)
ItemAmount
Municipality transfer tax1.5%
Penn Hills School District transfer tax0.5%
Commonwealth transfer tax1%
Occupancy Permit, single family$75
Dye test filing fee$25

What is Penn Hills like for a home seller?

Penn Hills is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, and Wikipedia calls it the county's second-largest municipality. It was formed from the north of Wilkins Township in 1850, carried the name Penn Township, became Penn Hills Township in 1958 and took home rule status in 1976. Its population peaked at 62,886 in 1970 and stood at 41,059 in the 2020 census, down from 42,329 in 2010. The Census Bureau lists no 2025 estimate for Penn Hills.

The municipality covers about 19 square miles, with the Allegheny River on its northern edge and Plum Creek marking the border with Plum Borough. It touches ten neighbors, among them Verona, Oakmont, Monroeville, Churchill and the Pittsburgh neighborhoods of East Hills and Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar. Neighborhood names include Lincoln Park, Milltown, Rosedale, Universal, Verona Hilltop and Frankstown Estates.

  • Owners report a middle home value of $134,700 in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates, and 74.6% of households own.
  • Households: 17,964, averaging 2.23 people.
  • Median gross rent: $1,103.
  • Residents 65 and older make up 24.3% of the population.
  • Commutes average 26.9 minutes.

Interstate 376 crosses the south end, with Penn Hills at exit 81, and Rodi Road (PA 791) connects the interstate to Frankstown Road. PA 130 and PA 380 are the other main routes. The Penn Hills School District runs Penn Hills Elementary, Linton Middle and Penn Hills High School.

How do Allegheny County taxes affect a Penn Hills sale?

Allegheny County uses base year values, and the current base year is 2012, so an assessment is not a present-day market price. The county portal lists parcels, and changes from appeals, permits and corrections post daily. The annual appeal window for tax year 2026 ran from July 1 to September 2, 2025, and the window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026. Both are closed.

Penn Hills tax collection is split among the county, the municipality and the school district. Ask the county treasurer and the Penn Hills tax collector for a paid-to-date statement before you set a closing date. Anything owed at the time of sale is normally settled from the proceeds, and the title company will search for open balances.

The county runs a Homestead exclusion under Act 50 for owner-occupied homes, with the application made through the county. A buyer who will live in the house should apply in their own name after closing.

What disclosures apply when selling a Penn Hills house?

A seller must deliver a signed property disclosure statement to the buyer before the agreement of transfer is signed. The statement must address the roof, basement, structural problems, plumbing, wiring, water and sewage, drainage and other topics listed in 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7304. Several creeks run through the municipality, so the land and drainage items deserve a careful answer.

An executor or other fiduciary who sells for an estate falls outside the chapter. Everyone else owes the buyer a truthful form, and a buyer who proves a violation can recover actual damages if the suit is filed within two years after settlement. If something on the form changes before closing, tell the buyer in writing.

How can I prepare a Penn Hills house for a fast sale?

Run the municipal steps first, because they are the ones with set lead times. A dye test needs a plumber's schedule and an occupancy inspection needs a weekday morning or early afternoon slot. Once those are lined up, the rest is the same as anywhere: a clean title, a payoff statement and a realistic price.

  • Book the dye test and, if the house has a septic system, the septic report.
  • Pick up the carbonless occupancy form at the Government Center rather than printing the sample.
  • Cut grass before inspection; the municipality treats grass over 10 inches as high.
  • Ask Code Enforcement whether any open permits or violations are on the address.

A buyer who purchases as-is still needs the municipal permit for the deed to move, so ask whether the buyer or the seller handles it and put the answer in the contract.

More questions about Penn Hills, PA

Does Penn Hills require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The municipality requires an Occupancy Permit and a dye test for a sale, with an inspection scheduled on weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. The permit is $75 for a single family home and the dye test filing fee is $25.

How much is the transfer tax in Penn Hills?

It totals 3%: 1.5% to the municipality, 0.5% to the school district and 1% to the state. Allegheny County collects it when the deed is recorded. The sales agreement decides who pays.

Can I download the Penn Hills occupancy permit form online?

No. The form on the municipal website is only a sample and will not be accepted. Pick up the three-part carbonless form at the Code Enforcement office at 102 Duff Road, or call (412) 342-1192 about other arrangements.

Who does the dye test in Penn Hills?

A plumber of your choice does it. The municipality's contractor list is only a suggestion. The plumber completes the form after the house passes, and you submit it with the $25 fee. A house on septic also needs a septic report.

Is there still time to appeal my Allegheny County assessment?

The 2027 window ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026 and has closed. Check the county's real estate portal for the next window.

How does selling a house in Cheltenham work?

A Cheltenham sale follows the normal Pennsylvania steps, with one township requirement layered in: the seller must hand the buyer zoning and use certifications issued by the township before settlement. Cheltenham is a home-rule township in the southeast corner of Montgomery County, so the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds records the deed and the county Board of Assessment Appeals handles values.

Allow time for paperwork, because a seller who needs to close quickly should file the township application as soon as there is a signed agreement of sale and a settlement date. The township's code says it will issue the certification statement and affidavits within 15 days of receiving the application, and no deed is registered by the township until the certifications are issued.

What is Cheltenham Township like?

Cheltenham is a 9.03-square-mile inner-ring suburb that borders Philadelphia on the south and east, Abington Township and Jenkintown on the north and Springfield Township on the west. Fifteen Quakers from Cheltenham, England, bought the land from William Penn in 1682, and Tookany Creek powered the mills that shaped early settlement.

Cheltenham became a first-class township in 1900 and a home-rule municipality in 1976. It has no mayor; a Board of Commissioners with one member from each of seven wards governs it, and a separate school board runs the schools. Sellers can reach the township office at 215-887-1000 on weekdays for permit questions.

The township has ten districts: Glenside, Laverock, Edge Hill, Wyncote, Cedarbrook, Chelten Hills, La Mott, Elkins Park, Melrose Park and Cheltenham Village. Zip codes are 19012, 19027, 19038 and 19095. Wealthy Philadelphians built estates here in the late nineteenth century, among them Lynnewood Hall, the Elkins estate and Grey Towers Castle, and the later housing stock includes rowhouses, twins and split levels. Cheltenham Township School District runs the public schools, ending at Cheltenham High School, and Arcadia University is in Glenside.

How good is transit from Cheltenham?

Transit is a selling point here, because SEPTA Regional Rail runs through the township and all lines north of Center City except Trenton pass through it. Stations carry the names of neighborhoods such as Glenside, Melrose Park and Jenkintown-Wyncote.

  • Bus: SEPTA City Division routes start at the Cheltenham-Ogontz bus loop at Ogontz Avenue (PA 309) and Cheltenham Avenue.
  • Roads: Cheltenham Avenue is the border with Philadelphia and links to PA 611 and PA 309; Old York Road, Limekiln Pike and Willow Grove Avenue continue from the city.
  • Commute: workers average 30.6 minutes each way, per the Census Bureau.

What do Census figures show for Cheltenham housing?

These figures are the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates for the township. About 62.6 percent of housing units are owner occupied, and the median owner-occupied value is $384,800.

Median gross rent is $1,608 and median household income is $109,022. There are 14,859 households averaging 2.47 people, and 58.1 percent of adults over 25 hold a bachelor's degree. The population was 37,452 in 2020 and an estimated 38,498 in July 2025, up 2.9 percent from the base.

What must a Cheltenham seller deliver at settlement?

Chapter 217 of the Cheltenham Township code, titled Property, Sale of, makes it unlawful to sell without delivering four items to the buyer at or before settlement. The township issues them on forms it provides and may inspect, though it is not required to.

  • A certification of the property's zoning district from the township Zoning Officer.
  • A certification that the current use does or does not comply with township ordinances.
  • An affidavit that the street address number is displayed as Chapter 114 requires.
  • For a single-family home, an affidavit that smoke detectors meet the Fire Prevention Code.

The agreement of sale must state the zoning classification and warrant that the use complies. An owner who skips the certifications and whose use violated zoning faces a summary offense with a fine up to $600 plus costs. The fire code also requires battery-powered smoke detectors in single-family dwellings when they are sold. Fees are in the township's Chapter A300.

What if the Cheltenham house is a rental?

Cheltenham requires a rental license before an owner enters a rental agreement, and Chapter 227 requires every rental property to pass inspection against the building, property maintenance and fire codes at least once every three years. The license is a mercantile or business privilege license under the township's tax chapter.

  • Within 30 days of a transfer of ownership, the owner must give the Code Administrator written notice with the new owner's name and address.
  • The township gives at least seven days' notice before an inspection, and the owner schedules required inspections.
  • A license can be suspended or revoked for unpaid fees, uncorrected violations or refusing an inspection.
  • A summary offense under the chapter carries a fine of $50 to $1,000 per violation.

A landlord selling to a buyer who will keep tenants should pass along license and inspection records. Gather the last inspection report and any correction notices before you list, because the buyer's lender and inspector will ask about the house's condition.

What are the property tax rates in Cheltenham?

Cheltenham's total 2026 millage is 73.4832 mills, the highest on the county's 2026 municipal list. The table shows the pieces from the county's published list.

Taxing body2026 mills
Montgomery County5.462

Cheltenham Township10.8512
School district (2026-2027)56.68
Total73.4832

Source: Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals. In the 2026 cycle the municipal bill dated February 1 and the school bill dated July 1. Because the school share is most of the bill, a buyer's monthly escrow depends heavily on the district.

What transfer taxes and permits apply in Cheltenham?

Montgomery County states the realty transfer tax is 2 percent, collected by the Recorder of Deeds, and Pennsylvania's share of that is 1 percent. The county page also lists the common level ratio factor, 3.36 for documents dated July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027.

Permits go through the township's OpenGov portal, and since March 26, 2025 the township accepts applications only there. Permits are needed for roofing, siding, decks, kitchen and bathroom renovations, fencing, sheds and HVAC. Painting, flooring and gutter replacement do not need one, and replacement windows with no change in rough opening are exempt unless the house is in a Historic District, where added review and inspection apply. A retaining wall that disturbs the Steep Slope Conservation District, a gradient of 15 percent or more, may need zoning relief first. Each permit carries a $4.50 state UCC charge. The township code also has chapters on rental licensing and inspection, sump pump standards and a vacant building registry, so landlords and owners of empty houses should check them.

More questions about Cheltenham, PA

Do I need a township certification to sell in Cheltenham?

Yes. Chapter 217 requires a zoning district certification and a use compliance certification, plus an address affidavit and, for single-family homes, a smoke detector affidavit. Apply on the township's form, and expect the answer within 15 days.

What happens if I skip the Cheltenham certifications?

The township will not register the deed, and an owner whose use violated zoning faces a summary offense with a fine up to $600 plus costs. The agreement of sale also must include the zoning and use warranty.

How much is the transfer tax in Cheltenham?

Montgomery County states the realty transfer tax is 2 percent. The Recorder of Deeds collects it at recording, with the state's 1 percent included.

Which school district serves Cheltenham?

Cheltenham Township School District serves the township, and its 2026-2027 millage is 56.68 mills, the largest piece of the bill.

Where do I apply for Cheltenham building permits?

On the township's OpenGov portal. Paper applications ended when the portal became mandatory on March 26, 2025, and each permit carries a $4.50 UCC charge.

What should I know before selling a house in Upper Merion, PA?

Upper Merion is a Montgomery County township of about 17 square miles with an estimated 36,674 residents, and the township does not require a use and occupancy permit when a single-family home changes hands. That one rule removes a step that sellers in several neighboring townships still face. What remains is the standard Pennsylvania sequence: disclosure form, agreement of sale, transfer tax, deed recording and tax proration.

The township sits about 16 miles from Philadelphia and takes in the villages of Gulph Mills, King of Prussia, Swedeland and Swedesburg, plus parts of Radnor and Wayne. A house in Swedesburg and a house near the King of Prussia mall draw different buyers, so the first job is matching your street to the right pool of buyers and the right sale route.

What makes the Upper Merion housing market different from nearby townships?

Upper Merion is an employment center as much as a bedroom suburb, which shapes who shops for a home here. The Schuylkill River forms its northern and eastern edge, Valley Forge National Historical Park fills most of the western end, and the King of Prussia retail and office district sits in the middle of the township. The township's 2024 financial report lists Lockheed Martin, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, US Liability Insurance, GlaxoSmithKline and CSL Behring among its largest employers, so many buyers want a short commute rather than a large yard.

Getting around is easy to sell. Buyers will look at these points on a listing:

  • The Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276) crosses the middle of the township and meets the Schuylkill Expressway (I-76) at the western edge.
  • US 202 runs parallel to the turnpike and connects to the eastern end of US 422 near the western border.
  • PA 23 runs east to west, and PA 320 runs north to south from its terminus at PA 23.
  • SEPTA's M line stops at Gulph Mills and Hughes Park, and several SEPTA suburban bus routes serve the township.
  • The Rambler community shuttle circles residential areas, the mall, medical sites and the municipal building Monday through Saturday.

How do Upper Merion home values and ownership compare?

Owners here hold higher-priced homes than in the neighboring townships of Upper Moreland and Warminster, and renting is common. The table below uses the Census Bureau's QuickFacts for Upper Merion.
