Does Upper Merion require a use and occupancy permit at sale?

No. The township's residential permit page says no Use and Occupancy Permit is required for a change of ownership of a single-family dwelling, as long as the use of the dwelling stays the same. Converting a house into a different use is a separate question for the township.

Permits still matter if you did work on the house. Buyers' inspectors and lenders ask about decks, finished basements, sheds, pools and replaced roofs, and the township's page lists the permit categories for each. Pull your own records before you list:

  • Permit review takes up to 15 business days, and inspections need 24 hours' notice, so finishing open work before listing takes weeks, not days.
  • Residential contractors must be registered with the State and list a Pennsylvania HIC number and a certificate of insurance on the application.
  • Accessory structures have setbacks by zoning district. In R-1 and R-1A a shed or pool sits 10 feet from the side and rear lines, while R-2 and R-3 require four feet from the side and five feet from the rear.

Call the township's safety and code enforcement office if you cannot tell which zoning district your lot is in.

Which school district serves Upper Merion homes?

Public school students in the township attend the Upper Merion Area School District, and its building layout is a talking point in every listing. Children start at one of five K-4 elementary schools: Bridgeport, Caley Road, Candlebrook, Gulph and Roberts. They move on to Upper Merion Area Middle School for grades 5 through 8 and Upper Merion Area High School for grades 9 through 12.

Mother Teresa Regional Catholic School is the parochial option in the township. Because the elementary school assignment depends on your street, confirm it with the district before you put a school name in your listing.

What do I pay and file when I sell in Upper Merion?

The state's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the value of the real estate, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue. Bucks County's recorder describes the full transfer tax as 2 percent, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, and says buyers and sellers usually split it. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds to confirm the rate that applies to your township and school district before you sign.

The seller's disclosure duty comes from 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. You complete the property disclosure statement and deliver a signed, dated copy to the buyer before the agreement of sale is signed. The form covers the roof, basement, plumbing, wiring, storm water facilities, hazardous substances and flood risk indicators. The Schuylkill runs along two edges of Upper Merion and annual precipitation runs near 48.5 inches, so answer the water questions with care. Act 74 of 2026 amended the land item and added a flood-insurance notice to the chapter.

If property taxes are behind, the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau holds upset sales each September and December for parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier, and buyers at those sales take the property subject to liens. Check with the Board of Assessment Appeals for the annual appeal deadline and forms listed on its page.

Which sale route fits an Upper Merion house best?

The right route depends on how much time and repair money you have. A listing can reach the large employee pool around King of Prussia but brings showings, inspection requests and a financing timeline. A private sale saves an agent's fee and adds legal and marketing work. A direct sale to an as-is buyer shortens the schedule and removes repair negotiations, usually at a lower price.

  • Ask every buyer for proof of funds and a written closing date.
  • Request a net sheet that shows transfer tax, payoff, tax proration and any repair credits.
  • Compare the net figure from each route, not the headline price.

More questions about Upper Merion, PA

Is a certificate needed to sell a house in Upper Merion Township?

No, not for a single-family home whose use stays the same. The township says no use and occupancy permit is required for the change of ownership. Ask the township office first for a multi-unit or non-residential property.

What does a home in Upper Merion cost compared with the rest of the county?

Owners in Upper Merion report a middle home value of $455,300 in the 2020 to 2024 survey. Your house will price off nearby sales, so ask an agent or appraiser for comparable sales on your street.

Who pays the transfer tax when an Upper Merion house sells?

The law does not assign it. Bucks County's recorder notes that most sale agreements split it between buyer and seller, and that the buyer is responsible if the amount paid is questioned. Put the split in writing in your agreement of sale.

Can I sell an Upper Merion house with unpermitted work?

Yes, but disclose what you know. Pennsylvania's disclosure form asks about additions, remodeling and structural changes, and a seller cannot make statements the seller knows are false. Many owners apply for a permit on the open work before listing.

How quickly can a cash sale close in Upper Merion?

A cash sale can close as fast as the title search, the deed and the transfer tax paperwork allow, because no lender is involved. The timeline is set in the agreement of sale, so ask the buyer for a written date and what must happen before it.

What makes selling a house in Norristown different?

Norristown requires a municipal inspection and an occupancy certificate whenever a residential or commercial property changes owners, so a sale here carries a code step that many Pennsylvania towns skip. Norristown is a home rule municipality and the Montgomery County seat, packed into about 3.5 square miles along the Schuylkill River, and its 2020 population of 35,748 makes it the second most populous borough in the state, per Wikipedia.

Because the inspection must happen before settlement, sellers who start early avoid a delayed closing. The next sections lay out the sequence, the tax bill calendar and the county appeal rules.

What are the steps to get a Norristown property transfer approved?

The process begins with zoning and ends with an Occupancy Certificate handed to the seller for use at settlement. The municipality's Use and Occupancy page lists the following order:

  • A Zoning Use Registration Permit confirms the intended use is allowed in that zoning district.
  • The seller then files a Property Transfer Permit application with the Code Department at least 30 days before the settlement date, with every field completed.
  • After fees are paid and the application is processed, an inspector contacts the owner or agent, which can take at least three business days.
  • The seller supplies a Heating Certification and a Chimney Certification from a contractor licensed and registered with Norristown.
  • If the building complies, the inspector issues an Occupancy Certificate.

The Code Enforcement Department answers questions at 610-270-0441, including whether a particular contractor is registered with the municipality.

What happens if the Norristown inspector finds violations?

Repairs must be finished before the Occupancy Certificate is issued, unless the buyer accepts responsibility in writing through a Letter of Intent. The buyer completes that form and returns it to the Code Department.

Depending on what the inspector finds, one of two temporary certificates may be issued. A Temporary Occupancy Certificate covers a violation that is not substantial and lets the purchaser live in the property while correcting it. A Temporary Access Certificate covers at least one substantial violation: nobody may occupy the building, though the owner may store belongings and enter to make repairs.

The municipality defines a substantial violation as one that makes a building or part of it unfit for human habitation. Examples include a significant fire or accident hazard, inadequate sanitary facilities, vermin infestation, or disrepair so deep that repair cost would exceed half the agreed purchase price. That last test is why a badly damaged house often moves to a buyer who is ready to take on the work.

How does Norristown rental licensing affect a sale?

Rental licensing matters because Norristown has more than 7,500 residential rental units, and the Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate at 42.7 percent. Many sellers here are landlords, and many buyers plan to rent the house out.

Every rental unit needs an annual license before it can be lawfully occupied. A new landlord submits an application, the Code Enforcement Department inspects the unit under the 2012 International Property Maintenance Code with local amendments, and a license issues only after violations are fixed and the invoice is paid. Owners who stop renting can file a De-Registration Request, and any later return to renting restarts the first-time landlord process.

Zoning limits how many separate units a building may hold. In single-family zones, converting a house to two or more rentals is illegal, and a long-vacant multi-unit may lose its legal status, so confirm the approved use with the Planning and Municipal Development Department at 610-270-0450 before pricing a property as a duplex.

What do Norristown real estate taxes look like?

Norristown bills real estate tax once a year on a fixed calendar, and the 2026 municipal rate is 19 mills after the council raised it by 0.75 mill. The Finance Department collects municipal and county real estate taxes plus the trash fee, and it does not accept partial payments on a bill.

Norristown real estate tax calendar (source: Norristown Finance Department)

For a closing, the finance office issues tax certifications for a $35 fee and asks for requests at least three weeks before settlement. Duplicate bills or receipts cost $5. The taxes phone line is 610-270-0431.

Unpaid taxes can end up with the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau, which holds upset sales each September and December. An upset sale buyer assumes the liens, while a judicial sale delivers parcels free and clear.

How do Montgomery County assessments and appeals work for a Norristown home?

The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals values every Norristown parcel for county, municipal and school taxes, and its annual appeal deadline is August 1 of the year before the year on appeal. An interim appeal must be filed within 40 days of the date on a notice of change in assessment.

Appeals must be hand-delivered or postmarked on or before the last day, and faxes are not accepted. Because postmarks can run late, the board suggests a post office counter postmark, certified mail, or delivery to its Norristown office on weekdays.

The assessment is presumed correct, so the appellant carries the burden of proof with an appraisal, comparable sales or witness testimony. The owner or a licensed attorney must appear at the hearing, and missing it gets the appeal dismissed as abandoned.

What should a seller know about Norristown's layout and housing?

Norristown sits on hilly ground where Stony Creek and Saw Mill Run split the town into thirds before emptying into the Schuylkill. The Wikipedia entry names four distinct areas: the West End, East End, North End and downtown. NOAA normals cited there show about 50.65 inches of precipitation and 25.3 inches of snow in a year, so basement moisture and roof condition often come up during buyer inspections.

Getting around is easy by regional standards. U.S. Route 202 runs through town as a one-way pair on DeKalb and Markley Streets, Main Street continues as Ridge Pike, and the Norristown Transportation Center connects SEPTA buses, the Norristown High Speed Line, a Regional Rail line and the Schuylkill River Trail.

QuickFacts reports a 2020 to 2024 median owner-occupied home value of $213,900 and median household income of $66,701 across 12,642 households. The population peaked at 38,181 in 1940 per the same Wikipedia history, and the Norristown Area School District serves the municipality.

What transfer taxes apply to a Norristown sale, and when does a cash offer help?

Pennsylvania's 1 percent state realty transfer tax is collected by the county Recorder of Deeds at recording, and local transfer tax is collected on top of it. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on a Norristown address, and plan on a Statement of Value form where the deed shows no price or claims an exemption.

A cash offer helps when the inspection cost or timeline is the obstacle. Sellers often turn to one in these cases:

  • Heating or chimney certifications and repairs would cost more than the seller can front.
  • The inspector is likely to issue a Temporary Access Certificate.
  • The house is a licensed rental with a tenant and open violations.

Any buyer still has to work through the Letter of Intent and certificate steps, so ask who handles them before signing.

More questions about Norristown, PA

Do I need an inspection to sell a house in Norristown?

Yes. Norristown requires a property transfer inspection before settlement, and the seller applies for a Property Transfer Permit at least 30 days before the closing date. A passing result produces an Occupancy Certificate for use at settlement.

Can a buyer take over Norristown repairs instead of the seller?

Yes, if the buyer assumes responsibility in writing by completing a Letter of Intent and returning it to the Code Department. Without that letter, repairs must be finished before the Occupancy Certificate is issued.

When are Norristown real estate taxes due?

Bills are due June 15 each year at face value. Payment through April 15 earns a 2 percent discount, and bills paid from June 16 through December 31 carry a 10 percent penalty.

How do I get a tax certification for a Norristown closing?

Submit the municipality's tax certification request form with the $35 fee at least three weeks before closing. The Finance Department taxes line, 610-270-0431, can answer questions about the request.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Norristown?

The annual appeal deadline set by the Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals is August 1 of the year before the year on appeal. Interim appeals must be filed within 40 days of the date on a notice of change in assessment.

Selling in Hampden?

Who is selling homes in Hampden Township, PA?

Hampden Township is one of the higher-priced, owner-heavy parts of the Harrisburg area. The 2025 Census estimate is 35,401 people, a gain of 8.1 percent over the April 2020 base, and the township is the largest municipality in Cumberland County.

Census survey years 2020 to 2024 show 76.9 percent of homes lived in by their owners, a typical owner-occupied value of $354,900 and rent of $1,466. Households earned a median $105,434, and 55.3 percent of adults finished a bachelor's degree. A seller here usually holds a family home with long equity, and buyers expect a house in good order.

If your Hampden house needs work, has tenants, or came to you through an estate, the usual listing path can drag. Many owners compare it with a direct as-is purchase before they spend money on repairs.

Where is Hampden Township and what is around it?

Hampden Township sits in the northeastern part of Cumberland County, with the Conodoguinet Creek running east toward the Susquehanna River. It covers about 17.3 square miles of land, with Blue Mountain along the northern edge and the creek bending through the middle.

  • Villages inside the township: Brennemans Mill, Good Hope, Mount Zion and Sporting Hill.
  • Neighbors: East Pennsboro Township, Camp Hill, Lower Allen Township, Shiremanstown, Mechanicsburg and Silver Spring Township, with Rye Township in Perry County to the north.
  • Roads: Interstate 81 crosses the north end with an exit at Mount Zion on Route 944, and Route 581 runs across the township with exits at Creekview Road, the Carlisle Pike (U.S. 11) and Route 641.

The area was settled in 1731 and incorporated on January 23, 1845. The Battle of Sporting Hill took place here in 1863, and the township became a first-class township on January 1, 1960. Growth since then has been steady: the Census count rose from 24,135 in 2000 to 32,761 in 2020.

Which school district serves Hampden Township homes?

The Cumberland Valley School District serves Hampden Township. Its school list includes Eagle View Middle School, Mountain View Middle School and Cumberland Valley High School, plus a group of elementary schools. School district boundaries matter for a sale because the district also sends its own real estate tax bill, covered below.

Hampden also keeps more than 100 acres of parks, including Hampden Pool and Park, Creekview Recreation Area, Salem Community Park and Conodoguinet Youth Park, and it runs Armitage Golf Club on Orrs Bridge Road. Buyers often ask about these, so mention the one closest to your street when you describe the house.

What property taxes and bills come with a Hampden Township house?

Three real estate bills reach a Hampden owner each year: a county bill that also carries the library and township charges, a school district bill, and a separate per capita tax for adults. The township tax collector's FAQ explains the schedule, and the county assesses every property at 100 percent of its 2010 value.

Hampden Township real estate bill calendar, from the township Tax Collector FAQ
BillIssued2 percent discountFace amount10 percent penalty starts
County, library and townshipMarch 1March 1 to April 30May 1 to June 30July 1
Cumberland Valley School DistrictJuly 1July 1 to August 31September 1 to October 31November 1

The same FAQ lists the combined county, library and township millage at 3.031 mills for 2025 (county 2.625, library 0.250, township 0.156) and the school district rate at 11.937 mills for 2024 to 2025. Apply those mills to the assessed value, not to the sale price.

  • County bills cover January 1 through December 31, and school bills cover July 1 through June 30.
  • The per capita tax is $10 at face for each resident 18 or older. It is not prorated, so someone who moves out of the township after March 1 still owes the full year.
  • Landlords must tell the tax collector about tenants over 18 under Chapter 24 of the township code.
  • The state Homestead credit on the school bill was $85.49 for 2024 for residents on file with the county assessor.

Before signing a sale contract, request a balance statement for your parcel from the tax collector. The Cumberland County Assessment Office, at (717) 240-6350, answers assessed value questions.

What township charges follow a Hampden house at sale?

Trash and stormwater are billed by the township and stay with the property, so settle them before the closing date. The township trash page lists each household's weekly pickup at $117.99 per quarter, and it includes one bulk item a week if you schedule it with the hauler.

The Sewer Authority's stormwater fee was set by a 2015 resolution at $13.25 per equivalent residential unit each quarter, and every single-family home counts as one unit of 3,534 square feet of impervious surface. Ask the township office about the sewer bill and any final reading when you set a closing date.

Leaf collection, yard waste and a bulk pickup schedule are on the township website. A clean, cleared yard helps a buyer walking the property, whether the buyer is a family or an investor.

Do permits and repairs matter before selling in Hampden Township?

Yes. The township's Community Development Department expects permits for most work above $500, and a buyer or lender may ask whether earlier projects were closed out. Its office works weekdays until 4:30 in the afternoon, and the phone is (717) 761-0119.

  • Building permits cover residential construction above $500 in total cost. Roof re-shingling that is not structural, window replacement, siding, gutters and like-for-like kitchen or bath replacement are listed exceptions.
  • Most standard residential permits are processed within 15 business days.
  • Zoning permits are needed for sheds, fences, accessory buildings and added impervious coverage.
  • A certificate of occupancy proves a building passed final inspection under the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code. The township says the owner, not the contractor, is responsible for making sure it was issued.

A deck, pool or addition that never got its last inspection can stall a financed sale. An all-cash buyer may accept that risk, but ask the department what it would take to close the file.

How does recording and transfer tax work in Cumberland County?

Your deed goes to the Cumberland County Recorder of Deeds, whose records reach back to 1750. In-person visits run weekdays until 4 in the afternoon and are by appointment, which you can set at 717-240-6370.

The state levies a 1 percent realty transfer tax, and the county recorder adds a local share that goes to school districts and municipalities. Property that heirs receive under a will or without one is exempt. The revenue department's Cumberland County valuation factor is 1.56 for deeds accepted in the year that began July 1, 2026.

Your title company can give you the exact local percentage and who pays each part.

Which sale route suits a Hampden Township house?

Three routes cover most Hampden sales. Which fits depends on the condition of the house and how soon you need to close.

  • Agent listing: often the top price for a tidy house, though you manage showings, an appraisal and a lender's schedule.
  • By owner: skips the listing fee, but marketing, forms and haggling are yours.
  • Cash offer: the buyer takes the house in its current state, with no showings or repair list, on a date you choose.

For a Hampden house with deferred repairs, an estate to settle or tenants in place, compare what you keep from each route, not the headline price.

More questions about Hampden, PA

Can a Hampden house be sold while a tax bill is unpaid?

Yes, a sale can go forward with an open balance. Call the township tax collector at (717) 737-4822 for the figure on your parcel and pass it to the title company so it appears on the settlement statement.

Who handles a wrong Hampden assessment?

Call the Cumberland County Assessment Office at (717) 240-6350. The township tax collector only bills the assessed value the county provides, so corrections and appeals start with the county.

Does the per capita tax follow me if I sell and move mid-year?

Yes, if you lived in the township on March 1 when the bills were mailed. The tax collector's FAQ says the bill is not prorated, so you owe the full amount to Hampden Township for that year, not to your new municipality.

Is a certificate of occupancy needed to sell in Hampden?

The township describes the certificate as proof that permitted work passed final inspection. If a past project needed a permit, call Community Development at (717) 761-0119 and confirm the final inspection happened before you list.

What does the Hampden stormwater fee cost?

The Sewer Authority set it at $13.25 per equivalent residential unit per quarter in 2015, with single-family homes counted as one unit. Confirm the present amount with the township before closing, since the authority can revise it.

What should I know before selling a house in Cranberry Township?

Cranberry is a fast-growing township in southwestern Butler County, about half an hour north of downtown Pittsburgh, and its housing market looks more like a family suburb than a small town. It covers roughly 22.8 square miles with almost no water, and it borders Jackson, Forward and Adams townships, Seven Fields, Pine and Marshall townships in Allegheny County, and New Sewickley Township in Beaver County.

Because Cranberry is a township with no separate city government, nearly every step of a sale runs through three offices: the township for permits and tax certifications, Butler County for assessments, deeds and delinquent taxes, and the Seneca Valley School District for school taxes. Knowing who handles what saves a surprising amount of time at closing.

If you own a house here and want to sell it, you can list it, sell it yourself, or take an as-is offer from a buyer. Each path has the same tax and paperwork steps, so it helps to know them before you compare offers.

Why did Cranberry grow so quickly?

The township was farmland before World War II. It took its name from the wild cranberries that once grew along Brush Creek. Its boundaries were redrawn in 1854, shrinking it from 81 to 25 square miles, and growth only took off after the western section of the Pennsylvania Turnpike opened in 1951 with an exit on Route 19.

Interstate 79 followed in 1966, crossing the Turnpike at the township's southern end, and Interstate 279 opened in 1989, cutting the drive to Pittsburgh to under half an hour. A nonprofit industrial development corporation formed by the township supervisors in the mid-1960s filled an industrial park, and office and retail followed.

  • More than 1,000 businesses operate in the township
  • About 20,500 jobs are located here, and more people commute in than commute out
  • Westinghouse Electric Company has its headquarters in Cranberry
  • Fernway and Fox Run are named neighborhoods that still appear on maps

What do Census figures show about Cranberry homes?

The Census Bureau estimates 35,244 people lived in Cranberry on July 1, 2025, up from 28,098 in 2010. Three out of four households own their home, and the median home value is above $420,000, which puts Cranberry well above most of Butler County.

Some 65.3 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and the mean commute is 27.1 minutes. For sellers, that means buyers are usually working households with mortgages, who care about school district boundaries, move-in condition and inspection results.

What taxes come due when a Cranberry house sells?

The township's own tax page lists a real estate transfer tax of 0.5 percent that goes to Cranberry, noting that the figure leaves out the state and school district shares. The Commonwealth takes 1 percent on top. Ask the Butler County Recorder of Deeds for the school district portion and the total on your deed, since the recorder collects the tax when the deed is filed.

The state Department of Revenue says both buyer and seller are legally responsible for the realty transfer tax, and some transfers are exempt, such as certain transfers between family members and property passed by will or intestacy. Your sales contract decides who pays.

  • County and township property tax: bills mailed March 1
  • Seneca Valley School District tax: bills mailed August 1
  • Township rate for real estate, apart from county and school: 15.75 mills
  • Earned income tax: 1 percent, split between township and school district (this one follows the owner's income, not the sale)

Your closing agent will prorate the current-year taxes between you and the buyer, so having the tax bills handy at the start speeds things up.

How do tax certifications and tax sales work in Cranberry?

An elected tax collector with an office in the Municipal Center on Rochester Road collects township, county and school taxes. The same office issues the certification required when a property or mobile home is sold or refinanced, reviewing the last three years of township, county and school tax records and breaking them down for the closing. The office works with real estate agents and closing attorneys, and appointments are available.

County and township bills offer a 2 percent discount within two months of the notice date. Payments after four months carry a 10 percent penalty. Taxes still unpaid after one year go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau, and a sheriff's sale follows if the balance remains unpaid for an additional year.

The Tax Claim Bureau holds its upset sale on the second Monday of September for properties two years delinquent. If a sale does not happen at that stage, the parcel goes to a judicial sale, then to a repository list. A seller with unpaid taxes should settle them or ask the Bureau for a payoff figure early, because the amount can include added costs.

How does Butler County assess property and handle appeals?

Butler County's Assessment Department builds the tax bills for the county, municipalities and school districts. Cranberry's township page notes that assessments are still based on 1969 dollars, which is why Butler County bills use mills against a base that does not track current market value.

The county assessment page lists the forms an owner may need: a Board of Assessment appeal form, a commercial or industrial appeal form, a mobile home appeal form, a homestead and farmstead exclusion application, and a change of address form. The office also publishes appeal hearing information and millage sheets.

Call the Butler County Assessment office before you assume anything about deadlines. It can confirm the current filing date and whether a recent sale changes how your property is reviewed. Ask the Seneca Valley School District about its homestead application window, since school districts run that program locally.

Which township rules affect the sale of a Cranberry house?

Cranberry's Code Administration staff review and inspect building, zoning, sign and fire permits and enforce the Property Code. The township follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code with the 2018 International Codes, effective October 1, 2018. Inspections are booked through the township's online portal at any hour.

Before you list, look at the work done on the house. Decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences all need residential permits, and a buyer's inspector will notice an unpermitted deck or a finished basement with no paperwork. The township's code of ordinances holds the fee schedule for permits, inspections and rentals.

  • Sidewalks belong to the abutting owner, who must clear debris and handle snow and ice removal
  • Home-based businesses have their own township page and rules
  • Mobile home removal permits come from the tax collector's office

Rental homes have fees in the ordinance schedule, so owners selling a tenant-occupied house should ask the Code Administration office what applies.

What are the ways to sell a Cranberry house?

A listing makes sense for a house in good condition that can wait for showings and a lender's appraisal. An as-is purchase suits an owner who needs a closing date: an inherited house, a relocation, a house with deferred repairs or one with unpaid taxes. In either case, compare offers by your net proceeds after transfer tax, payoffs, prorated taxes and repair credits.

Ask any buyer who is paying cash for proof of funds, the closing date, and who covers title and recording costs. Get the offer in writing before you stop marketing the house.

More questions about Cranberry, PA

Which county handles deeds and assessments for Cranberry Township?

Butler County. Its Recorder of Deeds records the deed and collects transfer tax, and its Assessment Department sets the assessment and prints the tax bills.

Who issues the tax certification when a Cranberry house sells?

The township's elected tax collector, whose office is in the Municipal Center. It reviews three years of township, county and school tax records and returns a breakdown for closing.

Which school district taxes a Cranberry house?

The Seneca Valley School District. Its tax notices are mailed August 1, with a discount through September 30 and face value through November 30, and the year ends December 31.

What happens if I owe back taxes on a Cranberry property?

Unpaid taxes go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau after one year. A sheriff's sale can follow, and the Bureau's upset sale covers properties two years behind. Pay or request a payoff figure before you list.

Does a deck or shed without a permit affect a sale in Cranberry?

It can. Cranberry requires residential permits for decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences, and an inspector may flag unpermitted work. Ask the township's Code Administration staff how to close it out.

Is a fast sale possible in Falls Township, PA?

It is. Falls Township owners can use an agent, handle the sale themselves, or accept cash from a buyer who takes the house as it is. The township asks for no home inspection, though a few resale steps must still be completed before closing.

Falls is a suburban Philadelphia township on the Delaware in Bucks County. Portions of Fairless Hills and Levittown are inside it, and a few addresses carry a Morrisville or Yardley mailing name though they lie in Falls. Residents numbered 34,716 in the 2020 Census and an estimated 34,282 by July 2025, down 1.3%.

How did Falls Township develop?

The township was chartered in 1692. Morrisville left it to become a borough in 1804, and Tullytown followed in 1891. Fallsington, a crossroads village, has stayed in continuous use since the colonial era. William Penn started building his Pennsbury Manor residence here in 1682, and the reconstructed site is open to the public.

Population stood at 3,540 in 1950 and 29,082 in 1960 as Fairless Hills and Levittown were built. Details a buyer will check:

  • Land and water: 26.6 square miles in total, 22.3 of land and 4.3 of water (16.11%), with Biles Island, Martins Creek and Queen Anne Creek among the features.
  • Highways: US 1 is a freeway across the north, US 13 follows the old King's Highway, and PA 32 starts at US 1 in the northeast corner.
  • Rail and bus: the Amtrak Northeast Corridor and SEPTA Trenton Line cross the township without a station in it. Levittown station is the nearest, and SEPTA buses 127 and 128 serve Falls.
  • Road upkeep: the township maintains 85.88 of its 131.48 public road miles.

What do the numbers say about Falls Township homes?

A typical owner's home in Falls was worth $361,900 for 2020 to 2024, and owners occupy 72.9% of homes. Households earn a median $93,223, and median gross rent is $1,465.

Falls Township by the numbers, Census QuickFacts
MeasureFalls township

Owners who still carry a mortgage pay a median $2,154 a month, against $808 for those who own free and clear. The population slipped slightly after 2020.

What must a Falls Township house pass before it is resold?

Four major components have to be certified before Falls issues a certificate of occupancy for a resale, and no township home inspection is required. A 2021 ordinance swapped the older resale inspection for certification of the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel. When the ordinance passed in January 2021, the township manager said a buyer's private inspection goes "far greater" than the township's, and that buyers are told of open violations or outstanding permit violations before they buy.

  • Who handles it: the Code Enforcement Department, which schedules use and occupancy, electrical and housing inspections and also takes permit applications.
  • Rentals: the ordinance also created a rental inspection program: apartment complexes get a yearly look at common areas, and any unit occupied three years or more gets an interior inspection.
  • Historic area: a Historic Architectural Review Board takes requests for review of plans, so ask whether your property falls under it.
  • Flood paperwork: the township posts a flood hazard area permit application and a FEMA substantial improvement form, relevant to a house near the river or a creek.

Ask the Code Enforcement Department which components your house must certify and whether any permit on the property was left open.

Does water or storm history matter in a Falls Township sale?

Buyers will ask about drainage and flood history, since water covers about 16% of the township and the climate station sits at 13 feet above sea level. Average precipitation is 47.78 inches a year, July is the wettest month, and the heaviest day since 1981 was August 27, 2011, at 6.49 inches. The warmest reading in that period, 103.4 degrees, came on June 7, 2010. Winter can bite as well: the coldest reading since 1981 was minus 10.2 degrees on January 22, 1984, in a township that sits in hardiness zone 7a, so the age of a heating system is a fair buyer question. The township also holds the easternmost point of Pennsylvania's southern half, a detail longtime owners like to mention.

Put what you know about basement water, sump pumps and past claims on the disclosure form. Keep permits and invoices for any storm repairs, and ask the township whether a flood hazard permit applies to your parcel.

How do Bucks County assessments and tax exclusions affect a Falls sale?

Values and appeals sit with the Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals at 55 East Court Street, Doylestown. Its 2026 annual appeal deadline fell on August 3, 2026, with a $75 per parcel fee that is not refunded, and any change applies from the 2027 tax year. The board convenes at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesdays of the month.

Acceptable proof of value is an appraisal by a Pennsylvania certified appraiser or sales of similar nearby properties from the last 18 months. An owner who bought within 18 months can add the settlement sheet, but it cannot stand alone.

  • Homestead: applications for the tax year starting July 1, 2027 are due March 1, 2027, and a newly recorded deed calls for a fresh application within 45 days.
  • New owners: Act 29 has a purchaser send contact information to the board within 30 days.

Pass the 45-day homestead rule on to your buyer, since a new deed starts the application over.

What transfer tax and state disclosure rules apply in Falls Township?

The state charges a 1% realty transfer tax, which the county Recorder of Deeds gathers with any local tax. Some family transfers and property passed by testate or intestate succession are exempt, and 15% of collections support the Keystone Recreation, Park and Conservation Fund. Ask the Recorder what local rate applies to your price.

For disclosure, 68 Pa.C.S. section 7312 allows a written amendment before the agreement is signed, and section 7307 obliges the seller to notify the buyer if facts change before final settlement. The law defines a material defect as a problem with a significant adverse effect on value or an unreasonable risk to people, and a system near the end of its useful life does not count by that alone. Municipalities may not add disclosure demands beyond the statute, except through ordinances that predate it.

When does a cash sale make sense in Falls Township?

It suits owners who want to sidestep repair bids and a buyer's financing contingency. Falls Township cases include an inherited house, a failed heating or sewer system that stalls the resale certificate, a rental unlikely to pass a township inspection, or a move on a fixed date. Measure the offer against a listing's net after repairs and transfer tax.

More questions about Falls, PA

Is a township home inspection needed to sell in Falls?

No. The township traded its resale inspection for certification of the heating system, chimney, sewer system and electrical panel, leaving any private inspection to buyer and seller.

What if the heating system or another component fails certification?

The certificate of occupancy waits until it is certified. Ask the Code Enforcement Department what repair or permit is needed, or sell as-is to a buyer who will finish the work.

What was the 2026 Bucks County appeal deadline?

August 3, 2026, and it has passed. Annual appeals go to the Board of Assessment Appeals, cost $75 per parcel and alter the assessment from the 2027 tax year.

Do Levittown and Fairless Hills belong to Falls Township?

Parts of both do. Pieces of Fairless Hills and Levittown lie inside the township, and the Morrisville and Yardley post office names also cover some Falls addresses.

How soon can a Falls Township sale close?

The contract sets the date, and a cash buyer has no lender to wait on. Title work, open permits and the resale certificate steps fix the earliest possible day.

What are my options for a fast sale in Lower Makefield Township?

Lower Makefield Township sellers can list with an agent, sell privately, or take a cash offer, and a cash sale is the shortest path because the closing date follows your calendar instead of a buyer's mortgage approval. The township's own sale steps are light: a moving permit, a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, and clean tax and utility balances.

Bucks County homes in this part of the Delaware Valley carry high values, so even a modest delay costs real carrying money in taxes, insurance and utilities. People who want a quick sale here usually have a reason beyond price: an estate that needs to be settled, a relocation, a divorce, a rental that has become a burden, or deferred repairs on a house that no longer fits the owner's plans.

  • Cash purchase: the buyer takes the house in its present condition and you set the closing date.
  • Agent listing: more exposure and often a higher price, with showings, repairs and a longer timeline.

What should I know about Lower Makefield Township before I sell?

The township covers about 18.3 square miles in Bucks County along the Delaware River, facing New Jersey across the water. It wraps around the borough of Yardley on the north, south and west, which is why most addresses carry a Yardley mailing label even though they are in Lower Makefield. Across the river are Hopewell Township, Ewing Township and Trenton, and on the Pennsylvania side the neighbors are Upper Makefield, Newtown, Middletown and Falls townships plus Morrisville.

Brock Creek, Common Creek, Core Creek and Jericho Creek run through it, and Edge Hill is a named local landform. Past and present villages include Schammels Corner and Woodside. The population rose from 25,083 in 1990 to 32,681 in 2000, and later office growth centered on the Stony Hill Road corridor near Interstate 295. Children attend the Pennsbury School District.

Interstate 295 is the main highway and crosses the Delaware on the Scudder Falls Bridge into New Jersey. PA Route 32 follows River Road along the water, PA Route 332 follows Newtown-Yardley Road through the middle, and US Route 1 clips the southern corner. As of 2018, 175.27 miles of public road ran through the township, and 138.20 miles of that were township maintained. SEPTA bus route 127 reaches the southern tip. The West Trenton regional rail line passes through the township without a station inside it, so commuters use Yardley station or Woodbourne station in Middletown Township. The area sits in hardiness zone 7a, so a buyer's inspector will look at roofs, gutters and basements with winter freezes in mind.

What do Census figures say about homes in Lower Makefield Township?

The Census Bureau estimated 34,028 residents on July 1, 2025. Of occupied housing, 87.6 percent is owner occupied, and the median value of an owner-occupied home was $630,200 over 2020 to 2024. Median gross rent was $2,340 and the median household income was $175,206 in 2024 dollars. A bachelor's degree or higher is held by 69.4 percent of adults, and 91.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

That profile means most sales are single-family homes where the owner lives, and values are well above most of Pennsylvania. Prices at this level make every percentage point of transfer tax and every month of carrying cost visible, so it pays to compare closing timelines as carefully as the offer price.

What taxes does a Lower Makefield property carry?

Real estate tax comes from three bills: township, county and the Pennsbury School District. The township tax collector page lists the 2025 combined rate at 256.403 mills, and the township levies no earned income tax.

One mill is one tenth of one percent of assessed value. Township and county bills are issued around March 1 for the calendar year, with a 2 percent discount for payment within two months, face amount within four months and a 10 percent penalty afterward. School bills are issued around July 1 for the school year. Unpaid taxes pass to the Bucks County Tax Claim Bureau after the collector's books close. When you sell, prorate these bills at settlement and ask the tax office at 267-274-1116 for current figures.

What does the township require when I sell?

The township's community development office lists three items for a sale, and it states that a resale use and occupancy certificate is not required in Lower Makefield Township. Confirm the current list with the office at 267-274-1100 before you schedule your closing, since a buyer's contract can add its own conditions.

  • A moving permit for both the buyer and the seller.
  • A sewer lateral inspection by the seller, to catch problems with the private line. Questions and submissions go to sewerlateral@lmt.org.
  • Calls to the taxing authorities and utility companies for any additional requirements they impose.

Allow time for a plumber to scope the line and for the township to review the report, since a failed line has to be fixed.

How does a property tax appeal work for Lower Makefield owners?

Bucks County sets annual appeals by a deadline in early August, and the 2026 deadline of August 3 has passed. Any change from a 2026 annual appeal takes effect in the 2027 tax year. Interim appeals follow the date printed on a recent assessment revision notice. The Board of Assessment Appeals meets on the first and third Tuesday of each month at the courthouse in Doylestown, and it can be reached at 215-348-6219.

Owner-occupants can also apply for the homestead and farmstead exclusion, which reduces the assessed value used for school tax. The county lists March 1 as the application deadline for the tax year that begins the following July 1. If you buy or sell an investment property, a Pennsylvania law added in 2026 asks owners to submit contact information to the Board within 30 days of a purchase, with owner-occupied homes excused.

What costs come with selling at closing?

The state transfer tax is 1 percent of the sale value, and the Lower Makefield Township page lists the local share as one half of one percent to the township and one half of one percent to the school district. On a $630,200 house, matching the township's median owner-occupied value, the combined 2 percent equals $12,604, split between buyer and seller by contract. Pennsylvania treats both parties as jointly responsible, so agree on who pays before signing.

Some transfers are exempt, including certain moves among family members and property passed by will or intestacy. Ask a title company to price the statement of value and recording fees at the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds, and check whether your sale involves a payoff, a lien or tenants.

More questions about Lower Makefield, PA

Does Lower Makefield Township require a resale certificate?

The township's community development FAQ says a resale use and occupancy certificate is not required. It does require a moving permit for buyer and seller and a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, so call the township office to confirm.

What is the transfer tax in Lower Makefield?

The state charges 1 percent, and the township page lists a local rate of one half percent for the township plus one half percent for the school district. That totals 2 percent of the sale price, divided by contract.

Who is responsible for the sewer lateral inspection?

The seller. The township expects the seller to inspect the private sewer line and submit the result, and its review can take time, so schedule the plumber early in your sale.

When can I appeal my Bucks County assessment?

Annual appeals are due in early August, and the 2026 deadline was August 3, so the next chance is the 2027 cycle. Interim appeals follow the date on an assessment revision notice.

Which school district serves Lower Makefield Township?

Pennsbury School District serves the township, and its 2025-2026 millage of 204.003 is the largest part of the combined 256.403 mills on a Lower Makefield tax bill.

What shapes a house sale in the city of Chester?

Chester is a dense river city in Delaware County, and what drives a sale there is local: an old housing stock, a city under state financial oversight, and a transfer tax that is higher than the county norm. The city covers about 6.0 square miles, of which 4.83 is land, and it lies along the Delaware River's western shore, between Philadelphia and Wilmington.

William Penn landed here in 1682, which makes Chester the oldest city in Pennsylvania. Chester Creek meets the Delaware inside the city limits, and the Port of Chester runs along the waterfront. Streets run on a simple grid: numbered streets go east and west, named streets go north and south, and the main spine is the Avenue of the States, which becomes Edgmont Avenue north of 9th Street.

An owner here has three routes: hire an agent, negotiate privately with a buyer, or take an as-is cash purchase. The right one turns on the roof, plumbing and wiring, any unpaid taxes, and your deadline.

How did Chester's industrial past shape its housing?

Chester grew around shipyards, rolling mills and textile mills along Chester Creek. During the two world wars, factory and dock jobs pulled in workers from southern and eastern Europe and from the American South, and the city's population went from 38,537 in 1910 to 58,030 in 1920. The Census count peaked at 66,039 in 1950.

Since then the city has lost people in nearly every decade, ending at 32,605 in 2020. Much of the housing was built for that larger workforce: rowhouses and twins on narrow lots, many a century old. Buyers and inspectors in Chester tend to look closely at foundations, old heating systems, lead paint and aging sewer laterals.

The waterfront has changed too. The Philadelphia Union plays at Subaru Park beside the Commodore Barry Bridge, Harrah's Philadelphia opened in 2008, and Widener University anchors the west side of the city.

  • Peak population: 66,039 in 1950
  • 2020 Census count: 32,605
  • Incorporated as a city on February 14, 1866
  • Water access that built the economy: the Delaware River and Chester Creek

How do Chester home values and rents compare?

The Census Bureau's figures for the city show more renters than owners and home values well below the Philadelphia suburbs next door. That matters for pricing: a buyer looking at a Chester rowhouse is comparing it with other Chester rowhouses, not with Media or Wallingford.

With 60 percent of households renting, a large share of the city's houses are investor-owned or have a tenant living in them. Sellers with occupied units should plan around the tenant's lease and the city's rental registration rules described below.

How does the city's financial recovery status affect a seller?

The effect lands on the tax side more than on the sale. Pennsylvania designated Chester a financially distressed municipality in 1995, declared a fiscal emergency in 2020, and in 2022 the city filed for Chapter 9 bankruptcy. The city's website lists meetings of the Municipal Financial Recovery Advisory Committee and identifies a receiver for the city, so the recovery process is still an active part of local government.

The practical points are narrow. Property tax rates and city fees can change as the recovery plan is revised, so an old tax bill is a weak guide to what the next owner will carry. Ask the City of Chester finance office for the current city millage, and ask the Delaware County treasurer for the county and school figures, when you work out your net.

None of this stops a sale. What a title company will want is a clean tax picture, so unpaid city bills, rubbish fees and liens should be sorted out before settlement.

What is the transfer tax on a Chester sale?

Chester is one of four Delaware County municipalities that charge more than the standard local rate: 1.5 percent for the city side, effective September 1, 2023, on top of the 1 percent that goes to the Commonwealth. That is 2.5 percent of the sale price in total, compared with 2 percent in most of the county.

The Delaware County Recorder of Deeds lists only four exceptions to its standard 1 percent local rate: Chester, Radnor, Upper Darby and Upper Providence. On a $90,000 sale, the difference between a 2 percent and a 2.5 percent total is $450.

Under the Commonwealth's rules the grantor and the grantee share legal liability, so the agreement of sale should name who pays. Certain family transfers and inherited property are exempt. For a doubtful case, the county sends questions to the revenue department's realty transfer tax unit at RA-BITRealtyTransferTax@pa.gov.

What city paperwork and rules apply to a Chester house?

The city's Licenses and Inspections department handles permits, rental registration and several exemption forms. Its page lists the forms a seller or landlord is most likely to touch.

  • Building permit application and the residential permit fee schedule
  • Rental registration application, FAQ, letter and a residential rental licensing policy summary
  • Use and occupancy fee schedule and a commercial use and occupancy permit form
  • Contractor license application
  • Homeowner exemption form and a senior citizen disability exemption form for residential property

If the house is rented, find out whether the unit is registered before you list it, because a buyer's lender or title agent may ask. If you did work on the house without a permit, contact L&I at City Hall before you market the property. Open permits are easier to close out while you still control the building.

The city assessor's page also posts the conditions and bid forms for repository properties, which are parcels that did not sell at county tax sales, along with a LERTA application for tax abatement on improvements. Those are useful if your house has sat vacant or you are buying next door.

How do Chester property tax bills and appeals work?

Chester property is assessed by Delaware County. The county's tax bill is mailed on February 1, and paying within 60 days earns a 2 percent discount; after April 1 the bill is due at face value by June 1. Chester Upland School District covers the city, Chester Township and Upland borough, and the city's website carries a link to pay property tax.

The county's Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion lowers the assessed value on a primary residence. The application comes from your school district, and the window runs every year from December 15 to March 1. If you are about to sell, the exclusion matters less to you than to the buyer, who will need to apply in their own name.

An assessment challenge is filed at the Board in Media, on paper with an original signature. Faxed or e-mailed forms are rejected, and because postmarks can lag, the county suggests hand delivery or a counter receipt at the post office. If you disagree with the Board's findings, you have 30 days to go to court. Look at the notice you were mailed for the filing date.

Does Chester's riverfront location affect the condition of a house?

It can. Chester is low and sits where Chester Creek and Ridley Creek reach the Delaware River, so flood exposure varies a lot by block. The climate is humid subtropical, averaging about 43.7 inches of precipitation a year, with July highs near 87 degrees. Damp basements, sump pumps and old drainage are routine inspection topics.

Before you list, find out whether your address is in a mapped flood zone and whether the house carries flood insurance. A buyer's lender will check the same thing.

Interstate 95 has three exits serving Highland Avenue, Kerlin Street and Edgmont Avenue, and U.S. 13 and U.S. 322 also pass through, with the Commodore Barry Bridge linking to New Jersey.

Which sale route fits a Chester owner in a hurry?

Putting the house on the market gives the widest exposure but needs showings, repairs and a lender's approval, which can stretch the timeline by months. An investor or cash purchase gives up some price for speed and certainty, and the buyer generally accepts the property with its flaws.

  • Inherited house with several heirs: confirm who holds title and whether the estate is open before accepting any offer
  • Tenant in place: read the lease and plan for notice requirements
  • Back taxes or city liens: get payoff figures from the county and the city
  • Code or permit issues: ask L&I what is open on the address

Whatever you pick, line up the offers by the check you would actually receive after transfer tax, payoffs and credits.

More questions about Chester, PA

How much is the transfer tax if I sell a house in Chester?

The combined rate is 2.5 percent: 1 percent to the state and 1.5 percent to the local side, which has applied in Chester since September 1, 2023. The contract decides who pays, though the state holds both parties responsible.

Can I sell a Chester house that has a tenant living in it?

Yes. The lease usually continues with the new owner unless it ends or the tenant agrees to leave. Check whether the unit is registered with the city's L&I department before you list.

Who do I ask about property taxes on a Chester house?

Start with the Delaware County treasurer and Board of Assessment in Media for county and school figures, and the City of Chester finance office for city charges. Both can confirm balances before closing.

Does Chester's bankruptcy stop me from selling?

No. Houses sell in Chester under the same Pennsylvania rules as elsewhere. The recovery process mainly affects city tax rates and fees, so confirm current figures before you price the house.

How do I claim the homestead exclusion on a Chester home?

Request the application from the Chester Upland School District between December 15 and March 1, then send it to the county Board of Assessment in Media. The county replies within 30 days.

What is the quickest way to sell a house in Lower Macungie Township?

Owners here choose between an agent listing, a private sale and a cash offer, and the cash route usually closes soonest because no buyer's lender is waiting on an appraisal. Whichever route you pick in Lower Macungie Township, the township's building sewer inspection and the deed recording at the county Recorder of Deeds still have to happen before the keys change hands.

Lower Macungie sits in southern Lehigh County, about 7 miles southwest of Allentown. The township grew from 16,871 residents in 1990 to 30,633 in 2010, so a large share of the housing stock is relatively recent. Sellers who ask for a fast close are often handling an inherited house, a job move, a divorce, a rental with tenants, or a roof and mechanical systems that need money they would rather not spend.

What is Lower Macungie Township like for a home seller?

It is a residential township of about 22.5 square miles with a mix of subdivisions, farmland and light industry. Little Lehigh Creek and Swabia Creek drain through it, South Mountain crosses the southern edge just below the boroughs of Macungie and Alburtis, and Alburtis sits entirely inside the township boundary. The Rodale Organic Gardening Experimental Farm in the township earned a listing on the federal historic register in 1999.

Students attend the East Penn School District. Ninth through twelfth graders go to Emmaus High School, middle schoolers go to Eyer Middle School or Lower Macungie Middle School, and the township has Wescosville and Willow Lane elementary schools. Buyers shopping the area often start with that district name, so it belongs in any listing or offer conversation.

Getting around is straightforward for commuters. Interstate 78 touches the extreme northern tip, PA Route 309 runs with it there, and US 222 crosses east to west. Local north to south routes include Route 100, Spring Creek Road, Willow Road and Brookside Road. Of 166.31 miles of public road, 125.26 miles are maintained by the township itself. LANta bus route 322 serves the northern tier. Police coverage has come from the Pennsylvania State Police rather than a township department.

The economy leans on manufacturing. Mack Trucks has its primary manufacturing facilities here, and Smooth-On and Allen Organ are also based in the township. Winters are cold and summers are warm and humid: the township sits in hardiness zone 6b with January averages near 29 degrees and July near 74 degrees, which is worth remembering when a buyer's inspector looks at the roof, gutters and basement.

What do Census figures show about housing in Lower Macungie Township?

The Census Bureau puts Lower Macungie Township at 33,507 people in its 2025 estimate, up 3.3 percent from the 2020 base. Housing here is overwhelmingly owner occupied, which means most sales are a family selling the home they live in.

Which inspection is required before a Lower Macungie house sells?

The township requires a building sewer inspection before a property is sold or transferred. The inspection looks at the private sewer line that runs from the house to the township's sewer lateral, a pipe the owner, not the township, is responsible for.

  • A licensed Journeyman or Master Plumber must perform the video inspection and submit a complete Building Sewer Inspection Report, a copy of the video and proof of licensure to the township.
  • Electronic video files are not accepted. The township keeps a physical copy, preferably on a USB flash drive, in the property file for at least five years.
  • Public works staff review the submission and issue a pass or fail letter to the owner by mail, and by email if an address was supplied on the report.
  • If the line fails, the owner is responsible for the repairs before the sale. A passing result is valid for up to two years.

The township's own page lists plumbers who have supplied proof of licensure for these inspections, and you may hire a plumber who is not on that list if the plumber submits proof of licensure. The program exists because stormwater and groundwater entering private lines contribute to overflows at the Allentown wastewater plant that serves the area. The ordinance also covers transfer without inspection, so read it or call the township office at 610-966-4343 before you assume anything about timing.

What bills and taxes come up at a Lower Macungie closing?

Expect a sewer and trash certification, a sewer inspection record, and two layers of transfer tax. Each has its own office and its own lead time, so start them as soon as you have a signed agreement.

  • Sewer and trash certification: the township's utility billing office issues it for a sale or refinance for a $50 fee, and the check has to arrive before processing starts. Sewer and trash bills go out quarterly and are due within 30 days.
  • Past due utility balances: amounts more than 90 days late move to a collection law firm and stop appearing on township invoices, so clear them before closing.
  • Pennsylvania realty transfer tax: 1 percent of the value, collected by the county Recorder of Deeds, and both buyer and seller are jointly liable.
  • Local transfer tax: the township ordinance sets its share at one half of one percent, and the township and any other taxing body together may not exceed 1 percent. Ask your title company for the school district's share and who pays what under your contract.

Water is billed separately by Lehigh County Authority, so a final water reading is a separate call. Transfers between certain family members, and property passed by will or intestacy, are among the exempt categories on the state's list, which matters for inherited houses.

How do property taxes and assessment appeals work in Lower Macungie?

Lehigh County assesses at 100 percent of fair market value as of a 2013 base year, the date of its last countywide reassessment, so your assessed value is a figure from that year adjusted for new construction or demolition. The Board of Assessment Appeals accepts only an original signed appeal with the filing fee received on or before August 1 each year. Postmarks and faxed appeals do not count as timely. Interim appeals are due by the date printed on a Change of Assessment Notice.

If you are selling a rental or other property you do not live in, note that a 2026 Pennsylvania law requires non-owner-occupant owners to file contact information with the county within 30 days of buying. Owner-occupied principal residences are exempt, so the rule matters mostly to the investor who buys from you.

What if my Lower Macungie house needs repairs or has tenants?

You can still sell it, and the sewer line is the first item to sort out. Order the video inspection early, because a failed line means repair work before closing and the township mails the pass or fail letter, which takes time. If a buyer will take the house as-is, ask whether that includes sewer repairs and who pays, and put the answer in the contract.

For tenants, review the lease end date and security deposit handling with your attorney, and ask the township office about any rental rules that apply to the address. Keep copies of the sewer inspection letter, the utility certification and the deed, since the buyer's title company will ask for them.

More questions about Lower Macungie, PA

Do I need an inspection to sell a house in Lower Macungie Township?

Yes, a building sewer video inspection by a licensed plumber is required before a sale or transfer. The township reviews it and mails a pass or fail letter, and a passing result stays valid for up to two years.

Who pays the transfer tax when selling in Lower Macungie?

The contract decides, but the law makes buyer and seller jointly liable. The state rate is 1 percent and the township's local rate is one half of one percent, with the county Recorder of Deeds collecting at recording.

How much is the sewer and trash certification in Lower Macungie?

The township charges $50 for a sewer and trash certification used for a sale or refinance. Email the utility billing office and mail the check, which must arrive before processing begins.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Lehigh County?

Lehigh County takes annual appeals on or before August 1 of each year. The original signed form and filing fee must be received by then, because postmarks and faxes are not accepted.

Which school district serves Lower Macungie Township?

East Penn School District serves it. High school students go to Emmaus High School, and the township has Eyer Middle School, Lower Macungie Middle School, Wescosville Elementary and Willow Lane Elementary nearby.

What is it like to sell a house in Warminster, PA?

Warminster is a Bucks County township of 10 square miles and an estimated 33,254 residents, and a sale there starts with the township's Licenses and Inspections Department, which expects a permit application for any property being sold. Applications go in online, and the department answers questions at 215-443-5423. After that, the sale follows Pennsylvania's normal disclosure, recording and tax steps.

The township has been on the map since 1711, when its borders were set, and it started as farmland under early English and Scotch-Irish settlers. Almost all of its housing came later. As recently as 1955 it had no residential subdivisions and one housing complex, and then the population jumped from 7,127 in 1950 to 34,900 in 1970. Most houses you will see on a listing sheet come from that postwar build-out.

Why did Warminster grow so fast, and what does that mean for sellers?

The Navy's presence at the Johnsville site drove the township's mid-century growth, and that shapes today's housing stock. The U.S. Navy took over an industrial site from Brewster Aeronautical Corporation in 1943, and the Naval Air Warfare Center there operated until 1996. The same site later trained astronauts for the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programs. Today the township's larger employers include ABB, Burpee Seeds, CRC Industries, Havis and a Penn State research laboratory.

One local issue deserves a straight answer in any sale. Several of the township's groundwater wells have been contaminated with PFOS and PFOA from the former Navy site, the Navy paid for treatment systems, and the Warminster Municipal Authority now buys more water from the North Wales Water Authority. The authority supplies water and sewer to about 10,300 customers. If your house is on public water, buyers may ask about it, so keep a recent water bill and the authority's contact details ready.

  • Neighbors include Warrington, Warwick, Ivyland, Northampton, Upper Southampton, Hatboro and Horsham.
  • Villages inside the township include Davisville, Hartsville, Johnsville, Rosewood Park and Warminster Heights.
  • The township maintains 13 parks covering 420 acres, led by the 243-acre Warminster Community Park.

What do Census figures show for Warminster homes?

Warminster has the highest share of residents age 65 and older of the four townships in this Census comparison, which points to a steady flow of long-held homes coming to market. These figures come from Census Bureau QuickFacts.

How do I get the township permit needed to sell in Warminster?

You apply through the township's online portal, and the Licenses and Inspections Department handles the review. Its page says plainly that making changes, renting a property or selling a property each need a permit, and that applications are submitted online. Staff can tell you which permit fits your situation if you call before applying.

Take these steps in order:

  • Call 215-443-5423 or email the department before you list so you know the permit name and fee for a residential sale.
  • Submit the application online and pay the fee through the portal.
  • Ask whether an inspection is part of the process, schedule it if so, and fix anything it flags.
  • Give your agent or settlement attorney a copy of the approved permit for the closing file.

Start the application early. If repairs are needed, time them against your settlement date, since a closing date in the agreement of sale does not move on its own.

Which schools and transit serve Warminster?

Warminster is part of the Centennial School District. The township's public schools are Davis, McDonald and Willow Dale elementary schools, Log College Middle School and William Tennent High School. Archbishop Wood Catholic High School and Nativity of Our Lord School are the parochial options inside the township.

For commuters, SEPTA's Warminster station is the terminus of the Warminster Line into Center City Philadelphia, and City Bus Route 22 runs south from the township through Willow Grove to North Philadelphia. The DART East bus runs weekdays along PA 132. Major roads include PA 132 (Street Road), PA 263 (York Road) and PA 332 (Jacksonville Road), and the township maintains 100.83 of its 113.97 miles of public roads. PECO supplies electricity and gas, and trash service runs under a township contract.

What do I owe at closing and how do Bucks County rules apply?

Bucks County's recorder says the realty transfer tax is 2 percent, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid when the deed is recorded. It is a tax on the value conveyed, which is not always the sale price, and the sale agreement usually divides it between buyer and seller. Since January 2026 the recorder no longer takes personal checks for the tax: cash in the office, cashier's check, money order or credit card only.

Family transfers can be exempt, but you must still present the state's Statement of Value (REV-183) where the exemption is not stated in the deed. Your attorney or title agent handles that paperwork. The seller must also deliver the property disclosure statement under 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303 before the agreement is signed, and Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information.

On the assessment side, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, which has passed, and annual appeal changes take effect the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year starting July 1. Buyers must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of purchase under Act 29, so tell your buyer.

Should I list or sell as-is in Warminster?

Listing suits a house in good condition on a street with recent sales, and an as-is cash sale suits a house that needs work or a seller on a short clock. Cash buyers usually offer less than a repaired, listed house would bring, in exchange for speed and fewer contingencies. Ask any buyer who takes the house as-is how the township permit will be handled.

  • Ask for a written offer with a closing date and proof of funds.
  • Find out whether the buyer will accept a house that has not yet received the township permit and who handles it.
  • Compare the offer against a net sheet for a listing sale, including permit costs and repairs.

More questions about Warminster, PA

Does Warminster require a permit to sell a house?

Yes. The Licenses and Inspections Department says selling a property needs a permit, and applications are made online. Call 215-443-5423 before applying to confirm the permit type and fee.

What is a typical home value in Warminster?

Warminster owners report a midpoint home value of $418,600 for 2020 to 2024. Your price depends on condition and nearby sales, so the median is only a reference point.

Should I mention the PFOS and PFOA wells to Warminster buyers?

Be ready to discuss it. The Warminster Municipal Authority has closed wells with PFOS and PFOA contamination from the former Navy site, installed treatment systems paid for by the Navy, and buys more water from a neighboring authority. Direct buyers to the authority for current water quality reports.

Where do I record the deed for a Warminster house?

At the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds, usually through your title company or attorney. The recorder collects the 2 percent transfer tax at recording and no longer accepts personal checks for it.

Can I sell a Warminster house that I inherited?

Yes, once the person with authority over the estate signs. Pennsylvania's disclosure chapter exempts transfers by an estate fiduciary, though many sellers still give buyers a condition statement. Ask the estate's attorney who may sign.

What should I know before selling a house in Radnor Township?

Radnor is a Main Line township in Delaware County with high home values, a mandatory township certificate for every resale, and a transfer tax that runs above the county default. A seller who plans around those three items can move quickly, whether the house goes on the market, sells to a neighbor, or goes to a cash buyer.

The township covers about 13.8 square miles and includes Wayne, St. Davids, Rosemont, Ithan, Garrett Hill and Villanova. It is home rule, run by a Board of Commissioners, and it was laid out in 1682 as part of the Welsh Tract. Lancaster Avenue follows the route of the 1794 Philadelphia and Lancaster Turnpike, and the Paoli/Thorndale rail line gave the area its commuter character in the nineteenth century.

Selling fast here mostly comes down to paperwork timing. Buyers, lenders and the township each have steps that can add days, and the sections below set them out in the order you will meet them.

What does the Census say about Radnor homes and owners?

Radnor is an expensive, owner-heavy market, and the figures below explain why pricing and buyer financing look different here than in much of Delaware County.

Radnor township housing and population snapshot (U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, 2020-2024 estimates unless noted)
MeasureRadnor
