A median value above $800,000 means many sales involve jumbo loans, appraisal scrutiny and long inspection lists. About a third of households rent, so investors and landlords are a real part of the buyer pool near Villanova University and Eastern University.

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell in Radnor?

Yes. The township's FAQ confirms that use and occupancy permits are required for resales, and the Engineering Department issues them. No new owner may occupy the property until the certificate is out.

The Engineering Department's transfer page sets the sequence:

  • The seller files the application at least 10 business days before settlement. The owner signs it, and the fee is $150.
  • Filing 10 days or less before settlement triggers a $300 expedite fee.
  • The township inspects for house number display and public sidewalk condition, then sends a violation notice for anything that needs repair.
  • If sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before closing, money goes into escrow with the department, and a sidewalk permit is needed for the work.
  • Sellers and buyers both sign a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification, and the application is not accepted unless the form, the fee and the signed application arrive together.
  • The owner books an inside look at the sanitary sewer soil pipe to confirm there are no illegal connections, and sump pumps must be disconnected from the sanitary system under Chapter 235 of the township code.

Call the Engineering Department at 610-688-5600, extension 129, to book the sewer appointment. Do it the day you file, because that appointment is the step most likely to push a closing date.

How much is the transfer tax when I sell in Radnor?

Delaware County's Recorder of Deeds lists the state share at 1% and the local share at 1%, with Radnor Township named as an exception at 1.5%. On a sale at the median value above, each additional half percent of local tax is about $4,200, so confirm the exact split with the Recorder before you set a net-proceeds number.

The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue explains that the county Recorder collects the state's 1% along with any local tax. Both the seller (grantor) and the buyer (grantee) are jointly liable, which is why a sales agreement states who pays. Certain transfers between family members, and property passed by will or intestate succession, are exempt under state rules, so an inherited house moving to an heir is treated differently from a market sale.

The county's recording office is at the Government Center in Media, and its transfer tax page lists the state's Statement of Value form (REV-183) for deeds that do not state full consideration. If a deed leaves the price off, that form is what carries the value to the Recorder.

When are Radnor property taxes due, and how do appeals work?

Township bills go out on or before February 1, and the face amount is due May 31. According to the township's FAQ, paying by March 31 earns a 2% discount, and a 10% penalty applies after May 31. The Radnor School District bills and collects its own tax separately, with school bills mailed in July.

An unpaid bill becomes a lien if it is not paid by the end of the calendar year, and the Delaware County Tax Claim Bureau adds interest and penalties. When a house sells, the township asks that you return the bill with the new owner's name, because the Recorder can take more than 60 days to process a title transfer.

  • Assessment appeals go to the Delaware County Board of Assessment Appeals before August 1 for a value effective the following January 1.
  • An appeal does not pause the bill. You pay what is billed and receive a refund or credit if the value drops.
  • The county reassessment that ran from December 2017 to 2020 took effect in January 2021, so current values reflect that base year.
  • A tax certification from the township finance office costs $25 per parcel, and title companies typically request one.

Sewer and stormwater are billed together on a separate mailing around April 1, due May 31. The stormwater charge depends on parcel size, and it applies to all developed properties in the township.

Which neighborhoods and schools affect a Radnor sale?

Schools drive demand more than any other local factor. Public students attend the Radnor Township School District, which runs Radnor High School, Radnor Middle School, and Radnor, Ithan and Wayne elementary schools. Private options inside the township include Archbishop John Carroll High School, the Agnes Irwin School, the Hill Top Preparatory School and the Valley Forge Military Academy and College.

Buyer groups differ by area. Downtown Wayne has historic districts, with North Wayne and South Wayne as residential pockets around a commercial core. St. Davids and Ithan are quieter residential neighborhoods, while Villanova and Garrett Hill have long-standing Catholic parish communities. Strafford, Bryn Mawr and Villanova straddle township lines, so a listing's mailing address may not match its municipality, and that matters for transfer tax and the certificate.

Commuting helps resale. The township has SEPTA Regional Rail stops at Wayne, St. Davids, Radnor and Villanova, plus seven Norristown High Speed Line stations. U.S. 30 runs along Lancaster Avenue, Route 320 follows Sproul and Spring Mill Roads, and Interstate 476 meets U.S. 30 inside the township.

Which selling route fits a Radnor house?

Three paths cover most sellers, and each handles the township certificate differently.

  • A traditional listing suits houses in good repair. The agent coordinates the certificate, but showings, inspection requests and buyer financing set the schedule.
  • A for-sale-by-owner sale saves the commission and leaves you running the certificate, the sewer inspection and the transfer tax paperwork yourself.
  • A cash sale to a company that buys as-is removes lender timing and repairs from the buyer side. The seller still files the township application and still schedules the sewer check, so ask any buyer who does the filing and who pays any sidewalk escrow.

Compare offers on net proceeds, not headline price. Subtract the transfer tax, the $150 or $300 township fee, any sidewalk or sewer repairs, and unpaid taxes before you decide.

More questions about Radnor, PA

Who applies for the certificate of occupancy in Radnor?

The seller does. The application goes to the Radnor Engineering Department at least 10 business days before settlement, signed by the owner, with the $150 fee and the smoke detector and carbon monoxide form signed by seller and buyer.

What happens if my sidewalk is damaged at the time of sale?

The township sends a violation notice after its inspection. If the sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before settlement, money is placed in escrow with the Engineering Department, and a sidewalk permit is required for the repair.

Is Radnor's transfer tax higher than the rest of Delaware County?

Yes. The county's Recorder of Deeds shows most municipalities at the 1% default local share and lists Radnor Township at 1.5%, plus the 1% state tax. Ask the Recorder to confirm the combined figure for your deed.

Can I sell a Radnor house that needs repairs?

Yes, but the sewer connection, sidewalk and house number items flagged by the township still have to be corrected or escrowed before the certificate is released. Cosmetic and structural repairs are a matter between you and the buyer.

Where do I get a Radnor tax certification for closing?

From the Radnor Township finance office at 301 Iven Avenue in Wayne. The township charges $25 per certification, and you need the parcel (folio) number, the owner name and the address.

How does selling a house in Mt. Lebanon work?

A Mt. Lebanon sale follows the usual Pennsylvania routes of listing with an agent, selling directly to a buyer, or taking a cash offer, with a few municipal and county steps layered on top. Mt. Lebanon is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, roughly four to six miles south of downtown Pittsburgh, and its Inspection Office, tax office and county records all influence the closing date.

The sections below cover the local pieces a seller should line up first, from open permits to the 2026 tax rates and the county appeal calendar.

What kind of homes do Mt. Lebanon sellers own?

Most Mt. Lebanon houses are early twentieth century commuter homes. The first streetcar line to Pittsburgh opened on July 1, 1901, the Liberty Tubes followed in 1924, and the population jumped from 2,258 in 1920 to 13,403 in 1930, according to Wikipedia. The municipality says 4,400 properties sit inside a National Register historic district established in 2014, with Foursquare, Tudor, Colonial Revival, Bungalow and Dutch Colonial styles all common.

Age shows up when a buyer inspects roofs, windows, porches, masonry and basement drainage. The municipality publishes an illustrated design guide for historic homes and a contractor vetting guide, which helps an owner decide whether to renovate before listing or sell without touching it.

Census QuickFacts puts the 2020 to 2024 typical value of an owned home in Mount Lebanon township at $378,300, with 72.3 percent of units occupied by owners across 13,646 households. Median household income over the same period was $123,771, and 67.9 percent of adults 25 and older have finished a four-year degree.

Which Mt. Lebanon permits and inspections can delay a closing?

Open building permits are the most common local snag, because the Inspection Office states that lien letters will not be issued while permits are open. A seller who finished a deck, remodel, furnace swap or fence should confirm every final inspection is on record before setting a settlement date.

  • Work started without a permit can draw fines set by the magisterial district judge, so ask the Inspection Office how to regularize it.
  • Residential building permits generally issue within 15 business days, while zoning permits for items such as an air conditioning unit, driveway, fence or shed take up to 30 days.
  • Fences in single-family districts may reach six feet in side and rear yards, are not allowed in front yards, and cannot be solid.
  • A front porch may extend no more than 10 feet into the front yard, and new or replaced front stairs need a building permit.
  • Every private swimming pool carries an annual operation permit and a safety inspection.

On the first Wednesday of each month the office holds Inspections Consultations from 2 to 5 p.m. Appointments last 30 minutes and require preregistering at 412-343-3408.

What do Mt. Lebanon owners pay in property tax?

A Mt. Lebanon parcel carried a combined 42.963 mills in 2026, divided among the municipality, the school district and Allegheny County. The municipal tax office, on the ground floor of the municipal building, collects real estate tax for both the municipality and the Mt. Lebanon School District.

2026 real estate millage on a Mt. Lebanon parcel (source: Mt. Lebanon tax office)
Taxing bodyMills
Mt. Lebanon Municipality4.50
Mt. Lebanon School District32.033
Allegheny County6.43
Combined42.963

Hypothetically, a house with a county assessed value of $200,000 would produce about $8,593 a year at that combined rate. Collection runs from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount period through July 31, a face period from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty after that. The school portion can be paid in installments, and unpaid balances move to private delinquent collectors each March.

The tax office can supply a bill or receipt, and a title company will usually ask for one before closing. For address changes, the Allegheny County Treasurer handles the request.

How are Mt. Lebanon assessments set, and when can an owner appeal?

Allegheny County assesses every Mt. Lebanon parcel on a 2012 base year, and the last county-wide reassessment took place in 2013. The county office may change a value only for omissions, mathematical or clerical errors, physical changes such as demolitions or building permits, and the occasional interim request from a school district or municipality.

The Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears challenges. The annual window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 through September 1, 2026, and the board mails residential hearing notices at least 14 days ahead. It applies a common level ratio to the market value in appeals, and that ratio is 49.3 percent for the 2027 tax year.

A catastrophic loss such as a fire allows a reduction request within six months of the event. Buyers of non-owner-occupied property now face a registry rule too: under Act 29 of 2026, effective September 18, 2026, they must send contact details to the chief assessor within 30 days of purchase, and a false filing can bring a fine up to $500.

What transfer taxes and recording steps apply to a Mt. Lebanon sale?

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax starts at 1 percent of the value transferred, and Allegheny County adds municipal and school district shares so the total ranges from 2 to 5 percent across the county. The county Department of Real Estate collects both the state and local portions at recording, and the tax goes on a separate check from the recording fees.

The county's own example splits a 2 percent total into 1 percent to the state, half a percent to the township and half a percent to the school district. Ask the Department of Real Estate for the rate list entry covering Mt. Lebanon and its school district, since the local share is set by those bodies.

Some family transfers are exempt, and a Statement of Value (form REV-183) is required when the deed lists no consideration or claims an exemption. The state notes that grantor and grantee are jointly liable, so the settlement statement should show who pays.

Which parts of Mt. Lebanon draw buyers?

Buyers tend to focus on walkable blocks near Uptown, which runs along Washington Road (U.S. Route 19 Truck) and holds 182 businesses and 72 storefronts. Beverly Road forms a second commercial strip on the north side, and the Red Line light rail stops at Mt. Lebanon Station beneath Uptown, running through the Mt. Lebanon Tunnel toward the city.

Named neighborhoods include Virginia Manor, Hoodridge, Mission Hills, Seminole Hills, Beverly Heights and Washington Park. The Mt. Lebanon School District operates seven elementary schools, two middle schools and one high school, and it is a walking district with no school bus service. Fifteen parks cover about 200 acres.

Retail news is also local: on October 29, 2026, the municipality posted that Wegmans will anchor a reimagined Galleria of Mt. Lebanon, with renovations expected to begin in 2028.

When does a cash sale fit a Mt. Lebanon house?

Cash works best when the closing date or the property's shape matters more than a retail price. A cash buyer purchases as is, so repairs and permit clean-up fall into the buyer's own plan. Typical situations include:

  • An inherited house with older systems that no one in the family wants to renovate.
  • A property with unfinished or unpermitted work that would take weeks of Inspection Office review.
  • A tenant-occupied house where the owner wants out of landlord duties.
  • A move on a short timeline, such as a job change that leaves two mortgages.

Whoever buys, ask the Inspection Office whether any permit is open before agreeing on a closing date, since municipal lien letters are part of the paperwork.

More questions about Mount Lebanon, PA

Does Mt. Lebanon require a resale inspection before I sell?

The municipality's permit page describes a Certificate of Occupancy for changes of use, enlarged buildings and new construction, and it does not list one for an ordinary resale. It does say lien letters are withheld while permits are open, so close those out first and call the Inspection Office at 412-343-3408 to confirm anything specific to your address.

When are Mt. Lebanon property taxes due?

Real estate tax is collected from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount through July 31, face value from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty afterward. School district tax can be paid in three installments, due September 30, December 31 and February 28.

What starts an Allegheny County assessment appeal for a Mt. Lebanon home?

File with Allegheny County's Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review during the annual summer window, which ran July 1 through September 1 for tax year 2027. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal, because the board applies the county common level ratio to market value.

What does the realty transfer tax cost on a Mt. Lebanon sale?

The state charges 1 percent and the local municipal and school shares come on top, so the countywide total ranges from 2 to 5 percent. Ask the Allegheny County Department of Real Estate for the figure that applies to Mt. Lebanon and its school district.

Can I sell a Mt. Lebanon house that has unpermitted work?

Yes, but the municipality warns that work done without a permit can lead to fines set by the magisterial district judge. Ask the Inspection Office how to bring the work into compliance, or discuss an as-is sale with a buyer who will take the house in the condition it is in.

What should a seller know about Ross Township, PA?

Ross Township is a large suburb on the northern edge of Pittsburgh in Allegheny County, with a retail-heavy McKnight Road corridor, an older population and a transfer tax that is split between the township and the North Hills School District. A sale here is handled through the Allegheny County Division of Real Estate and the township's Building office.

The township was incorporated on June 26, 1809 and was named for James Ross, a Pittsburgh attorney and U.S. Senator. It covers 14.47 square miles, surrounds West View Borough, and shares eleven borders with municipalities including McCandless, Hampton, Shaler, Franklin Park and the Pittsburgh neighborhoods of Perry North and Brighton Heights. Northway Mall opened in 1962 as the first enclosed mall in Pennsylvania, and the Big Mac was created in 1967 at a McDonald's on McKnight Road.

The notes below cover what buyers see, what the township and county require, and how a fast sale compares with a listing.

What do Census figures show about Ross homes and owners?

Ross has a mature, mostly owner-occupied housing market, with a high share of older residents and a population estimate that has slipped since 2020.

With nearly a quarter of residents 65 or older and an average of 2.22 people per household, a share of Ross houses are held by older owners, and a sale of a long-held home often needs a repair estimate before pricing.

Do I need an occupancy certificate to sell a house in Ross Township?

Ask the Building office before you list. The township's Building page says that department handles permit applications, plan review, inspections and Certificates of Occupancy under the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, but it does not describe a separate resale inspection.

Call the Building Inspections office at 412-931-7048, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. at 1000 Ross Municipal Drive, and ask whether your address needs anything for a transfer. If you did work on the house without a permit, resolve it before a buyer's inspector finds it.

  • Permits are applied for online through iWorq.
  • Inspections need 48 hours' notice, and requests must include the permit number, address, inspection type, preferred date and an on-site contact.
  • Plumbing permits and inspections run through the Allegheny County Health Department, and electrical inspections go through the township's third-party agency.
  • For flood questions, the township says it cannot certify flood zones. Properties in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area face added requirements, so check the FEMA map for your parcel.

Projects submitted after January 1, 2026 follow the 2021 International codes as amended by the state, so a buyer's renovation plans will be reviewed under the newer codes.

How much transfer tax do sellers in Ross pay?

Allegheny County says its realty transfer tax runs from 2% to 5% of the price, with 1% going to the state and the rest split between the municipality and the school district. For Ross, ask the Division of Real Estate for the exact municipal and North Hills School District rates, which the county posts on its local rate page.

The county provides two examples. In Shaler Township, a $40,000 house carries 1% state, 0.5% township and 0.5% school tax for a 2% total of $800. In the City of Pittsburgh, the same house carries a total of 5%, which is $2,000. Use those as a guide to the arithmetic only, because Ross has its own rates.

  • The county collects state and local transfer tax when the deed is recorded, paid on a separate check from the recording fees.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) is required when the deed does not list the consideration or when an exemption applies.
  • Certain transfers between family members may be exempt, and the deed should say so, for example by stating that the transfer is familial and exempt from realty transfer tax.
  • The Department of Revenue can answer exemption questions at 717-783-8104.

At the Census median value of $268,900, each 1% of tax is about $2,690, so a 2% total would be near $5,400 and a 3% total near $8,100.

How do assessments and appeals work for Ross homeowners?

Allegheny County assesses Ross properties, and the first level of appeal is the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Owners and any taxing body with an interest in the parcel can file. Hearings are held by telephone, and a lawyer is optional, although most school districts and municipalities bring counsel.

If the BPAAR result is unsatisfactory, either side can take the appeal to the second level, the Board of Viewers at the Court of Common Pleas. Only the filing party can withdraw an appeal, using the county's withdrawal form. The county also allows year-round special appeals when the Office of Property Assessments issues a written determination in certain circumstances.

The school district and the township can appeal an assessment too. If you receive a hearing notice for an appeal filed by the school district or the municipality on your home, you may attend but you are not required to. A buyer who learns of a pending taxing-body appeal will ask about it, so mention it during negotiations.

Which neighborhoods, schools and roads matter in Ross?

Ross and West View together form the North Hills School District, which also uses Northland Public Library, shared among several municipalities. North Hills High School is the district's high school, and the school district is a recurring point in listings.

The township's named areas include Perrysville, McKnight, Evergreen Hamlet, Berkeley Hills, Highcliff, Laurel Gardens, North Hills Estates, Kinvara, Greybrooke, Holly Hill, White Oak Heights, Glenshaw, Keown Station and Northway. Commercial districts cluster along McKnight Road, U.S. Route 19 (Perry Highway) and Babcock Boulevard.

The township's population rose from about 15,700 in 1950 to about 35,100 in 1980, so homes in Evergreen Hamlet, Perrysville and the newer plans differ widely in age. Describe your street, lot and era in your listing or offer request, because buyers search by those features.

Should I list or take a cash offer in Ross?

List when the house shows well and you can wait for lender timelines. Take a cash offer when the house needs work, an estate is involved or the date matters more than the last few thousand dollars.

  • Compare offers by net proceeds after transfer tax, any commission, repairs and unpaid taxes.
  • Ask each buyer in writing who pays transfer tax and what happens if an inspection finds a defect.
  • Confirm the closing date and whether the buyer can close without a mortgage contingency.

More questions about Ross, PA

Who issues Certificates of Occupancy in Ross Township?

The township Building department. It handles permits, plan review, inspections and Certificates of Occupancy under the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, and its inspections line is 412-931-7048.

What is the transfer tax range in Allegheny County?

Allegheny County reports a range of 2% to 5% of the price, with 1% to the state and the remainder to the municipality and school district. Ask the county for the specific Ross and North Hills School District rates.

Can I appeal my Ross assessment before selling?

Yes. The owner or any taxing body can file with the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. A lawyer is not required, and the county lists the appeal forms and a withdrawal form on its Appeals page.

Is a house in a FEMA flood zone harder to sell in Ross?

It can be, because properties in a Special Flood Hazard Area face added requirements. The township cannot certify flood zones, so check the FEMA map for your parcel and tell buyers early.

Which school district serves Ross Township?

The North Hills School District, which also serves West View Borough. North Hills High School is the district's high school.

What kind of community is Bethel Park?

Bethel Park is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, about 7 miles south of Pittsburgh, with an estimated 32,074 residents on July 1, 2025. That is 4.5 percent below the 2020 estimates base, and the borough also has an older population, with 25.5 percent of residents 65 or over.

It began as Bethel Township in 1886, named for Bethel Presbyterian Church, and became a borough on March 17, 1949. The interurban trolley lines of the early 1900s made it an early streetcar suburb, and population doubled from 11,324 in 1950 to 23,650 in 1960. Nine wards each elect one member of the municipal council, and the mayor is elected at large. The municipal building is at 5100 West Library Avenue.

The borough covers 11.70 square miles, all land, and it touches seven neighbors: Castle Shannon, Whitehall, Baldwin, South Park, Upper St. Clair, Mt. Lebanon and Peters Township in Washington County. The primary ZIP code is 15102, while 15234, 15236 and 15241 serve border communities, so confirm the municipality on the parcel record.

Why does coal mining history matter when selling a Bethel Park house?

Bethel Park sits on the Pittsburgh coal seam, and the borough's geology summary, which cites the state environmental agency, says all of Bethel Park was undermined. The Pittsburgh Terminal No. 8 Mine, known as the H Mine and the Coverdale Mine, opened around 1920 and is closed.

Raise mine subsidence early in a sale. Ask your homeowner's insurer whether the policy covers mine subsidence, and ask the buyer's title company what it will search. Land in the borough ranges from 980 feet at the creek junction in the southeast corner to 1,370 feet at Rocky Ridge in the southwest.

What must a Bethel Park seller complete before the deed transfers?

A seller in Bethel Park must complete a dye test and a camera lateral inspection before any deed is transferred. The Camera Lateral Inspections Ordinance took effect on January 1, 2025, and the municipality's dye test page sets the rules.

  • The dye test and camera inspection must be finished 21 days before closing or deed transfer.
  • The municipality charges a $50 processing fee.
  • The camera lateral inspection must come from a contractor certified by the National Association of Sewer Service Companies, and the plumber must be registered through the health department.
  • An Allegheny County licensed plumber performs the dye test, and a municipal building code official signs off if a defect is corrected.
  • A test already performed and certified within the last two years can satisfy the rule.
  • A deed cannot be transferred until needed repairs are made and pass inspection.

Paperwork has a 48-hour turnaround, and the form request goes through the municipal office at 412-831-6800, extension 205. The page also states that an occupancy inspection is not required for a sale. Owners who deeded a property without the test receive an official letter, and non-compliance leads to a citation.

What do Census figures show about Bethel Park housing?

Bethel Park is a market of owners. For 2020 to 2024, 76.4 percent of homes were owner-occupied, the median household income was $107,090, and 53.5 percent of adults 25 and over held a bachelor's degree or higher.

What permits and fees apply to a Bethel Park home?

The municipality's development fee schedule, effective September 9, 2025, lists a Certificate of Occupancy at $50, a written Certificate of Zoning at $50, and a Short-Term Rental Permit at $50 initially and $25 for each annual renewal. Building permits for work under $1,000 cost $50.

Permits go to the Community Development Department on the second floor of the municipal building, or by email to the permits address on the municipality's site. Residential questions go to extension 131 at 412-831-6800. Pennsylvania adopted the 2021 I-Codes under the Uniform Construction Code effective January 1, 2026, so permits for repairs before a sale follow the newer code. Code enforcement also treats grass over 8 inches as a violation, so mow before photos and showings.

How do Allegheny County assessments and appeals work for Bethel Park owners?

Allegheny County's Office of Property Assessments sets values for Bethel Park, and appeals go first to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. A party who disagrees with that result can appeal to the Board of Viewers at the Court of Common Pleas.

  • Hearings take place by telephone.
  • Legal representation is optional, and an authorized representative may appear for the owner.
  • A taxing body, such as a school district or municipality, can also file an appeal on a property.
  • Special Appeals can be filed year-round in response to a written determination notice from the assessment office.

Ask the Office of Property Assessments for the annual filing window, because the county sets it by ordinance. The county's real estate page also covers state and local realty transfer taxes, the municipal and school shares, and recording requirements for deeds.

How do transit, schools and shopping shape Bethel Park?

Pittsburgh Regional Transit's three light rail lines all run through the borough. The Blue and Red lines end at South Hills Village, and the Silver Line passes through the central business district to Library. Park-and-ride lots operate at South Hills Village, West Library, Lytle and Washington Junction.

PA Route 88 and US Route 19 carry most commercial traffic, and the Yellow and Orange Belts of the county belt system serve the borough. Interstate 79 and the Mon-Fayette Expressway stay outside the boundary, each about a 15-minute drive. Bethel Park High School is the comprehensive high school of the Bethel Park School District, and South Hills Village is a two-level mall inside the borough.

What are the ways to sell a house fast in Bethel Park?

An owner here can list the house, sell privately or accept a cash offer. Because the lateral inspection deadline is 21 days before closing, a sale that closes in under three weeks needs the dye test and camera work done before a contract is signed.

Start by requesting the forms from the municipality, hire the certified plumber, and keep the video and paperwork together for the buyer's title company. If the camera finds a defect, price the repair in early, because the deed cannot move until the repair passes inspection.

More questions about Bethel Park, PA

Do I need a dye test to sell my Bethel Park house?

Yes. Bethel Park requires a dye test and a camera lateral inspection before a deed transfers, unless one was done and certified within the last two years.

How much does the Bethel Park lateral paperwork cost?

The municipality charges a $50 processing fee. The plumber's fees are separate and depend on the contractor you hire.

Does Bethel Park require an occupancy inspection when a house is sold?

No. The dye test page states an occupancy inspection is not required for a sale. A $50 Certificate of Occupancy appears on the fee schedule for other situations.

Is Bethel Park built over old coal mines?

Yes. The borough's geology summary says all of Bethel Park was undermined, and part of it lies over the closed Pittsburgh Terminal No. 8 Mine.

Where do I appeal an Allegheny County assessment?

Appeals go to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Hearings are held by telephone, and later appeals go to the Board of Viewers.

What should a seller know about Tredyffrin Township?

Tredyffrin is the most populous township in Chester County, with 31,927 residents at the 2020 census, and it covers 19.9 square miles on the Philadelphia Main Line. Welsh settlers gave it its name, which joins the Welsh words for town and wide valley, and the township was incorporated in 1707. Wikipedia's account notes that part of Valley Forge National Historical Park lies inside the township, along with the quarters used by several Continental Army generals.

The township's communities include Chesterbrook, Strafford, Howellville and East Howellville, plus portions of Paoli and Wayne. Rail service that terminated in Paoli drove the first big wave of suburban building in the 1800s. Population then more than doubled between 1950 and 1960, rising from 7,836 to 16,004, and it has stayed above 28,000 since 1990.

That history shows up in the housing. The township's historic buildings include seven colonial log houses and cabins, an 1818 octagonal schoolhouse and a 1788 school, alongside the postwar subdivisions, so age and condition vary widely from street to street.

How do the roads and schools of Tredyffrin shape home values?

Tredyffrin is cut by some of the busiest roads in the western suburbs. The Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-76) crosses the northwest, U.S. 202 runs through the center, U.S. 422 starts at 202 in the northeast corner as the County Line Expressway, U.S. 30 follows Lancaster Avenue along the south, and PA 252 runs north to south. As of 2018 the township counted 150.13 miles of public roads, of which the township itself maintained 106.89 miles.

Schools come from the Tredyffrin-Easttown School District. The township's 2025 annual report says it approved turning an office building at 1200 Swedesford Road in Berwyn into a new elementary school, which is expected to open for the 2027-28 school year. A new school building near a street can change how buyers talk about that neighborhood, so check the district's attendance map before you price.

  • Note whether your street is near a turnpike, 202 or 422 interchange, since noise comes up in showings.
  • Ask the district which school your address feeds, and say so in the listing.
  • Mention commuter rail access in Paoli if you are within a short drive.

Does flooding or stormwater matter when selling in Tredyffrin?

It can, depending on your street. The township's 2025 annual report lists a run of stormwater projects at Crabby Creek, Strafford Park, Bair Road, the Willis, Woodcrest and Upper Weadley Roads area, and Gregory Lane. The Willis project had construction expected to run through fall 2026, and the Gregory Lane work has a second phase planned to start in fall or winter 2026.

The same report describes flood buyouts. The township received more than $697,000 to acquire the home at 595 Park Ridge Drive, demolish it and return the lot to vegetation, and further acquisitions were underway on Park Ridge Drive and Yellow Springs Road. If your home sits near Trout Creek or one of those streets, expect buyers and their insurers to ask about flood history, and gather any repair records before you list.

Rainfall in 2025 was 39.7 inches against an area average of about 43 inches, and the report noted no tropical storm events that year, so recent seasons say little about worst-case flooding.

Does Tredyffrin require an inspection or occupancy permit to sell?

No resale inspection appears on the township's permit pages. The Permits and Inspections page states that Use and Occupancy permits are needed for new residential construction and that the permit "is not required for changes in residential ownership or tenancy." Commercial properties are different: a change of occupant, change of use or commercial alteration needs a U&O permit before occupancy.

Open permits are the practical risk. Applications go through the Clariti online portal, and final inspections must pass before a U&O is issued, so a deck or finished basement built without sign-off can surface during a buyer's inspection review. Residential plans get a maximum review of 15 business days. Email permits@tredyffrin.gov or call 610-644-1400 and press 4.

The township lists repairs that need no building permit, including painting, window replacement without structural change, replacing siding, replacing gutters, and re-roofing up to 25 percent of the roof in a 12 month span. Larger work and any change to plumbing, gas, mechanical or electrical systems does need one.

  • Removing more than five trees six inches or wider in diameter within 12 months needs a tree removal permit, unless the trees are dead or hazardous.
  • A student home is limited to three tenants and needs a special exception and registration.
  • Zoning certificates are requested by letter to the zoning officer, with the address and tax parcel.

What does the Chester County transfer tax cost on a Tredyffrin sale?

The Chester County Recorder of Deeds collects transfer tax for all 73 municipalities and the state. It lists the usual rate as 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality, with Coatesville, Malvern and Tredyffrin as exceptions. Tredyffrin is listed at 1.5 percent, so the municipal side here is higher than in most of the county.

Tredyffrin recording and tax facts. Sources: Chester County Recorder of Deeds, Pennsylvania Department of Revenue, Tredyffrin Township 2025 Annual Report
ItemDetail
State realty transfer tax1% of consideration or computed value
Tredyffrin municipal transfer tax1.5%, listed as an exception to the county's 1%
Payment method at recordingBusiness check, cashier check or money order to the Recorder of Deeds
Parcels billed by the township in 202511,989
2025 township real estate tax collected99.38% of the amount billed

The Recorder does not take cash or credit cards for transfer tax. Tax is figured on the price or on the computed value, which the county says is usually the higher figure. Pennsylvania makes both buyer and seller liable to the state, so settle in the contract who pays. Recorded documents usually show up in the county's online records within 48 hours, and a lender has 60 days to record a satisfaction after a payoff.

How do I appeal a Tredyffrin assessment, and when?

Chester County sets assessments, and the appeal goes to the county Board of Assessment Appeals. An annual appeal can be filed from May 1 through August 1, or the next business day if August 1 is a weekend. The decision takes effect with the next year's tax bills. If a change notice follows a new addition or permit, an interim appeal must be filed within 40 days of the notice.

Filing costs $25 for a residential parcel, paid by check or money order to the Chester County Treasurer. Forms must be printed and delivered, with no fax or electronic copies, to the Assessment Office at 313 W. Market Street, Suite 4202, West Chester. Hearings take place in the Government Services Center on Westtown Road, and you can bring recent sales of similar homes, an appraisal and exterior photographs from the last six months. A further appeal to the Court of Common Pleas must be filed within 30 days of the Board's notice.

Chester County's assessment represents 100 percent of market value at the base year, so it reflects that older value, which can sit well away from what a buyer would offer.

What are my options to sell a Tredyffrin house quickly?

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is. In a township where permits issued in 2025 totaled 1,312 with $237,174,301 in construction costs, buyers are used to renovating, so a house that needs updating still draws interest.

  • List when the house is in good shape and you can handle showings.
  • Sell for cash when there are open permits, tenants, an estate to settle or repairs you cannot fund.
  • Pull the permit history from the township before any offer, because unresolved work can slow either route.

Compare offers on net proceeds after the 2.5 percent combined transfer tax, any agent fees and repairs, and ask each buyer in writing about closing dates.

More questions about Tredyffrin, PA

Does Tredyffrin Township require a use and occupancy permit when I sell my house?

No for an ordinary residential sale. The township says the permit is not required for changes in residential ownership or tenancy, and it applies to new residential construction and to commercial occupancy changes.

What is the transfer tax rate in Tredyffrin?

The county lists 1 percent to the state and 1.5 percent to Tredyffrin, a combined 2.5 percent. Most Chester County municipalities charge 1 percent on the local side.

When can I appeal my Chester County assessment?

An annual appeal window runs from May 1 through August 1 each year. An interim appeal must be filed within 40 days of the date on an assessment change notice.

Can I sell a Tredyffrin house with open permits?

You can try, but open permits are a title and inspection problem. Ask Permits and Inspections at 610-644-1400 (press 4) which permits remain open, and finish the inspections first if you can.

Where do I record a deed after closing in Tredyffrin?

Deeds are recorded with the Chester County Recorder of Deeds. The office takes transfer tax by business check, cashier check or money order, and posts records online within about 48 hours.

How does selling a house in North Huntingdon work?

North Huntingdon sellers deal with a township, a county and a school district that each tax and record separately, and the township's permit schedule lists no resale inspection for an ordinary house. North Huntingdon is a first class township in Westmoreland County covering about 27 square miles, governed by a board of commissioners with one commissioner from each of seven wards.

Census QuickFacts counts 31,880 residents in 2020 and 31,697 in its 2025 estimate. The township is crossed by the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-76) and the Lincoln Highway (U.S. Route 30), with the Youghiogheny River touching its southwestern corner, as described on Wikipedia.

What are North Huntingdon's housing and neighborhoods like?

North Huntingdon is mostly a township of owner-occupied houses, with 90.1 percent of housing units owner occupied in the 2020 to 2024 Census figures. The survey puts a typical owned home at $232,400, household income at $101,200 at the median, and 94.4 percent of residents at the address they occupied the prior year.

Older sections of the township grew around settlements such as Circleville, Cavitt's Mills and Robbin's Station, and the Fullerton Inn and the McFarlane House carry federal historic register listings. Students attend the Norwin School District.

About 21.3 percent of residents are 65 or older, so estate sales and downsizing moves are part of the local picture. QuickFacts also reports about $826 million in retail sales for 2022.

Does North Huntingdon require an inspection before a house sale?

The township's permit fee schedule lists a residential occupancy permit for new construction only, at $25 and included in the building permit fee, which means an existing owner-occupied house changing hands does not go through an occupancy inspection. Commercial occupancy for a new use or tenant costs $150.

Permits still matter for projects a seller finishes before listing:

  • Residential building permits are charged per square foot plus a state fee and review fee, and the application will not be accepted without a property survey.
  • Accessory buildings under 200 square feet skip the building permit but need a $50 zoning permit.
  • Demolition requires proof of utility shut-offs, and the township inspector checks the sewer cap before backfilling.
  • Inside and outside sanitary sewer inspections on permitted construction are handled by the North Huntingdon Township Municipal Authority.

The Planning and Zoning Department takes questions at 724-863-3806, extension 220, and inspections need 24 hours of notice.

How is North Huntingdon property tax calculated?

The tax bill multiplies the Westmoreland County assessed value, divided by 1,000, by each millage rate, and three bodies levy: the township, the county and the Norwin School District. The township's 2026 budget document describes a general real estate rate of 10.73 mills, up from 9.23, and uses a $24,000 assessed value as the median household example.

How do Westmoreland County assessment appeals work?

An owner can appeal an assessment to the Westmoreland County Board of Assessment Appeals every year, and annual appeals must be filed on or before August 1 to take effect for the following tax year. Anyone who receives a notice of change in assessment has 40 days from the mailing date to appeal.

Appeal forms are posted in the Forms section of the county site and are available from the Tax Assessment Office at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue in Greensburg. The board meets on the second Thursday of each month at 9:00 a.m. in the Tax Assessment Office, Suite 440.

Because the township uses county values, a successful appeal changes the township and school bills together. A seller who plans to list should file before the August 1 deadline if the assessed value looks high compared with similar houses nearby.

What recording and transfer tax steps apply in North Huntingdon?

A deed for a North Huntingdon house is recorded with the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds, which requires the 10-digit parcel identifier number on every document. The recorder's list also calls for original signatures, a certified grantee address, and either transfer taxes or a completed Statement of Value (REV-183) unless a family exemption appears in the deed.

The state portion is 1 percent of the value transferred, and the state revenue agency notes that grantor and grantee are jointly liable. The township's 2026 budget lists real estate transfer tax revenue of $650,000, which shows a local share applies as well, so ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on your parcel.

If a deed's transfer tax covers more than one municipality, it must state how the tax is divided.

How are North Huntingdon's roads, fire protection and utilities arranged?

The township's fire levy is shared equally among the seven volunteer fire companies inside its borders, and a separate hydrant levy applies only within 600 feet of a hydrant. The fire service line appears on every tax bill.

Wikipedia puts the township's road network at about 125 miles, and the 2026 budget message names roads and stormwater as its main spending emphasis. Sanitary sewer service and inspections run through the North Huntingdon Township Municipal Authority, which a seller can contact about a lateral line before a buyer's inspector raises it.

When does a cash sale fit a North Huntingdon house?

A cash sale suits owners who need certainty on timing or who would rather not spend on updates before a buyer's inspection. A cash buyer purchases as is, which fits several common situations:

  • A long-held house that needs a new roof, furnace or sewer line.
  • An inherited property that heirs live far from.
  • A home with delinquent township, county or school taxes that moved to a collector.
  • A landlord who wants out of a rental on a short schedule.

Compare any offer with a likely net from a traditional listing, after agent fees, repairs and the transfer tax, and ask for a copy of the purchase terms before agreeing to anything.

More questions about North Huntingdon, PA

Does North Huntingdon require a resale occupancy permit?

The township's fee schedule lists a residential occupancy permit for new construction only, so an ordinary resale of an existing house is not covered by it. Call the Planning and Zoning Department at 724-863-3806, extension 220, to confirm for your address.

What is the North Huntingdon real estate tax rate?

The township's budget document shows a general real estate rate of 9.23 mills for 2025 and 10.73 mills for 2026, plus 1.32 mills for fire service. Westmoreland County and the Norwin School District tax the parcel separately, so check your bill for the full total.

Who collects North Huntingdon taxes?

Keystone Collections Group collects the township's occupation, local services and delinquent real estate taxes, and its phone number is 724-978-0300. Norwin School District bills its school taxes separately.

By what date must a Westmoreland County assessment appeal be filed?

Annual appeals must be filed on or before August 1 and take effect for the next tax year. A notice of change in assessment gives the owner 40 days from the mailing date to appeal.

How much is transfer tax when selling in North Huntingdon?

Pennsylvania charges 1 percent at the state level, and local shares are added on top. The Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds can give the combined rate for your parcel before you sign a sales agreement.

How quickly can a York Township, PA house sell?

Quickly, if the price matches the condition and the paperwork is clean. York Township is a large suburb of the City of York with a steady stream of buyers, and the route you choose (agent listing, owner sale or direct cash purchase) decides how much time you give up and how much price you keep.

Dallastown, Red Lion and Yoe grew out of the township's old southeastern corner, and what remains is the most populous suburb of York. The Census Bureau puts the township at 31,479 residents in mid-2025, a 5.8% rise from a 2020 starting count of 29,748. Growth keeps buyers active, yet a house with liens, tenants or deferred repairs usually waits longer on the open market than a tidy one.

What kind of place is York Township for a seller?

Mostly suburban, with older postwar tracts next to newer streets. Wikipedia dates settlement to 1748 and incorporation to 1753, and says the land stayed largely rural until after World War II. Head counts show the shift: 4,502 residents in 1950, 8,506 in 1960, 12,702 in 1970 and 29,740 in 2020.

About 25 square miles in size, the township contains Queens Gate, Spry and Tyler Run, three census-designated places, and answers to a Board of Supervisors. Many residents drive to work, with an average trip of 24.9 minutes.

Survey figures for 2020 to 2024 sketch the likely buyer pool and the likely sellers:

  • 12,939 households of about 2.3 people each.
  • Seven in ten homes are lived in by their owners, so roughly three in ten are rentals.
  • Household income in the middle of the range is $80,190, and 38.7% of adults 25 and over hold a four year degree.
  • Nearly a quarter of residents (22.5%) are 65 or older, which feeds downsizing and estate sales.

What are houses worth in York Township?

The Census Bureau's middle value for an owner occupied home is $260,800. Owners in the middle pay $1,914 a month in housing costs with a mortgage and $768 with none, while renters in the middle pay $1,389. A township wide figure hides a lot, so a dated ranch and a fully updated home in a newer plan will price far apart.

Which permits and inspections can affect a York Township sale?

The township's Building and Zoning Department issues permits, enforces codes and handles property maintenance. It applies the statewide Uniform Construction Code, adopted locally through Ordinance 2004-7 on May 11, 2004. A finished basement, deck or shed built without a permit may come up when a buyer's inspector or lender looks the house over, so check the file before you list.

  • Plan review is allowed up to 15 business days for a residential building permit and 30 for a commercial one.
  • A zoning permit is due in 10 days, unless a special exception or variance must go before the Zoning Hearing Board.
  • Building inspections are booked on weekdays between 7:30 a.m. and 2:15 p.m. with a day's notice, by calling (717) 428-5641.
  • Plumbing jobs go to a plumber licensed by York Township under Resolution 93-2; swapping a fixture or a water heater on the same fuel needs no permit.
  • Anyone running a business from home registers each year and pays $25.

Zoning and code staff answer questions on weekdays until 4:00 p.m. at (717) 741-3861, and the township asks you to call for an appointment first. The department also lists a LERTA tax assistance program for certain deteriorated areas, worth a question if your parcel might fall inside one.

How does recording work after a York Township closing?

The York County Recorder of Deeds records the deed, since the township does not. County fee notes set the base charge for a deed at $86.25, which covers four pages and four names. Pages past the fourth cost $2 each, extra names cost $0.50 each, and each parcel identification number on the paper adds $20.

Filing a PA Realty Transfer Tax Statement of Value costs $2. Business checks, personal checks and cash are accepted, and a bounced check brings a $50 charge. The county also posts a Common Level Ratio for each stretch from July 1 to June 30; the 2025 to 2026 figure was 1.98.

Pennsylvania taxes the transfer at 1 percent of value, and the Department of Revenue notes the buyer and the seller answer for it together. Municipal and school shares can sit on top, so ask your title company or the county recorder what the total comes to on your deed. Some gifts to family and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt.

Which selling route suits a York Township house?

Three routes cover most cases.

  • Agent listing. Best exposure for a house in good order. You pay a commission, host showings and wait on the buyer's loan, appraisal and inspection.
  • Owner sale. You keep the commission and take on pricing, marketing, contracts and negotiation, and the transfer tax and recording costs still apply.
  • Cash offer. A direct buyer buys the property in its present state, so cleanouts, repairs and tenants stop being obstacles. The price usually runs below a fully prepared retail sale, so compare it against your net after commission and fix-up.

The cash route tends to suit inherited homes, tenants who will not leave, long deferred repairs or a hard deadline such as a job move. To see the gap, request a written offer for your York Township address and set it next to a listing estimate.

What paperwork should a York Township seller gather first?

Begin with the deed and the newest tax bill, then pull permit records for any work done on the house. Request a payoff statement for each mortgage or lien, since those get paid from your proceeds at closing. If the house came from a relative, the estate papers need to show who may sign.

Then walk the property the way an inspector would: roof, furnace, electrical panel, sump area and outbuildings, noting anything built without a permit. Decide whether to repair, offer a credit or sell as is. Once you know the repair bill, choosing between a listing and a direct offer comes down to arithmetic.

More questions about York Township, PA

What is the typical timeline to sell in York Township?

Listed houses commonly take weeks to a few months depending on price, condition and the buyer's loan. A cash sale can close sooner because no lender or appraisal is involved, and the seller often sets the closing date.

Is a permit required before selling a York Township house?

No permit is needed just to sell. Earlier unpermitted work is the concern, because a buyer's inspection can raise it. Call the Building and Zoning Department at (717) 741-3861 to ask what the township file shows.

Which office records the deed for a York Township sale?

The York County Recorder of Deeds. Its base fee for a deed is $86.25 for four pages and four names, plus charges for added pages, names and parcel numbers.

Who owes Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax?

Buyer and seller are both liable, per the Department of Revenue. The state takes 1 percent of the value, and local shares can be added; your sales agreement sets who pays what.

Can a house that needs repairs still be sold here?

Yes. A direct buyer takes it in its current condition, while a financed buyer tends to ask for repairs or a lower price after inspection. A repair estimate up front lets you compare what each path would net.

What should a seller know about Ridley Township, PA?

Ridley Township is a compact, mostly built-out suburb in southeastern Delaware County where owners are long-settled and the housing stock is older. A sale here depends on a short call to the township's Code Enforcement office, the county's 1% local transfer tax default, and a buyer pool that is mostly local.

The township covers about 5.1 square miles of land, with more water along the Delaware River at its southern edge. It includes the communities of Folsom, Woodlyn, Crum Lynne and Holmes, plus parts of Morton and Secane. Rutledge Borough sits entirely inside Ridley's boundaries, and Ridley Park Borough is surrounded on three sides by the township, so the municipal line is not always obvious from a street address.

Ridley was named for Ridley in Cheshire, England, and its tax collectors were appointed as early as 1684. Continental Army troops camped along its roads after the Battle of Brandywine in 1777, and the township grew sharply after World War II, from about 8,600 residents in 1940 to nearly 36,000 by 1960.

A 93.3% same-house rate means most owners stay put, so houses that do come up often belong to long-term owners, estates or retirees. If you have owned the house for decades, get a repair estimate before you pick a price.

What does Ridley Township require when I sell my home?

Call the Code Enforcement office before you go to settlement. The township's code page says plainly that sellers should contact it for the necessary information, and the phone number is 610-534-4803.

The page also notes that owners of rental units must hold an annual certificate of use for each dwelling unit, whether occupied or empty. If you are selling a duplex or a house that was rented, confirm that the certificate is current so it does not become a closing problem.

  • Ask which inspections or forms the township wants for a sale at your address.
  • Ask whether any open violations, stormwater issues or unpermitted work are on file.
  • Ask for the township's current fee list, since permit and certificate charges are set locally.
  • Keep sidewalks and shared driveways clear of snow and ice within 24 hours after snow stops, because the township enforces that rule and buyers walking a property in winter will notice.

The township also publishes its code book, zoning map and a stormwater management ordinance, which matter if a buyer plans an addition or paving.

How much is transfer tax on a Ridley sale?

Delaware County's Recorder of Deeds lists a default of 1% to the state and 1% to the local municipality, and Ridley Township is not among the exceptions it names. Radnor, Upper Darby, Upper Providence and Chester are the ones that pay more.

At the Census median value of $265,200, 1% is about $2,650, so the combined 2% comes to roughly $5,300. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue says both parties are jointly liable and that some transfers, such as certain family transfers and property passing through an estate, are exempt. The contract should still say who pays.

  • The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 108 of the Government Center at 201 West Front Street in Media, phone 610-891-4152.
  • Recording hours are 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., a full hour before the 4:30 p.m. office close.

  • If the deed does not state the full price, the state's Statement of Value (REV-183) goes with it.

Because deeds for several municipalities are filed in the same office, check that your deed names Ridley Township as the municipality. A mistake there changes the local tax line.

Which schools, roads and neighborhoods shape demand in Ridley?

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District, and Our Lady of Angels Regional School, which formed in 2012 from two parish schools, is the nearby Catholic option. Families searching in this area often use the district as a filter, so a listing's school assignment is worth stating in the first lines.

Access is a selling point. Interstate 95 crosses the southern part of the township, Interstate 476 begins at I-95 and runs northwest across the southwest corner, U.S. 13 follows Chester Pike, PA 291 follows Industrial Highway and PA 420 follows Kedron Avenue. SEPTA city bus route 37 and suburban routes 113 and 114 serve the township. The nearest regional rail stations are in neighboring municipalities, since the Media/Wawa and Wilmington/Newark lines only clip the edges.

The township maintains about 72 miles of road, and PennDOT maintains about 14 miles.

How do property taxes and assessments work for a Ridley seller?

Ridley homeowners pay Delaware County, Ridley Township and the Ridley School District, each on its own bill. Ask the Delaware County Assessment Office for the current appeal deadline and form, and ask the township treasurer for the township's tax certification before closing.

Delaware County's countywide reassessment took effect in January 2021, so values across the county were reset at the same base year. A seller who thinks the assessed value is out of line can appeal, but filing an appeal does not stop the bill from coming due.

Stormwater is its own cost. Ridley adopted a stormwater management ordinance, last updated in September 2022, and publishes a stormwater fee schedule on its code page. Ask the township how the fee is billed on your parcel and whether any credit applies.

Which way to sell is best in Ridley?

A listing makes sense when the house is updated and priced against recent nearby sales. A cash sale works better when the house is dated, an estate is involved or the owner has to move on a deadline.

  • For an estate sale, confirm who has legal authority to sign the deed before listing.
  • For a tenant-occupied house, confirm the annual certificate of use and the lease terms.
  • For a quick sale, ask the buyer to put the closing date and who pays transfer tax in writing.

Whichever route you choose, gather the tax bills, the deed and any township notices before you call anyone. With 73.7% of Ridley homes owner-occupied and few households moving in a given year, a clean file and a firm closing date set one offer apart from another.

Does Ridley Township require an inspection before I sell?

Call the Code Enforcement office at 610-534-4803 to find out. The township's own page tells sellers to contact that office for the necessary information before settlement, so the answer for your address comes from them.

What is the transfer tax rate in Ridley Township?

The county's default is 1% state and 1% local, and Ridley is not listed among Delaware County's higher-rate exceptions. Confirm the figure with the Recorder of Deeds before you finalize your closing numbers.

Can I sell a Ridley rental property with tenants?

Yes. The township requires an annual certificate of use for each rental dwelling unit, occupied or not, so keep that current. Review the lease for how the buyer takes over the tenancy.

Which school district serves Ridley Township?

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District. Parts of Morton and Secane lie inside the township, so check the school district on your tax bill.

In Room 108 of the Government Center, 201 West Front Street, Media. Recording hours run 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and the office phone is 610-891-4152.

  • Easton is in Northampton County.
Selling in Easton?

Is a quick sale realistic for an Easton house?

It is. Easton owners choose among an agent listing, a sale without an agent, and an as-is cash purchase, and the house's condition, any tenants and your closing date usually settle which one. Deferred repairs, a tenant lease or a clouded inheritance are the usual reasons an owner here looks at cash.

Easton is the seat of Northampton County and the eastern end of the Lehigh Valley, where the Lehigh River joins the Delaware. Allentown lies 14 miles to the southwest, Philadelphia 51 miles south and New York City 64 miles east. The Delaware marks the city's eastern edge, and Phillipsburg, New Jersey, sits across it, so some buyers commute over the bridges.

What should I know about Easton's districts and roads?

Easton's four districts are Downtown, College Hill, South Side and West Ward. Census QuickFacts lists 4.26 square miles of land and 6,597.9 people per square mile in 2020, so houses sit tightly together. Downtown is low ground at the river junction with hills rising north, west and south. Lafayette College anchors College Hill, and South Easton, across the Lehigh, was its own borough until 1898.

  • Roads: US 22, the Lehigh Valley Thruway, crosses the middle of the city. PA 611 hugs the Delaware, and PA 248 begins where those two meet. I-78 touches the southeast corner, but its nearest interchange is in Williams Township.
  • Bridges: the Northampton Street Bridge and the Easton and Phillipsburg Toll Bridge connect to New Jersey.
  • Downtown landmarks: Centre Square, the Crayola Experience and the National Canal Museum.
  • Weather: winters bring about 30 inches of snow, the hardiness zone is 6b, and the record low is minus 15 degrees Fahrenheit, so inspectors look at roofs, gutters and plumbing in older houses.
  • Schools: Easton Area School District covers the city, Forks and Palmer townships and part of Lower Mount Bethel, and its high school is in Palmer Township.

How did Easton get its housing and its reputation?

Easton was named in 1752 for the Easton Neston estate of Thomas Penn's wife's family, and the Lenape called the place Lechauwitank, the Place at the Forks. The Delaware and Lehigh canals made it a coal transfer point in the 19th century, and railroads followed the same corridor. Historians of angling credit an Easton gunsmith, Samuel Phillipe, with the six-strip split-cane fly rod in 1845.

The city's population peaked at 35,632 in 1950, fell to 26,027 by 1980 and has climbed since to 28,127 in 2020. Easton Area School District reported about 8,289 students in 2020 to 2021 across seven elementary schools, a middle school campus in Forks Township and the high school. Crayola's maker is based in nearby Forks Township, and Larry Holmes Drive honors the city's heavyweight champion. Buyers value these town details, so mention what you know of your block's history in the listing or the offer conversation.

How do Easton housing costs compare with local income?

On paper Easton is affordable: an owner's home has a median value of $196,300 for 2020 to 2024, set against household income of $69,348. Owners live in just 44.5% of the city's homes, and the population grew 8.2% from the 2020 base to 30,402 in July 2025.

Citywide medians blur big differences between a renovated Downtown block and an unrenovated College Hill one. Price your house against recent sales close to it.

Which city offices touch an Easton sale?

Start with Code Enforcement, then the Historic District Commission, then the rental licensing desk if anyone rents the house. Code Enforcement applies the city Property Maintenance Code and the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, and it can tell you whether permits on your address are still open.

  • Permits: building, enlarging, altering, repairing, moving or demolishing a structure, changing its use, or installing electrical, gas, mechanical or plumbing systems all need one.
  • Historic review: facade and signage work may also need a certificate of appropriateness from the Historic District Commission.
  • Occupancy cap: a single housekeeping unit may hold no more than three unrelated people, and an Occupancy Limitations Certificate states the limit for each dwelling unit.
  • Rental paperwork: an owner who rents files each tenant's name and address with the Rental Licensing Officer, and a moving permit comes from the Finance Department.
  • Fire check: the fire inspector will do a free fire safety inspection if you doubt a building has the required smoke detectors.

For a rented house, gather the lease, rental license papers and tenant form in one folder. A buyer's attorney will ask for them.

What taxes and recording steps come with an Easton sale?

Expect separate bills from the city, the county and the school district. Easton levies 24.95 mills on the value the Northampton County Assessment Office sets, and residents pay a city earned income tax of 1.45% plus 0.5% to Easton Area School District, for 1.95% in all.

The county mailed 2026 bills in mid-January, with the discount ending March 31 and the face amount due June 1. Taxes still unpaid at the close of business on January 31 of the next year pass to the Tax Claim Bureau, which meant January 31, 2027 for the 2026 bill. Clear any balance from the sale proceeds.

The state's realty transfer tax is 1% of value, and the law holds the grantor and the grantee jointly liable. The Recorder of Deeds, at (610) 829-6210, takes it with any local tax at recording, and the city's tax list includes a real estate transfer tax. Request the combined rate for your price before you sign a contract.

The county's 2026 appeal hearings ran from August 5 through October 29. For the present filing deadline, ask the Assessment Division on the second floor of the courthouse at 669 Washington Street. School homestead exclusions come from Act 72 of 2004, so an owner-occupant should ask the school district how the exclusion is handled when the deed changes.

What must an Easton seller tell the buyer?

Pennsylvania's disclosure rule, 68 Pa.C.S. section 7303, reaches anyone selling one to four dwelling units. The seller gives the buyer a completed, signed and dated statement ahead of signing the sales agreement. The state form has 16 topics, from the roof and basement to hazardous substances and legal title problems.

If a seller willfully or negligently skips a duty, the buyer's actual damages are owed, and suit must start within two years of final settlement (section 7311). An executor or other fiduciary selling for an estate is outside the chapter (section 7302). Paying cash earns the buyer no exemption.

When is cash the better route for an Easton house?

Cash fits best when condition, occupancy or timing would stall a listing. Examples from Easton's housing mix:

  • A house left by a relative that no heir wants to keep.
  • A rental where the unit or the license paperwork needs attention.
  • Open permits or code notices that scare off buyers who depend on a mortgage.
  • Roof, plumbing or heating damage after a hard winter.
  • A job transfer, divorce or court date that fixes your move.

Weigh any cash figure against what a listing nets after repairs, concessions and transfer tax. To get a figure for an Easton address, call or text with the details, including tenants and any open code items.

More questions about Easton, PA

What controls the speed of a cash closing in Easton?

Title work and the date you choose control it, since there is no loan to underwrite. The deed then goes to the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds, and taxes or liens come out of the proceeds.

Who owes the Pennsylvania transfer tax in Easton?

Under state law both the person giving the deed and the person receiving it are liable for the 1% state tax. Your sales agreement decides how the cost is divided, and the Recorder of Deeds collects any local share with it.

Is a tenant a problem when selling in Easton?

No, but paperwork matters. The city expects owners who rent to keep tenant names and addresses on file with the Rental Licensing Officer, so give the buyer the lease and those records.

Where does a deed get recorded for an Easton property?

At the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds, which records deeds and mortgages and collects the fees and taxes due on transfers. The office number is (610) 829-6210.

Can I sell an inherited Easton house?

Yes. Pennsylvania exempts property passed by will or intestate succession from realty transfer tax, and a fiduciary selling for an estate falls outside the seller disclosure chapter. Settle title questions with the estate's attorney before setting a closing date.

Who is selling homes in Hazleton, PA?

Hazleton is a compact, fast-changing city in Luzerne County where homes are affordable and about half are rented. The 2025 Census estimate is 30,286 people, compared with 25,340 in the 2010 count and 29,963 in 2020.

In the 2020 to 2024 survey, 51.1 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the typical owned home is valued at $151,600 and rent is $1,089. Households earn a median $46,177. Hispanic or Latino residents make up 63.4 percent of the population, 38.0 percent were born abroad, and 57.8 percent of people over age 5 speak another language at home. The city posts major notices in both English and Spanish.

Sellers here include longtime owners of older rowhouses, landlords with several units and heirs to a house they do not plan to keep. If a buyer or tenant speaks mainly Spanish, plan for bilingual paperwork and a translator at the closing table.

Where is Hazleton and how does its setting affect a house?

Hazleton sits on a plateau called Spring Mountain in northeastern Pennsylvania, 35 miles northwest of Allentown, 82 miles north-northwest of Philadelphia and 106 miles west of New York City. The city covers 5.97 square miles, all land, and Wikipedia gives its highest point as 1,886 feet, which makes it the highest incorporated city in the state. It straddles the divide between the Delaware and Susquehanna River watersheds.

Height brings weather. The climate is warm-summer humid continental, with roughly 47 inches of snow a year and 50 inches of rain. The city's building codes list a frost depth of 42 inches, a ground snow load of 40 pounds per square foot and a design wind load of 115 miles per hour. Buyers and inspectors in Hazleton look closely at roofs, chimneys, gutters, foundations and basement moisture, so a recent repair record helps.

How did Hazleton's coal history shape its housing?

Anthracite built Hazleton. Coal was found at nearby Beaver Meadows in 1818, the Hazleton Coal Company was incorporated in 1836, the town became a borough on January 5, 1857 and a city on December 4, 1891. Small company towns called patches grew around it, including Jeddo, Stockton, Jeansville, Tresckow and Freeland.

  • German and Irish immigrants arrived in the 1840s and 1850s.
  • Italian, Polish, Russian, Lithuanian, Slovak and Montenegrin workers followed from the 1860s to the 1920s.
  • Since the early 2000s, new residents from the Dominican Republic and New York and New Jersey have reshaped the city again.

The result is a housing stock of narrow, older homes on steep, close lots. Many have been in a family for generations, which is why a good number of Hazleton sales involve an estate, several heirs or a house with deferred maintenance.

What does Hazleton's economy and transportation look like?

Mining and garment work have mostly disappeared. Distribution and manufacturing now dominate through the Humboldt Industrial Park in neighboring Hazle Township, where employers have included Amazon, Coca-Cola, American Eagle Outfitters, Hershey, General Mills and Steelcase. Residents commute 21.3 minutes on average.

Three interstates reach the area: I-80, I-81 and I-476, the Northeast Extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike. Five state routes enter the city: PA 93 on Broad Street, PA 309 on Church Street, PA 424, PA 924 and PA 940. Hazleton Public Transit runs nine routes through the city and surrounding towns, and jitney companies run to Stroudsburg and New York City via I-80.

The Hazleton Area School District serves the city, with Hazleton Elementary/Middle, Heights-Terrace Elementary/Middle and Arthur Street Elementary inside city limits and Hazleton Area High School in Hazle Township. Greater Hazleton, which includes parts of Luzerne, Schuylkill and Carbon counties, had 77,187 residents in 2010.

Outdoor options matter to buyers relocating from larger cities. Memorial Park, the Greater Hazleton Rails to Trails, Hickory Run State Park and Lehigh Gorge State Park are all within reach, and you can mention the nearest one when you describe the house.

What city rules apply to Hazleton rentals, permits and inspections?

Several Hazleton rules can affect how a sale closes, and City Hall at 570-459-4960 can point you to the Code Enforcement Office. Residential rental units must be registered with the Code Enforcement Office within 30 days of a new owner taking title, with one application and one license per property.

  • An owner who lives more than 10 air miles outside the city must appoint an agent who lives within 10 air miles.
  • Building permits are required for interior renovation, new siding, a new roof, sidewalks, sheds, fences, paving and concrete work.
  • Residential permit applications can take up to 15 days, and all outstanding fees and fines, including property taxes, garbage, water and sewer, must be paid before a permit is issued.
  • A residential zoning permit costs $75 per unit and takes about 15 days.
