Extra copies of a certificate of occupancy cost $5, and a cancellation, reschedule or no-show adds $50. Because the city ties permits to unpaid taxes and utility bills, clear those before you ask for any permit.

Can the Hazleton Land Bank or code violations affect my sale?

If the house is vacant, blighted or tax-delinquent, yes. The City of Hazleton Land Bank exists to return vacant, abandoned and tax-delinquent properties to productive use, and its board meets on the first and third Wednesdays of each month. Ask City Hall whether any code or fee balance is attached to your property before you sign a sale contract.

Hazleton voters approved a Home Rule Charter in the November 3, 2026 general election. Call the Code Enforcement Office to confirm whether the charter changes any permit or inspection step that applies to your sale.

How are recording and transfer tax handled in Luzerne County?

A Hazleton deed is filed with the Luzerne County Recorder of Deeds. The commonwealth taxes the transfer at 1 percent of the property's value, and a local share is collected beside it. Seller and buyer are jointly liable, so the closing statement should show who covers what.

Inheritance transfers are exempt, which helps an heir putting a house in their own name. The revenue department's Luzerne County valuation factor is 1.14 for deeds accepted during the year that began July 1, 2026. Ask the Recorder's office or your title company for the local rate and recording fees.

Which sale path fits a Hazleton house?

Hazleton owners usually pick one of three paths.

  • Use an agent for a sound house and a seller who can wait out financing and inspections.
  • Sell yourself to keep the commission, taking on pricing, showings and contracts.
  • Take a cash offer for an inherited, vacant, damaged or rented house, bought as-is on a closing date you pick.

Total the repairs, taxes owed, rental registration items and holding costs before you decide.

More questions about Hazleton, PA

Must I register a Hazleton rental after buying it?

Yes. The City's Code Enforcement Office wants rental units registered within 30 days of a change in ownership. An owner living beyond a 10-mile air radius of the city must name an agent who lives inside it.

Can I get a Hazleton building permit with city bills unpaid?

No. The city requires every outstanding fee and fine, among them property taxes, garbage, water and sewer, to be paid before it issues a permit.

What does a Hazleton occupancy inspection cost?

The fee is $75 per dwelling unit with 15 days of notice, $150 with less and $300 inside 72 hours. Extra certificate copies cost $5, and a no-show adds $50.

Does an inherited Hazleton house trigger transfer tax?

Not on the inheritance itself, which state rules exempt whether or not there is a will. The heirs' later sale to a buyer is a separate transfer with the 1 percent state tax plus the local share.

Which district covers Hazleton schools?

The Hazleton Area School District does. Three of its schools sit inside city limits, and Hazleton Area High School is in Hazle Township.

Upper Macungie at a glance

Selling in Upper Macungie?
We buy Upper Macungie houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Where is Upper Macungie Township, and how big has it grown?

Upper Macungie is a Lehigh County township about 11.5 miles southwest of Allentown, 60.8 miles northwest of Philadelphia and 99.2 miles west of New York City. It spans 26.3 square miles and was created in 1832 when Macungie Township was divided into Upper and Lower Macungie. Wikipedia lists seven villages: Breinigsville, Fogelsville, Krocksville, Kuhnsville, Newtown, Ruppsville and Trexlertown.

The growth numbers are the story here. The township counted 13,895 people in 2000, 20,063 in 2010 and 26,377 in 2020, a gain of 44.4 percent in the first decade and 31.5 percent in the second. The 2020 census found 9,313 households with an average size of 2.65 people. A township that added so many residents in two decades has plenty of newer housing, so look at what comparable recent homes on your side of the township listed for.

The ZIP codes are 18031, 18051, 18087, 18104 and 18106. Lower Macungie lies to the southeast and South Whitehall to the northeast, while Maxatawny and Longswamp Townships in Berks County border the township on the west and southwest.

How do roads, buses and schools in Upper Macungie affect a listing?

Interstate 78 and U.S. 22 cross at exit 49 in Fogelsville, where Pennsylvania Route 100 also meets them. U.S. 222 cuts from southwest to northeast, and PA 100, Interstate 476 and PA 863 carry traffic north and south. Schantz Road links several industrial and commerce parks across the township. As of 2022 the township had 182.81 miles of public roads, with 135.94 miles maintained by the township, 45.97 by PennDOT and 0.90 by the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission. LANta bus routes 213, 218 and 322 serve it.

The Parkland School District covers the township. Grades 9 through 12 attend Parkland High School, and most middle schoolers go to Springhouse Middle School, except those in the far north. Fogelsville, Fred J. Jaindl and Veterans Memorial Elementary Schools are located in the township. Parkland Community Library on Walbert Avenue is free to residents of Upper Macungie, North Whitehall and South Whitehall townships.

  • Spell out the drive to I-78, Route 100 and the industrial parks off Schantz Road.
  • Name the elementary school only after confirming the attendance zone with Parkland.
  • Mention the library, parks and the Lehigh Valley hospital campus if they are close.

Does the weather or land in Upper Macungie matter to buyers?

Freezing Januaries shape the house. Fogelsville averages 28.5 degrees Fahrenheit in January and 73.3 in July, and the township falls in plant hardiness zone 6b. Buyers therefore look hard at the furnace, roof and insulation, and an aging boiler will come up in their inspection.

Water flows to Little Lehigh Creek and Jordan Creek, which both feed the Lehigh River, so walk the lot for low spots and check where downspouts discharge. The township's permit list includes a Low Pressure Sewer System Connection form. A house on that system will draw questions about maintenance, so get the facts from the township before you list.

Farm and forest parcels may be enrolled in Clean and Green, a county program that taxes land on how it is used. Enrolled owners should check the conveyance form the county posts before a sale closes.

What permits and zoning rules affect selling in Upper Macungie?

No resale inspection is listed among the Permit Department's forms. The department works from Suite 311 at 7540 Windsor Drive, keeps weekday hours of 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. and enforces the state's building codes. Its form list covers basements, decks, kitchens, bathrooms, roof re-shingling, water heaters, HVAC replacement, pools, oil tank removal and sheds, and it also lists a Business Use and Occupancy application. Nothing on it covers an ordinary house sale, so call the department and ask what, if anything, your address needs at transfer.

Pennsylvania moved to the 2021 ICC code series for enforcement on January 1, 2026. Work under contracts signed before that date could use the older 2018 code if the permit was filed by June 30, 2026, and anything signed or filed after that must meet the 2021 code. If you have an unfinished project, ask the township which code applies to it.

  • Zoning permits are issued when a use or structure conforms to the zoning ordinance.
  • If the township denies a zoning permit, you can take it to the Zoning Hearing Board, which sits most months on the second and fourth Wednesday evenings.
  • The township wants a hearing application roughly four weeks ahead to meet advertising rules.
  • The township is rewriting its zoning ordinance, and printed copies of the current one cost $35.

What does Lehigh County charge and record when an Upper Macungie house sells?

Your deed gets recorded in the Courthouse in downtown Allentown, in the Recorder of Deeds division on West Hamilton Street, Room 122. Staff are reachable at 610-782-3162 on weekdays. The Commonwealth takes 1 percent of the value at recording, and the county collects a local portion with it. The local portion can be divided between township and school district, so confirm the exact rate for your deed with the Recorder before you run net proceeds.

Lehigh County rules that touch an Upper Macungie sale. Sources: Lehigh County Assessment Office and Recorder of Deeds

Conveyances among spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are generally exempt. A statement of value form goes with any deed that claims another exemption or leaves out the full price. Deeds are public record, so the county cannot keep a sale price out of print.

How does the Lehigh County assessment and appeal work for Upper Macungie owners?

Values at the Lehigh County Assessment Office trace back to the 2013 countywide reassessment, which set assessments at the full fair market value of that year. An owner who disagrees files with the county Board of Assessment Appeals. The yearly cutoff is August 1, and the Board wants the original signed form and fee in hand by then. A mailed postmark or a fax does not prove a timely filing, so deliver the paper yourself or mail it well ahead.

A newer state law, Act 29 of 2026, signed July 20, 2026, adds a duty for buyers who will not live in the home: they must send the county a contact record within a month of purchase. An investor who buys your house will handle that after closing. County assessment staff can be reached at 610-782-3038.

Township and school tax rates come from the township office and the Parkland School District tax office, so pull your latest bill before you price the house.

How can I sell an Upper Macungie house quickly?

Most owners weigh a traditional listing against a direct sale to a buyer who pays cash and takes the house in its current state. With so much newer housing around you, buyers compare condition closely, and a dated or worn property may fit a cash buyer better.

  • A listing suits a recently updated house and an owner who is fine with weeks of showings and lender timelines.
  • A direct sale suits an inherited house, a tenant-occupied one, or a seller with a fixed moving date.
  • Collect permit records for any finished basement, deck or kitchen project, because buyers and title agents ask for them.

Get each offer in writing and compare what you would actually net after transfer tax, fees and repairs.

More questions about Upper Macungie, PA

Is a resale inspection part of closing on an Upper Macungie house?

The Permit Department's forms list shows no residential resale inspection. Call the department to learn whether your address needs anything, and close out any open permits before listing.

Which school district serves Upper Macungie Township?

Parkland School District. Students in grades 9 through 12 attend Parkland High School, and most middle schoolers attend Springhouse Middle School. Confirm your attendance zone with the district.

What is the cutoff for contesting an Upper Macungie assessment?

August 1 each year for annual appeals. The Board needs the original signed form and fee in its hands by then, and it gives no credit for a fax or a postmark.

How much transfer tax applies when an Upper Macungie house sells?

The state takes 1 percent, and the county adds a local portion when the deed is recorded. Call the Recorder of Deeds at 610-782-3162 to confirm the local figure for your property.

What if my Upper Macungie land is enrolled in Clean and Green?

Talk to the county Assessment Office before signing a contract. The program taxes qualifying land on its use value and generally starts at ten acres, and the county posts a conveyance form for land that changes hands.

What should I know about selling a house in Whitehall Township?

Whitehall is a home rule township in Lehigh County, so the rules that matter most to a seller come from the township building on MacArthur Road. The big one is a mandatory resale inspection, and it shapes how fast a sale can close.

The township covers about 12.6 square miles on the north side of Allentown, with the Lehigh River marking its eastern edge. The Census Bureau estimates 29,405 residents for July 2025, a gain of 0.8 percent over the 2020 base. Owners live in about 62 percent of homes, and the 2020 to 2024 midpoint for home value is $262,100. Households count 11,664, with a median household income of $75,658.

Local history explains the housing stock. Farming and then the Lehigh Canal, iron furnaces and the "Cement Belt" built villages such as Hokendauqua, Cementon, Fullerton and Egypt, and after World War II the township became an Allentown suburb. The villages merged under a single Whitehall post office identity in 1968, and voters adopted the home rule charter in 1974.

Does Whitehall Township require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The township's FAQ says it requires an inspection for the resale of your property, and its permits page adds that a change of use or occupancy, including a home sale, needs a certificate of occupancy.

The township says each time a property is offered for sale or lease it needs a fresh inspection and a new certificate, even when a rental has several tenants in a year. Its Certificate of Occupancy Application and Guide lays out the steps:

  • Submit the inspection request form with the fee to the Bureau of Development at 3219 MacArthur Road.
  • An inspector contacts you within 1 to 3 business days, and the visit is set within 5 to 10 business days.
  • If nothing is wrong, the clear certificate is issued within 1 to 3 business days.
  • Payment is by cash, check or money order only. The form says cards are not accepted.

Add those windows up and the paperwork alone can take two to three weeks, so ask for the inspection as soon as you pick a settlement date.

What does the Whitehall inspection cost, and what do inspectors check?

Whitehall Township charges listed on the township inspection form (revised May 2023) and FAQ page
ItemCharge
Single-family resale inspection$65
Apartment unit inspection$35 per unit
Conditional certificate for an as-is single-family sale$65 plus a $100 deposit
Conditional certificate for a rental of up to five units$100 plus a $250 deposit
Moving permit$5

Call the township at 610-437-5524 to confirm amounts before you mail a check, since the form carries a 2023 revision date.

The township describes the visit as a targeted safety inspection that is narrower than a full home inspection. Items on its checklist include working smoke detectors on every level and in each sleeping area, a carbon monoxide alarm near bedrooms where a fireplace, attached garage or fuel-burning heater exists, GFCI outlets in kitchens, baths and laundry areas, handrails on stairs of four or more risers, a 100-amp minimum electrical service, a concrete basement floor and visible house numbers at least four inches tall. Missing items are the usual reason for a failed first pass.

What happens if the inspection finds problems?

You have two paths. Fix the violations and have the inspector return, or sell as is with a conditional certificate. The guide says repairs must be corrected and reinspected within 30 days or before settlement.

For an as-is sale, the seller gives the inspection report to the other party, and a notarized Buyer or Seller Acceptance Form goes back to the township with the added fees. The conditional certificate allows the transfer only. Nobody can move in until all required repairs pass inspection, and the deposit comes back once a clear certificate is issued inside the allotted time.

This matters for homes that need work. Heirs, landlords and owners with deferred repairs often cannot finish a punch list before closing, which is why buyers who purchase as is tend to pair well with the conditional certificate route. Ask any buyer, cash or financed, who will sign the acceptance form and who will complete the repairs.

What transfer taxes and recording steps apply in Lehigh County?

Pennsylvania charges a realty transfer tax of 1 percent of the value, and the state holds both grantor and grantee jointly and severally liable. County recorders usually collect it alongside any local transfer tax, so the deed cannot be recorded until the tax is paid.

  • The Lehigh County Recorder of Deeds sits at the courthouse, 455 W. Hamilton Street, Room 122, in Allentown, with weekday hours of 8:00 AM until 4:30 PM. The phone is 610-782-3162.
  • Transfers between spouses, parent and child, grandparent and grandchild, and siblings are generally exempt, and a family exemption has to be stated on the deed.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) accompanies any transfer that does not pay the full tax, does not state full consideration or claims an exemption.

Ask the Recorder or your closing agent for the local rate that applies to a Whitehall address, because the municipal and school district share is set locally.

How do rental properties change a Whitehall sale?

Landlords face one extra rule. The township requires every non-owner-occupied property to name a local responsible agent whose office or home is within 10 miles of the township boundary. That person must be reachable in an emergency and authorized to accept legal service for the owner.

The inspection request form asks whether the property will be a rental and, if so, for the agent's name, address, daytime and after-hours phone numbers. Tenants who leave before closing also trigger paperwork, because the township asks for a moving permit when anyone moves into, out of or within the township. The FAQ prices that permit at $5 and says it is issued at the Township Tax Office from 8:00am to 4:00pm.

An owner with a tenant in place can still sell, but the inspector needs access to every room, attic and the exterior, so plan notice to the tenant early.

How do schools and neighborhoods affect resale in Whitehall?

Buyers looking at Whitehall compare it with other Lehigh Valley suburbs, and the Whitehall-Coplay School District is the main draw. It serves the township and neighboring Coplay, and ninth through twelfth graders attend Whitehall High School. Several parochial and private schools sit inside the township too, including Good Shepherd Catholic School, Lehigh Valley Lutheran School and St. Elizabeth Regional School.

Shopping and commuting add appeal. The Lehigh Valley Mall is the largest shopping mall based in the Lehigh Valley, and MacArthur Road (PA 145) carries retail traffic past an interchange with US 22, the Lehigh Valley Thruway. PA 329 crosses the northern part of the township, and LANta buses serve the MacArthur Road corridor. As of 2018 the township maintained about 97.6 miles of its own roads, with PennDOT handling roughly 23 miles.

More questions about Whitehall, PA

Can I sell my Whitehall house without a certificate of occupancy?

No. Whitehall Township requires an inspection and a certificate of occupancy for a resale, and the new owner cannot occupy the property until one is issued. A conditional certificate is available for as-is sales.

How much is the Whitehall resale inspection?

The township's form lists $65 for a single-family home and $35 per apartment unit. An as-is sale adds a $100 deposit for a house, per the form revised in May 2023, so confirm the current amount with the township.

Can I sell a Whitehall house as is if it fails inspection?

Yes. The seller or buyer signs a notarized acceptance form, pays the added fees and receives a conditional certificate that allows the sale only. All listed repairs must pass inspection before anyone occupies the home.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Whitehall home sale?

The state says buyer and seller are both liable for the 1 percent state tax, and the contract decides how the cost is split. The deed is not recorded until the tax is paid, so your closing agent usually collects it at settlement.

Do I need a local agent if my Whitehall house is a rental?

Yes. Non-owner-occupied properties must have a responsible agent within 10 miles of the township. The inspection request form asks for that person's contact details whenever the property is a rental.

How do I sell my house fast in Spring Township, PA?

A direct cash sale is the fastest route for a Spring Township house, but the township's property transfer inspection has to be scheduled either way. Spring Township is in Berks County, west of Reading, and it requires an exterior inspection of every single and multiple family dwelling before title changes hands.

The inspection is the step that most often decides the calendar, so this page puts it first and then covers the township itself: where it sits, what its housing looks like in Census figures, how the creeks and hills affect lots, and what the buyer and seller each pay.

What is the Spring Township property transfer inspection?

It is a required exterior check under the township's Property Transfer Ordinance 341, in effect since August 1, 2007, and the Code Enforcement Officer must inspect before title transfers. The seller, buyer or either side's agent can file the application.

The application goes to the Code and Zoning Office no later than 30 business days before settlement. The fee is $150 per property, and it rises to $250 if the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. After a complete application, the officer inspects within 10 business days.

  • Utility and storm drainage easements and road rights-of-way must be clear of obstructions, including landscaping.
  • Fences, pools, spas, sheds and decks must be permitted and sit within setback and yard rules. Pool fencing needs a self-closing, latching gate.
  • Sanitary sewer connections must control inflow and infiltration, and sump pump discharge must be properly placed.
  • The number of dwelling units, bedrooms and smoke detectors is checked against township records.

How much does the inspection cost and how long does it take?

Spring Township property transfer inspection. Source: Township of Spring, Property Transfer page.
When the application is filedInspection feeInspector's response
30 business days or more before settlement$150Within 10 business days
Fewer than 15 business days before settlement$250Within 10 business days

The inspection covers only exterior, observable conditions, and nobody has to be home as long as the inspector can reach the backyard. Add a note with a phone number to the application if you want to be there.

What happens if the inspection finds problems?

Seller and buyer both sign the report to confirm they read it and agree to correct what it lists, and the township then issues a Property Transfer Certificate once the deficiencies are done. That can happen before or after settlement.

You do not have to fix everything before closing. If the buyer is willing to take on the repairs, an addendum to the agreement of sale normally settles who is responsible and how the money works. The township suggests ordering the inspection soon after you decide to sell, because the report has to be disclosed to the buyer and an early look leaves time to permit anything that was built without approval.

Common findings are an unpermitted shed or deck, a fence in an easement, or a pool without the right barrier. Those are fixable, and a cash buyer who plans to renovate will often accept them as part of an as-is purchase.

Where is Spring Township and what is the area like?

Spring Township covers about 18.4 square miles of land in Berks County, west of Reading and next to Wyomissing, Sinking Spring and Adamstown. The Census Bureau counted 28,407 residents in 2020 and estimates 28,873 for 2025, a gain of 1.7 percent. It is the second largest municipality in the county after Reading.

The township was split from Cumru Township in 1850 and takes its name from a large spring that appeared and disappeared with the limestone beneath it, which early settlers called the Sinking Spring. Terrain varies a lot: low ground in the north, with Cacoosing Creek on the northwest edge and Tulpehocken Creek on the northeast, and hills toward the Lancaster County line in the southwest. Communities inside the township include West Lawn, Whitfield, Spring Ridge, Vinemont and Montrose Manor.

Wertz's Covered Bridge, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, is one of the landmarks. The township shares the main western Reading retail district with Wyomissing, and Penn State Berks sits in the northeast corner.

What do Census figures say about Spring Township homes?

Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 show 11,495 households, a 75.3 percent owner-occupied rate and a median owner-occupied home value of $286,900. Median gross rent is $1,416, and median household income is $94,837.

About 17.6 percent of residents speak a language other than English at home, and 9.1 percent are foreign-born. Median selected monthly owner costs are $1,754 with a mortgage and $819 without. About a quarter of homes are rented, so some sellers here are small landlords who should check lease dates before setting a closing date.

How do the roads, bus routes and schools matter to buyers?

Spring Township has 130.6 miles of public roads, of which 112.16 miles are maintained by the township and the rest by PennDOT. U.S. 222, U.S. 422 and Pennsylvania Route 724 cross it, and U.S. 222 south gives expressway access toward the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Lancaster. Mean travel time to work is 23.6 minutes.

BARTA bus routes 12, 14, 15 and 16 serve residential and business areas and connect to the transportation center in Reading. Public schools are in the Wilson School District, which has five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. For a buyer, a house near a bus line or the bypass reads differently from one in a quieter subdivision, so mention it in any listing or offer discussion.

Which township rules can catch a seller by surprise?

Spring Township reviews more than 700 permits a year and enforces its fence, shed and pool rules closely. Fences in a front yard are limited to 4 feet and must be open style, rear-yard fences can reach 6 feet, and sheds are not allowed in required front or side yards.

Residential grass and weeds may not exceed 8 inches. After a verified complaint the township sends a notice, cuts the property after 7 days if the owner does not, and bills the owner, and unpaid amounts become a lien on the real estate. Sidewalks must be cleared of snow and ice within 24 hours after it stops, with the same lien risk. Clear both before you list so the inspection comes back clean.

How are taxes and transfer costs handled in Spring Township?

County and municipal tax payments can be made online through the Berks County Treasurer, and Wilson School District taxes are paid at Fulton Bank, according to the township tax collector's page. Call the tax collector's office for a payoff figure before closing.

Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent state realty transfer tax, collected with any local share by the Berks County Recorder of Deeds when the deed is recorded. Ask the Recorder for the combined local rate, and expect the buyer and seller to split it unless the sales agreement says otherwise.

More questions about Spring, PA

Does Spring Township require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes. Ordinance 341 requires an exterior property transfer inspection by the Code Enforcement Officer before title changes. Apply at least 30 business days before settlement to pay the $150 fee.

What is the late fee for a Spring Township transfer inspection?

The fee is $250 instead of $150 when the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. The inspector still responds within 10 business days of a complete application.

Do I have to fix every item before closing?

No. A buyer can agree to make the corrections, and an addendum to the agreement of sale usually covers it. The Property Transfer Certificate is issued once the deficiencies are completed, before or after settlement.

What is the population of Spring Township?

The Census Bureau estimates 28,873 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 28,407 in the 2020 census. It is the second most populous municipality in Berks County.

Which school district serves Spring Township?

The Wilson School District serves the township, with five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. School real estate tax is paid separately from county and township tax.

What should I know before selling a house in McCandless?

McCandless is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, officially called the Town of McCandless, and a sale there carries a 2.5 percent combined transfer tax that is higher than in several neighboring communities. The town also issues its own lien letter and points sellers to the sanitary authority for a dye test.

The town covers about 16.6 square miles in Pittsburgh's North Hills and had 29,709 residents in the 2020 census. It sits on the Allegheny Plateau at roughly 1,024 feet of elevation, and hilly ground defines most streets. Pine Creek cuts a deep valley through the middle of the town, with a floodplain along the creek.

Because of its home rule status, the town no longer operates under the First Class Township Code, although it is treated as a first-class township for certain purposes. McCandless borders Pine Township to the north, Hampton Township to the east, Ross Township to the south and the borough of Franklin Park to the west. Its public schools belong to the North Allegheny School District, and the Northland Public Library is shared with nearby municipalities.

How did McCandless grow into a North Hills suburb?

The first European settler, James Duff, bought 400 acres in 1796, and the area stayed farmland through the 1800s. The township was organized in 1851 as Taylor Township and was renamed McCandless in 1857 after a district judge.

Several events shaped the housing map you see today:

  • A 1908 interurban rail line, the Harmony Line, let residents commute to Pittsburgh until it closed in 1931.
  • Allegheny County created North Park in 1927, and about 1,600 acres of it, roughly 15.2 percent of the town, lie inside McCandless.
  • Population jumped from 2,653 in 1930 to 6,488 in 1950 and 14,582 in 1960.
  • McKnight Road opened in the mid-1950s as the main route into the north suburbs.
  • The Community College of Allegheny County opened a campus in 1972.
  • McCandless Crossing, a mixed-use center with apartments and townhomes, was completed in 2016.

The population has been roughly flat since 1990, with 28,781 residents then and 29,709 in 2020, so listings compete with a mature, established housing supply.

Which McCandless neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

Buyers commonly search by named plan or community, and McCandless has many. Allison Park is one community inside the town, and the list also includes Meadow Oaks, Guyton Farms, Greybrooke, Bennington Woods, Pin Oak, Briarwood, Park Meadows, Foxcroft Village, Sample Manor, Colington Square, Royal Manor, Pinnacle Pointe and Longvue Acres.

Five ZIP codes cover the town: 15237, 15090, 15044, 15101 and 15127. That matters for a listing because a house inside the town can carry more than one postal city. Confirm the municipality on the tax bill, not the postal city, before checking local rules.

Homes near Pine Creek deserve a floodplain check. Ask the town whether your lot sits in the mapped floodplain before you write the listing description.

What is the transfer tax when you sell in McCandless?

The total realty transfer tax on a McCandless sale is 2.5 percent. That figure combines the state's 1 percent, a 1 percent municipal share and a one half of 1 percent North Allegheny School District share, based on the county's published rate table.

The municipal rate is the notable part. Allegheny County's table lists McCandless at 1 percent, the same as Hampton and Pine townships, while Ross Township and Franklin Park borough list one half of 1 percent. On a $300,000 sale, the difference between a 2 percent and a 2.5 percent total is $1,500, so the rate belongs in your net sheet.

The county collects the tax when the deed is recorded. The state says buyer and seller are both liable, and contracts decide the split. Some transfers, including certain deeds between family members and property passed through an estate, are exempt from the state portion, so ask the county's Real Estate office how an exemption is documented.

What does the Town of McCandless need from a seller?

A seller should order a municipal lien letter and arrange a dye test. The lien letter costs $30 by mail or $35 if the results are emailed, and the request needs the owner's name, property address, parcel number and the reason, such as a sale. Checks are payable to the Town of McCandless.

McCandless sale paperwork. Source: Town of McCandless Tax Information FAQ and Allegheny County transfer tax table.

The sanitary authority and the water authority can each file liens for unpaid service, so call both before the closing. The lien letter request is handled by the town's tax office at 412-364-0616.

How are real estate taxes billed in McCandless?

The deputy tax collector, Jordan Tax Service, collects both Town and North Allegheny School District real estate tax. Beginning in 2026, owners receive two separate invoices, one for the Town and one for the school district.

  • The Town millage for 2026 is 1.236 mills.
  • The North Allegheny School District rate is 20.43 mills for the 2025 to 2026 school year, or $2,043 per $100,000 of assessed value.
  • Allegheny County lists 6.43 mills.
  • Taxes unpaid after December 31 are delinquent and can lead to a lien on the property.

An installment plan with three equal payments is open only to owners with a homestead or farmstead exclusion. The first payment is due August 31, followed by October 31 and December 31, and late installments carry a 10 percent penalty. Owners approved for the Act 77 senior citizen discount receive 30 percent off the Town portion. Pay tax on time even while an appeal is pending, because the higher amount must be paid once a deadline passes.

Payments cannot be left in the Town Hall drop box. Send them to Jordan Tax Service or use the options printed on the statement. Jordan representatives also sit at Town Hall on select dates, which are posted on the Town calendar, and owners should bring the full tax statements. Earned income tax and business privilege tax are handled separately by the Keystone Collections Group.

Can I still appeal my Allegheny County assessment?

The 2027 annual appeal window ran from July 1 through September 1, 2026, and it has closed. The Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears appeals, and it sends residential hearing notices at least 14 days ahead.

The county set its 2027 common level ratio at 49.3 percent, a factor applied to market value in appeals that started in September 2026. Owners who missed the window should ask the Office of Property Assessments about the next annual period and about special appeals tied to a change notice.

Should I list a McCandless house or accept a cash purchase?

Cash works best when the house needs repairs or the closing date matters more than the last dollar of price. A listing suits a house in good condition in a popular plan, where several buyers may compete.

  • Get the lien letter and dye test started before you accept any offer.
  • Compare offers after the 2.5 percent transfer tax, any payoff and the unpaid portion of the year's Town and school taxes.
  • Ask each buyer how they treat the dye test result if the sewer lateral needs work.

More questions about McCandless, PA

What is the total transfer tax in McCandless?

2.5 percent. The state charges 1 percent, McCandless charges 1 percent, and the North Allegheny School District charges one half of 1 percent.

How do I get a lien letter from the Town of McCandless?

Mail a request with the owner's name, address, parcel number and reason, along with a $30 check. The email option costs $35. Write the check to the Town of McCandless.

Who collects real estate tax in McCandless?

Jordan Tax Service collects both Town and North Allegheny School District real estate tax. Owners receive two separate invoices starting in 2026.

Which school district serves McCandless?

North Allegheny School District. McCandless is also part of the shared Northland Public Library.

Is the 2027 Allegheny County appeal window still open?

No. The 2027 annual appeal period ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026. Contact the county's Office of Property Assessments about later options.

What does a Susquehanna Township, PA home seller need to know first?

Susquehanna Township is a first-class township on the north side of Harrisburg in Dauphin County, with the ZIP codes 17109 and 17110. Three offices matter: the township for permits, the county treasurer for tax bills, and the Dauphin County recorder for the deed.

The township was carved out of Lower Paxtang Township on May 1, 1815 and takes its name from the Susquehanna River along its western edge. Its first settlement, Coxestown, was laid out in 1757 and later renamed Estherton. The Rockville Bridge, the long stone-arch rail bridge that links the township to Marysville across the river, was added to the National Register in 1975.

How big is the township, and where do its neighborhoods sit?

The township covers 15.3 square miles, of which 13.3 are land and 1.9 are water, and elevations climb from about 300 feet at the river to about 1,150 feet in the northeast on Blue Mountain. That range matters to a seller because a hillside lot and a riverside lot raise very different buyer questions about drainage, access and views.

  • Named communities: Beaufort Farms, Edgemont, Estherton, Lucknow, Montrose Park, Paxtang Manor, Progress and Rockville.
  • Main roads: Interstate 81, U.S. 22, U.S. 322 and Pennsylvania Route 39, plus local arteries such as Elmerton Avenue and Progress Avenue.
  • Neighbors: Middle Paxton and Lower Paxton townships, Swatara Township, Paxtang, Penbrook and Harrisburg, with East Pennsboro Township across the river in Cumberland County.
  • Attractions: the National Civil War Museum sits just inside the boundary, and the Capital Area Greenbelt runs through the township.

How is the housing market in Susquehanna Township put together?

The 2025 Census estimate is 28,434 people, up 6.2 percent from the 26,762 April 2020 base and well past the 24,036 of 2010. No other place in this four-way Census comparison grew as quickly.

Owners live in 62.9 percent of the homes, and the middle owned home was valued at $227,100 in the 2020 to 2024 survey. Rent runs $1,487, above neighboring Swatara, and household income is $84,832. The township has 11,894 households of 2.26 people on average, and 19.9 percent of the population is 65 and over.

Close to 37 percent of homes are rented, so landlords shop alongside owner-occupants. Tell any buyer up front whether the house is occupied and on what lease terms.

What permits and building codes apply to a Susquehanna Township seller?

Residential permits go to the municipal office at 1900 Linglestown Road in Harrisburg, and the township number for questions is 717-909-9251. Every application needs a site plan, and commercial plans go electronically to the Middle Department Inspection Agency.

Pennsylvania adopted the 2021 International Construction Codes effective January 1, 2026, so repairs done after that date follow the newer edition. The township adopted the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code on July 14, 2022, effective July 19, 2022, and that is the standard code enforcement uses on existing houses.

A contractor who disagrees with a ruling can appeal to the Joint Uniform Construction Code Appeals Board. Hearings are held as needed on the fourth Tuesday of each month at 5 p.m. in the Hampden Township Municipal Building in Mechanicsburg.

A public hearing on a Linglestown Road Overlay zoning map and text amendment was scheduled for November 12, 2026. A house along that corridor deserves a call to the township about the final text before you list.

Which office bills property tax in Susquehanna Township, and what transfer tax applies?

Here the Dauphin County Treasurer acts as tax collector, from 101 Market Street, Room 105 in Harrisburg, phone 717-780-6550. Neighboring Swatara Township has its own collector, so the two townships do not share an office.

The county Recorder of Deeds supplies that split and keeps deeds dating to 1785. Find it in the courthouse at 101 Market Street, Room 102, phone 717-780-6560. Recording fees can be paid by cash or check, and family transfers are generally exempt.

Ask the treasurer what is owed on your parcel before closing, since the title company deducts any balance from your proceeds.

How does Susquehanna Township compare with its neighbor Swatara?

Susquehanna Township's middle home value of $227,100 runs about $12,700 above Swatara Township's $214,400, and its median household income of $84,832 beats Swatara's $80,444. The two townships touch along the south side, and a buyer shopping the Harrisburg suburbs will often look at both.

The housing mix differs. Swatara has 69.9 percent owner occupancy against 62.9 percent here, and median gross rent is $1,487 in Susquehanna and $1,252 in Swatara. The township also has 1,793 veterans, 12.7 percent foreign-born residents and 90.6 percent of households with a broadband subscription.

These comparisons matter at the negotiating table. If you price against a Swatara sale, remember that the two townships have different rental shares, different school districts and different tax collectors.

How is Susquehanna Township governed, and why does that matter to a seller?

Susquehanna became a first-class township through a Dauphin County Court order on January 2, 1952, and a Board of Commissioners with nine members elected by ward runs it today. Appeals of zoning decisions go to a Zoning Hearing Board, and a separate Township Authority also holds regular meetings.

The township's November 2026 calendar listed meetings of all three bodies, including a Zoning Hearing Board session on November 4, an Authority meeting on November 10 and a Commissioners meeting on November 12. Agendas and minutes are posted in the township's online Agenda Center, so a seller facing a zoning question can read what has already been decided. The township keeps its own police department, which began with a single officer sworn in during September 1955.

Which schools serve Susquehanna Township buyers?

Susquehanna Township School District covers the township with a primary school, an elementary school, a middle school and a high school, and its offices sit on Elmerton Avenue in Harrisburg.

On education, 92.5 percent of adults hold at least a high school diploma and 40.7 percent a bachelor's degree or beyond. A 20.3 minute average commute suits a township beside Harrisburg and along I-81.

What are the practical ways to sell a Susquehanna Township house quickly?

Selling straight to a buyer avoids showings and lets you pick the closing day, while a listing puts the house in front of the most people. Sellers here often face an inherited house, a tenant in place or repairs they would rather skip.

  • Pull your deed copy from the county and request a loan payoff before talking to buyers.
  • Walk the house against the 2021 maintenance code and fix peeling paint, broken steps and loose railings.
  • Write into the offer who pays the 2 percent transfer tax.
  • Compare what a listing would net after fees and repairs with a direct offer, including timing.

Either way the deed is recorded in Harrisburg and the county tax split is the same.

More questions about Susquehanna, PA

Who bills real estate tax in Susquehanna Township?

The Dauphin County Treasurer, at 101 Market Street, Room 105 in Harrisburg. The treasurer's 2026 collector list shows the county office handling Susquehanna Township, and the phone number is 717-780-6550.

What transfer tax comes with a Susquehanna Township sale?

Two percent of the price: 1 percent to the state and half a percent each to the municipality and school district, according to the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

Where is a Susquehanna Township deed recorded?

Dauphin County. The Recorder of Deeds is in the courthouse at 101 Market Street, Harrisburg, and the office holds deeds back to 1785.

Which building codes does the township follow?

Pennsylvania's Uniform Construction Code governs building work, and the township adopted the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code for existing buildings, effective July 19, 2022. Residential permit questions go to 717-909-9251.

How much has Susquehanna Township grown?

The Census Bureau counted 24,036 residents in 2010 and 26,736 in 2020, and estimated 28,434 on July 1, 2025. That is growth of about 6.2 percent since the 2020 base.

Where is Swatara Township, and what is it like to sell a house there?

Swatara Township is a Dauphin County township just south of Susquehanna Township in the Harrisburg area, and selling a house there means working with a township codes office, a private real estate tax collector and the county recorder. The township's municipal building is at 599 Eisenhower Boulevard in Harrisburg.

A 1799 court order split Lower Paxton Township in two and the southern half took the name Swatara, from Swatara Creek. The word is thought to come from a Susquehannock term meaning where we fed on eels. The township covers 15.5 square miles, with 13.05 of land and nearly 16 percent water along the Susquehanna River, and it holds Calver Island, which was added to the National Register in 2007.

What do the numbers say about Swatara Township?

The 2025 Census estimate is 27,936 residents, far above the 23,362 of 2010 and a hair above the 27,824 counted in 2020. Density is about 2,132 people per square mile.

Owners occupy 69.9 percent of homes, and the middle owned home was valued at $214,400 in the 2020 to 2024 survey. Rent runs $1,252 and household income $80,444. The township has 10,640 households of 2.47 people on average. Foreign-born residents make up 17.2 percent, and 24.7 percent of residents speak another language at home.

  • Named places: Bressler, Enhaut, Oberlin, Lawnton and Rutherford are census-designated places inside the township.
  • Retail and logistics: retail sales in 2022 reached $1,147,259,000, or $41,104 a head, while transportation and warehousing receipts were $509,815,000, the largest figure reported among the four places in this comparison.
  • Education: among adults, 87.5 percent finished high school and 28.5 percent have a bachelor's degree or more.

How does Swatara's codes office affect a sale?

Building and zoning permits come from the township's codes department, and Approved Code Services, Inc. does the plan reviews and construction inspections as the township's sole third-party agency. Property maintenance complaints and enforcement of the International Property Maintenance Code run through the same department.

Expect to need a building permit for new construction, additions and alterations. Routine maintenance, repairs and like-for-like equipment replacement generally need none. Stormwater management permits and quarterly waste fee exemption requests also go through the department.

When an inspector flags unpermitted work, phone the department at 717-564-2551 before replying; the office is open weekdays from 8 until 4:30. The township also runs a fall brush collection, and the 2026 round ran September 21 to 26, a handy moment to clear yard waste before showings.

Who collects real estate tax in Swatara, and what does closing cost in transfer tax?

Real estate tax is collected at a separate office, 6400A Chambers Hill Road in Harrisburg, and the municipal building does not accept those payments. The collector takes payment for the current year only. Tax certification requests go to that office at 717-832-4908.

Keystone Collections Group, with a Dauphin County office on Vartan Way, collects local services tax and earned income tax instead. Knowing the split helps when a title agent asks which office issues which certificate.

What schools and travel times will Swatara buyers weigh?

Central Dauphin School District covers Swatara Township together with Lower Paxton, Middle Paxton and West Hanover townships and the boroughs of Dauphin, Paxtang and Penbrook. Its schools include Swatara Middle School and Lawnton, Rutherford and Chambers Hill elementary schools. Within the county it is the biggest district, and statewide it ranks ninth.

Commutes average 20 minutes. The township reaches the Susquehanna River and is named for Swatara Creek, so a house near the water can raise questions that an interior lot does not. Ask your agent or a surveyor to confirm flood zone status if the property sits close to the creek or the river.

What does Swatara Township's local economy look like?

About 61.9 percent of residents 16 and older are in the labor force, and 61.5 percent of women in that age group are. Census business data for 2022 show $138,896,000 in accommodation and food service sales and $267,885,000 in health care and social assistance receipts, alongside the retail and warehousing figures above.

Household income of $80,444 sits next to a poverty rate of 8.3 percent, and 8.2 percent of residents under 65 lack health insurance. Veterans number 1,357. Buyers who commute to Harrisburg jobs, warehouse work or health care roles will compare this township's prices with the township to its north, so price your house with both in mind and ask your agent for recent sales from each.

What should you collect before closing a Swatara Township sale?

A clean closing depends on a short list of documents, and most of them come from offices named on this page.

  • A tax certification from the township's tax collector, so the title agent sees what has been paid this year.
  • Your lender's payoff letter and a deed copy from the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.
  • Permit records for any addition, deck or alteration, from the Building and Codes Department.
  • Sewer and stormwater bills, which the township lists on a separate online payment page from real estate tax.
  • Receipts for work done since you bought, because buyers who finance will have an appraiser and an inspector look at condition.

Roughly 88.3 percent of people stayed at the same address for a year, so many owners have been in place a long time and may not have handled a sale recently. Children under 18 are 19.3 percent of the population and people 65 and over are 15.4 percent. Broadband reaches 93.0 percent of households.

Which routes work for a quick Swatara Township sale?

You can list with an agent, sell privately or sell straight to an investor or cash buyer. A listing may fetch the most but ties you to showings, repair requests and a lender's calendar.

  • Listing: fits a sound house when you can wait out financing and inspections.
  • Private sale: avoids a commission and leaves pricing and paperwork with you.
  • Direct purchase: cuts out financing and showings and lets you choose the closing day, at a price that reflects repairs.

On any route, line up a tax certification, a lender payoff letter and your deed copy. Have each buyer state in writing who pays the 2 percent transfer tax, because the deed will not record until it is paid.

More questions about Swatara, PA

Where does Swatara real estate tax get paid?

At the township's real estate tax collector at 6400A Chambers Hill Road, Harrisburg, or online through the link on the township's tax page. The municipal building does not accept real estate tax payments.

What does the transfer tax cost on a Swatara sale?

The Dauphin County recorder describes a 2 percent tax, with 1 percent to the state and one half percent each to the municipality and school district. On the $214,400 Census median value, that is $4,288.

Are permits needed for repairs before a Swatara sale?

New construction, additions and alterations generally need a building permit, while routine maintenance and replacement of existing equipment generally do not. Call the Building and Codes Department at 717-564-2551 if you are unsure.

Who collects Swatara's earned income tax?

Keystone Collections Group, which keeps a Dauphin County office on Vartan Way in Harrisburg. This is separate from the real estate tax collector.

What school district serves Swatara Township?

Central Dauphin School District. Its list of schools includes Swatara Middle School and elementary schools in Lawnton, Rutherford and Chambers Hill.

What comes first when a Horsham homeowner decides to sell?

Horsham Township asks every seller of a residential property to complete a township inspection and certification before settlement, so build that step into your timeline from day one. The rest of the sale follows the usual Pennsylvania pattern, with Montgomery County handling assessment, recording and transfer tax.

Horsham sits in Montgomery County about ten miles north of Center City Philadelphia. Its 17.32 square miles held an estimated 27,882 residents by mid-2025, according to the Census Bureau, which is 5.0 percent above 2020. Homes here are worth far more than in older Pennsylvania cities, so a delay of even a few weeks costs real money in carrying costs and interest.

A fast sale to a cash buyer is one route, a listing is another, and a for-sale-by-owner deal is the third. All three need the township certification below, because the rule attaches to the property transfer rather than to the type of buyer.

What is Horsham Township like for homeowners?

It is a suburban home-rule township that grew mostly after World War II. William Penn's surveyors laid out the township's lines, and Horsham was established in 1717. Early settlement clustered around the Friends meeting house at Horsham and Easton Roads, and the township had only about 1,300 people in 1890. The count climbed from 3,663 in 1950 to 8,933 in 1960 and 13,888 in 1970.

Today the township includes the villages of Horsham, Hallowell, Prospectville and Maple Glen. Mail comes through five ZIP codes: 19044 for Horsham, plus parts of the township that use Hatboro, Ambler, Chalfont and North Wales codes. Natural features include Park Creek, Little Neshaminy Creek, Pennypack Creek and Wissahickon Creek.

  • Schools: the Hatboro-Horsham School District, with Keith Valley Middle School and Hatboro-Horsham Senior High School.
  • Parks: about 815 acres of township parkland, a trail network that includes the Power Line Trail, and the 42 acre Graeme Park with its colonial governor's house.
  • Climate: a hot summer humid continental climate, averaging about 32 degrees in January and 77 in July.

Local government is a five-member council elected at large for four-year terms, with a township manager running daily operations and Horsham Fire Company No. 1 providing fire protection. Because the township works under a home rule charter, its rules, including the transfer inspection below, come from its own ordinances rather than the state's township code.

The township's biggest recent land story is the former Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Willow Grove, which closed in 2011 after 68 years. Surplus land from the base is about 8 percent of the township's area and is subject to a redevelopment plan, while the Air National Guard remains on the 200 acre site as Biddle Air National Guard Base.

Which roads and employers shape Horsham home values?

Buyers here shop by commute and by corporate campus. Easton Road (Route 611) runs north to south through the eastern side, Horsham Road (Route 463) crosses the center, and Welsh Road (Route 63), Limekiln Pike (Route 152) and Bethlehem Pike (Route 309) frame the edges. The Willow Grove interchange of the Pennsylvania Turnpike sits just south in Upper Moreland Township.

SEPTA bus Route 55 follows Route 611, and the township runs a weekday rush hour shuttle called h.o.p.s. between the office parks and the Fort Washington station on the Lansdale/Doylestown Regional Rail line. The Census Bureau reports a mean commute of 28.6 minutes for Horsham workers.

Employers named for the township include Janssen Biotech and Janssen Pharmaceuticals, both Johnson & Johnson subsidiaries, plus corporate offices for Bimbo Bakeries USA, Penn Mutual and SofterWare, and a UPS hub.

How do Horsham's housing numbers compare?

Horsham is a high value, mostly owner occupied township, and the figures below show how far it sits from the state's older cities.

What does Horsham's property transfer certification require?

The township requires an inspection of every residential property before a transfer. The application and fee are submitted to the Horsham Township Municipal Building at 1025 Horsham Road within the 90 days before settlement.

  • A township inspector checks the curb and sidewalk in front of the property.
  • The street address must be posted and easy to see from the road.
  • The seller certifies that working smoke detectors are in the house.

Schedule the inspection early enough to fix a cracked sidewalk slab or a missing house number before settlement. Questions go to the Code Enforcement department at (215) 643-3131.

The township also issues tax certifications through the township tax collector. Send the requester's contact details, the parcel number, the property address, the owner's name and a $30 check per parcel made out to Horsham Township, along with a stamped return envelope if you want it mailed. A title company normally handles this, but a seller handling a sale directly will need to order it.

How do Montgomery County assessments and tax sales touch a Horsham sale?

The county Board of Assessment Appeals sets the values behind county, township and school bills. Yearly appeals are due August 1 and change the tax year after. That same August 1 date applies to real estate tax exemption applications. State law requires annual appeals to be decided by October 31 so changes reach the rolls and taxing bodies by November 15.

The board advises mailing deadline filings with a hand-cancelled postmark, a Certificate of Mailing or certified mail, because postal delays can mark a timely envelope late. You can also hand deliver in Norristown on weekdays between 8:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. The board's phone line is 610-278-3761.

If the house carries unpaid taxes, the county Tax Claim Bureau enters the picture. It holds an upset sale each September and December and a judicial sale at least once a year in August and December. Upset sale buyers take the property subject to its liens, while a judicial sale presents it free and clear. Clear any delinquency before listing so it does not surface at closing.

When is a cash sale the better choice in Horsham?

A cash sale helps most when the property does not fit a conventional buyer's loan, or when the seller cannot wait through showings. Examples are a house with deferred roof or mechanical work, an estate property that needs to close before the next tax bill, or a seller relocating out of the area.

Because Horsham values are high, compare any cash figure with a full net sheet: list price, agent commission, transfer tax, repairs to pass the township inspection, and carrying cost. If you would like a cash figure for your Horsham house, Cash Home Buyers can provide one to set against that sheet.

More questions about Horsham, PA

Is an inspection required to sell a house in Horsham Township?

Yes. The township's Residential Property Transfer Certification Program requires an inspection of every residential property before transfer, covering the curb, the sidewalk and the posted address, plus a seller certification of working smoke detectors. Submit it within 90 days before settlement.

How much does a Horsham tax certification cost?

The township's tax collector charges $30 per parcel, paid by check to Horsham Township. Include the parcel number, property address and owner name, and say how you want the certification returned.

What date closes the yearly Montgomery County assessment appeal?

August 1, and the result applies to the next tax year.

Which school district serves Horsham?

The Hatboro-Horsham School District serves the township, along with neighboring Hatboro. Its schools include Keith Valley Middle School and Hatboro-Horsham Senior High School.

Can I sell a Horsham house with unpaid property taxes?

Yes, but the unpaid amount must be cleared at or before closing. Taxes that reach the county Tax Claim Bureau can put the property into an upset or judicial sale, so settle the balance before then.

Where is Monroeville, Pennsylvania, and how is it laid out?

East of Pittsburgh in Allegheny County, Monroeville is a home rule municipality that counted 28,640 people in 2020. It covers about 19.7 square miles, and its elevation ranges from 735 to 1,319 feet, a spread of more than 580 feet from the lowest ground to the highest.

The municipality touches nine neighbors: Plum to the north, Murrysville, Penn Township and Trafford in Westmoreland County to the east and south, North Versailles, Wilmerding and Turtle Creek to the southwest, Wilkins Township to the west and Penn Hills to the northwest. The borough of Pitcairn sits entirely inside Monroeville, near the south-southwest edge, so check the parcel record to see which municipality's rules and tax rates apply to a given address.

How did Monroeville become a municipality?

The area takes its name from Joel Monroe, its first postmaster, and was settled in the mid to late 1800s. It was organized as Patton Township in 1849, became the borough of Monroeville on January 25, 1951, and adopted a Home Rule Charter on May 21, 1974.

Growth followed the highways and the retail boom. Population rose from 22,446 in 1960 to 29,011 in 1970 and 30,977 in 1980, then slipped to 28,386 by 2010 and 28,640 in 2020. The 2025 estimate of 27,685 is 3.3 percent under the 2020 base. That slow, flat pattern means most homes here belong to established neighborhoods rather than new subdivisions, and many were built in the decades when the population was climbing.

What drives Monroeville's economy and housing demand?

Monroeville is best known for the Monroeville Mall, the surrounding office parks and a cluster of high-rise hotels that went up from the 1960s onward. The Monroeville Convention Center, once called the ExpoMart, sits near the mall. U.S. Steel's research laboratory here employed nearly 1,800 people at its 1979 peak.

The Census Bureau reports retail sales of about $2.59 billion in 2022, which works out to $91,813 per resident. That is far more than 27,000 residents spend alone, which shows how much shopping and service business Monroeville draws from the wider region. Health care and social assistance receipts were about $1.0 billion the same year.

Which schools, roads and trails serve Monroeville homes?

Public school students from kindergarten through grade 12 attend the Gateway School District, which has about 3,800 students. Higher education nearby includes the Community College of Allegheny County's Boyce Campus, an Indiana University of Pennsylvania satellite site in Penn Center East and the Western School of Health and Business.

Getting around is straightforward:

  • Interstate 376, the Parkway East, carries traffic toward Pittsburgh and joins the Turnpike at Exit 57.
  • U.S. Route 22 is the main business route, with PA 48 and PA 286 serving other parts of the municipality.
  • Pittsburgh Regional Transit runs two bus lines to downtown from park-and-ride lots in Monroeville.
  • The Westmoreland Heritage Trail follows an old rail line to Trafford and Murrysville for cyclists and walkers.

Owners without a mortgage pay a median of just $611 a month in housing costs, so a long-held home can be cheap to keep and still need expensive repairs.

Does Monroeville require an occupancy permit when a house is sold?

Yes. Monroeville requires a residential occupancy permit tied to the sale, and an inspection has to be completed before the new owners occupy the home. The municipality's application sets the fee at $100 for a single-family dwelling or townhome, and a second reinspection can add $50 under the municipal fee schedule.

The application works like this:

  • The current owner or the owner's agent files it.
  • It lists the property address, the buyer's name, who will meet the inspector and whether the electricity is on or off.
  • It has a line to mark the house as being sold as is.
  • The permit is issued in the name of the new owners who will live there.

The application lists 412-856-3340 for the municipality. Call before listing so the inspection can be scheduled early, and keep the electricity on if you can, since the form asks whether it is on or off.

What rules apply if the Monroeville house is a rental?

Rental units need their own occupancy permit, and an inspection must be completed before a tenant moves in. The fee is $75 for multi-family units and $100 for a single-family dwelling or townhome, and the permit is issued in the tenant's name. Units occupied before inspection can face penalty fines under the municipal ordinance.

A tenant in place changes the sale. Ask the municipality whether the permit on file is current and pass the paperwork to a buyer who plans to keep the tenant. An investor who will rent the house after closing applies under the rental rules separately from the sale permit. If the tenant is moving out anyway, put the move-out date in writing so the sale inspection can happen in an empty house.

What does a Monroeville sale cost in transfer tax, and how do appeals work?

Monroeville is one of the higher-tax spots in the county table: 1 percent to the municipality and one-half percent to the Monroeville-Gateway school district, plus the state's 1 percent, for 2.5 percent in all. On a $210,000 sale that comes to $5,250. The tax goes to the county at the deeds office with its own check, apart from recording fees. Some family transfers escape it, and form REV-183 covers deeds that show no price.

A challenge to your valuation starts with BPAAR, the county's first appeal level, and all of its hearings take place by phone. You can speak for yourself, send an attorney or appoint a representative. A losing party may carry the case to the Board of Viewers in the Court of Common Pleas. The Gateway school district or the municipality can file an appeal against an owner too, and the owner is free to attend or skip those hearings.

How can I sell a Monroeville house quickly?

Speed depends on the inspection, the title and the buyer's financing. A cash buyer takes away the loan approval step, but the municipal occupancy inspection still applies.

  • Order the occupancy inspection early and fix any items it flags.
  • Pull the county parcel record for the owner of record and school district.
  • Collect mortgage and lien payoffs, and leave the power on for the inspector.
  • Weigh a listing, a cash offer and an as-is investor sale against what repairs would cost.

Monroeville sits where I-376, the Pennsylvania Turnpike at Exit 57, U.S. 22, Business 22 and PA 48 meet, and two Pittsburgh Regional Transit bus lines run to downtown Pittsburgh from park-and-ride lots here, so a listing can highlight the commute.

More questions about Monroeville, PA

What is the occupancy permit fee when selling a house in Monroeville?

$100 for a single-family house or townhome under the municipal fee schedule, with a possible $50 charge if a second reinspection is needed. The buyers cannot occupy the home until the inspection is done.

How much is the transfer tax on a Monroeville sale?

The county table gives 2.5 percent in all: the state takes 1 percent, the municipality 1 percent and the Monroeville-Gateway school district one-half percent.

Is Monroeville a city or a borough?

It is a home rule municipality. The area began as Patton Township in 1849, turned into a borough in 1951 and adopted its charter in 1974.

Which school district serves Monroeville?

The Gateway School District serves students from kindergarten through grade 12. The Allegheny County transfer tax table lists it as the Monroeville-Gateway district for the municipality.

Can I appeal my Monroeville property assessment?

Yes. Go through the county's BPAAR board, which hears cases by phone. An owner may appear alone, use an attorney or name an authorized representative.

How can I sell my house fast in Springettsbury, PA?

Selling to a cash buyer is the fastest way to move a Springettsbury house, with no township sale inspection described on its published pages. Springettsbury Township sits east and northeast of the city of York in York County, and the steps that set the calendar are tax certification, payoff letters and title work.

This page covers what is particular to Springettsbury: its history and neighborhoods, the retail and industrial base around the York Galleria and Interstate 83, the two school districts that split the township, and the tax calendar that determines what the closing company asks you for.

What is Springettsbury Township like?

Springettsbury is a supervisor-manager township of about 16.4 square miles, home to the York Galleria mall and a large Harley-Davidson manufacturing campus. The Census Bureau counted 27,058 residents in 2020 and estimates 27,617 for July 1, 2025, a 2.2 percent increase.

The name comes from Springett Penn, a grandson of William Penn, and the township was incorporated on April 20, 1891 out of the northeast part of Spring Garden Township. It includes the census-designated places of East York, Pleasureville, Yorklyn and Stonybrook. East York was first developed in 1903, and the housing built there in the 1930s sits alongside postwar subdivisions such as Fayfield and Haines Acres and newer developments.

Codorus Creek forms the western and northwestern boundary and Mill Creek runs along the southwest. Major roads are Interstate 83, U.S. Route 30, Route 462 (East Market Street), Route 24 and Route 124.

What are the Census numbers for Springettsbury housing?

Census Bureau data for 2020 to 2024 shows 10,202 households, a 72.5 percent owner-occupied rate and a median owner-occupied home value of $243,900. Median gross rent is $1,339, median household income is $86,335 and mean travel time to work is 22.0 minutes.

About 85.8 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and more than a quarter of homes are rented. Retail sales in 2022 were $1,356,251,000, or $50,118 per resident, which reflects how much shopping in the York area concentrates here.

Which school district is my house in?

Springettsbury is split between the York Suburban and Central York school districts, and your tax bills follow whichever one serves your address. The township tax collector bills school real estate tax for both districts inside the township.

That split matters when you sell. School tax is billed separately from the county and township bill, on a different date, and a closing company needs the right district and the right year to prorate it correctly. Look at your most recent school tax bill, which names the district, before you give a title company the parcel number.

When are Springettsbury tax bills mailed and paid?

Springettsbury tax calendar and fees. Sources: Springettsbury Township property tax page and Real Estate Tax Certification Request Form.

The collector goes by postmark date for mailed payments, so allow time. Cash is not accepted in the drop box. If your mortgage company pays through escrow, forward any bill that reaches you rather than paying twice.

How does the tax certification work for a sale?

The closing company asks the township Tax Collector for a Real Estate Tax Certification, which shows whether York County, township, street light and school taxes are paid, with the year, face amount, discount and penalty for each. The request form lists the property address, parcel number, owner, buyer and settlement date and whether the deal is a sale or a refinance.

The fee is $20, payable by check to the Springettsbury Township Tax Collector. Delinquent taxes from prior years go through the York County Tax Claim Bureau instead. The township also keeps a sewer account certification request form among its documents, so ask the title company whether a sewer certification is on its list.

What property rules does the township enforce?

Springettsbury employs a full-time Codes Enforcement Officer who responds to complaints about property maintenance. The township's property maintenance page lists the issues that come up most often:

  • Fences, pools, decks, sheds and patios built too close to a property line.
  • Signs of the wrong size, type or location.
  • Cars, RVs, tractors, construction equipment and boats parked on grass, plus abandoned or junk vehicles.
  • Weeds, tall grass, trash, uncleared sidewalks, dilapidated buildings and unsafe structures.

Owners are asked to correct a violation voluntarily, and a finding can sometimes be appealed to the Zoning Hearing Board. If a violation stays open, the township can pursue legal action and the District Magistrate can impose fines for each violation. Fix open notices before listing, or tell a cash buyer about them up front so the price reflects the work.

What happened to the big employers nearby?

Springettsbury has seen several large facilities change hands. A 101-acre Caterpillar plant operated here from 1953 until the 1990s, and the vacant site was sold in 2002 and redeveloped as the York Business Center. The McCrory Stores headquarters was in the township from 1963 until the chain closed in 2002, and Bon-Ton Stores closed its township headquarters in August 2018.

More recently construction of a Post Consumer Brands logistics center on the Harley-Davidson campus finished in January 2017, and Hollywood Casino York opened in August 2021. For a homeowner, these shifts matter mostly through job access and traffic on Market Street and Route 30.

What about transfer tax and recording?

The state realty transfer tax is 1 percent of value, and local governments can add a share, with the York County Recorder of Deeds collecting it at recording. Certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestate succession are among the exemptions the Department of Revenue lists.

Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined local rate for Springettsbury and for current recording fees, then subtract both from your estimate of net proceeds. The sales agreement decides who pays, though both buyer and seller are legally liable if the tax is not paid.

Is a cash sale the right choice in Springettsbury?

A cash sale makes the most sense if the house needs repairs, has an open code violation, is a rental with a tenant leaving, or you need a firm date. Get at least one cash offer in writing, then compare it with the net from a listing after commission, repair credits and the carrying cost of waiting.

Ask any buyer who covers the tax certification fee, the sewer certification and the recording costs, and ask for the closing date in writing.

More questions about Springettsbury, PA

Does Springettsbury Township require an inspection before I sell?

The township's published pages describe code enforcement for complaints and permits, and they list no sale inspection. Check with the township office about any open violation or permit on your address before listing.

How much is the tax certification in Springettsbury?

The fee is $20, paid by check to the Springettsbury Township Tax Collector. The closing company sends the request form with the parcel number, owner, buyer and settlement date.

Which school districts serve Springettsbury Township?

York Suburban and Central York both serve parts of the township. Their tax bills go out July 1 for York Suburban and July 15 for Central York.

What is the population of Springettsbury Township?

The Census Bureau estimates 27,617 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 27,058 in the 2020 census. The township covers about 16.4 square miles.

Where do I pay back taxes on a Springettsbury house?

Delinquent taxes from prior years go to the York County Tax Claim Bureau at 717-771-9232. Current-year bills are paid to the township Tax Collector, who goes by postmark date.

What makes selling a house in Williamsport, PA different?

Williamsport is the seat of Lycoming County and the commercial center of north central Pennsylvania, so its housing market follows college calendars, hospital hiring and the river as much as it follows the wider region. Renters make up most households here, which affects who buys and what they expect from a property.

The Census Bureau estimates 27,384 residents for July 2025, down 1.3 percent from the 2020 base. Only 43.0 percent of housing units are owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024, the median home value is $154,300 and median gross rent is $855. The city counts 11,320 households with 2.14 people each, a median household income of $48,851 and a poverty rate of 25.4 percent.

Population peaked at 45,729 in 1930 when lumber money built the mansions on West Fourth Street. It stood at 27,754 in the 2020 census. That is a drop of about 40 percent from the 1930 peak.

What fees does the Williamsport Bureau of Codes charge?

The city's Bureau of Codes publishes a fee schedule, and several lines apply to owners who are selling or renting a property. It is open Monday to Friday from 8:00am to 4:00pm, closed for lunch from 12:00pm to 1:00pm, at 200 Reighard Ave., and the main number is (570) 327-7517.
