Most permits issue within 15 business days of a completed application, except new construction or major reconstruction. Ask the Bureau which occupancy or certification letter your buyer or lender expects, and request it early.

How does the Williamsport rental inspection affect a sale?

If the house has tenants or is used as student housing, the rental inspection fee schedule applies, and the Bureau lists inspection of rental properties among its core duties. A landlord selling a unit should find out whether the inspection is current and whether a re-inspection is open.

  • Gather any inspection reports and repair receipts for the buyer.
  • Check the unit count, because the fee grows with each unit in a building.
  • Sobriety houses, rooming houses and student residences have their own license line at $60 plus $15 per room, capped at $500.
  • Zoning matters for conversions. Variances and special exceptions each carry a $500 application fee, so confirm the legal use before you advertise a duplex or apartments.

A purchaser paying cash for a tenant-occupied building can accept the inspection history as is, yet the closing agent will still want clean paperwork on each unit.

Which Williamsport neighborhoods and schools shape buyer interest?

Williamsport's neighborhoods each draw a different buyer. Downtown runs between Hepburn Street and Basin Street, and Millionaires' Row along West Fourth Street is a National Register historic district. Newberry lies west of Lycoming Creek, Vallamont sits north of Rural Avenue, Grampian Hills spreads around Grampian Boulevard, Park Avenue and East End fill in the south and east, and West Hills occupies the hillside and hilltop.

The Williamsport Area School District serves the city with Cochran, Hepburn Lycoming and Jackson primary schools, Curtin and Lycoming Valley intermediate schools, a middle school and Williamsport Area High School. The district was recognized for its music program, and Stevens Primary School closed in 2022. Lycoming College and Pennsylvania College of Technology are both in the city, which keeps a steady pool of student renters and staff buyers.

Little League Baseball began here in 1939, and the Little League World Series is held every late summer in neighboring South Williamsport, a draw for visitors.

How do floods and winters affect a Williamsport house?

Water is the first thing buyers ask about. The West Branch Susquehanna River borders the city on the south, and the March 1936 flood crested at 33.9 feet and reached High Street. June 1972, when Hurricane Agnes struck, set the wettest month on record at 16.80 inches. A flood control levee and the Susquehanna Riverwalk now run along the river.

Winter is the second factor. Williamsport averages about 36 inches of snow a season, January is the coldest month, and the first freeze typically arrives around October 16, so roofs, gutters and heating systems get tested every year. Yearly precipitation averages roughly 43 inches over about 136 days, which keeps basement moisture on every inspector's list.

Gather your flood insurance history, any basement repair records and roof dates before you talk with a buyer. Those documents answer the questions that slow offers down.

How is a Williamsport deed recorded and taxed?

Pennsylvania imposes a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value transferred, and county recorders collect it along with any local tax. Both buyer and seller are jointly liable, and the contract decides who pays what. Some family transfers and transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

The Lycoming County Recorder of Deeds keeps land records back to 1795, with images online at the county's search portal. The county lists eleven school districts for transfer tax purposes, and Williamsport is one of them, so the local share can be divided between the municipality and the school district. Ask the Recorder or your title company for the exact local rate and the current recording fee before closing.

To add or remove a name, a new deed must be drawn and recorded. The county suggests a real estate attorney or title company for that job.

What should I prepare before listing a Williamsport house?

A short checklist saves weeks in a city with several overlapping offices: the Bureau of Codes on Reighard Avenue, the county Recorder downtown and the title company handling settlement.

  • Pull the parcel number and the names exactly as they appear on the deed.
  • Collect rental inspection letters, re-inspection results and any open permit paperwork.
  • Photograph the basement, roofline and any river-side flood marks, and keep insurance claims on hand.
  • Confirm the zoning use, particularly for duplexes, rooming houses and student residences.
  • Decide how you want to split the 1 percent state transfer tax and any local tax with the buyer.

With those items in a folder, you can compare a listing, a private sale and an as-is purchase on the same footing, and a buyer's questions get quick answers.

What do getting around and local jobs mean for Williamsport sellers?

Interstate 180, US 15 and US 220 meet at Williamsport, and Harrisburg is about 85 miles away. River Valley Transit runs local buses, Fullington Trailways connects downtown to Harrisburg, New York and Philadelphia, and Williamsport Regional Airport in Montoursville has flights to Washington Dulles. The Census puts the mean commute for 2020 to 2024 at 15.8 minutes.

Major employers include UPMC Susquehanna, Penn College, the school district and several manufacturers, including a large Lycoming Engines plant. The city sits in Marcellus Shale gas country, which has added another layer to the local economy. For sellers, that mix means buyers include nurses, instructors and plant workers who value short drives and move-in-ready homes.

More questions about Williamsport, PA

Does the City of Williamsport require an inspection when I sell?

Ask the Bureau of Codes at (570) 327-7517, because the published fee schedule lists occupancy and certification letters that a lender or buyer may request. Rental properties have a separate inspection fee of $85 per building plus $15 per added unit.

How much is a rental inspection in Williamsport?

A rental property inspection costs $85 per building plus $15 for each additional unit in the building. A re-inspection visit costs $30.

Who records the deed on a Williamsport sale?

The Lycoming County Recorder of Deeds records it. Pennsylvania's 1 percent state realty transfer tax is collected there, together with any local tax and recording fee, and the deed is not recorded until payment is made.

Does flooding affect selling in Williamsport?

It can, because the city borders the West Branch Susquehanna River and has a flood history, including a 33.9 foot crest in 1936. Have your insurance and repair records ready, and any buyer will still ask about them.

How long does a permit take in Williamsport?

Most permits are issued within 15 business days of submitting the required application. New construction and major reconstruction can take longer.

What shapes a house sale in East Hempfield Township?

East Hempfield is a suburban township west of the city of Lancaster, and a sale there turns on three local facts: Lancaster County is in the middle of a countywide reassessment, the Hempfield School District sets the biggest piece of the tax bill, and the township charges its own transfer tax. Each affects what you net.

The township covers about 21 square miles of land in west-central Lancaster County. It is one of six immediate suburbs that share the Lancaster mailing designation, so many East Hempfield houses carry a Lancaster address. Within the township are Landisville, Mechanicsville, Rohrerstown, Bamford, Centerville, Chestnut Ridge, Donerville, Chestnut View and Wheatland, plus part of Salunga.

This page covers what a seller needs to know about the tax steps, the county assessment cycle and township inspections, followed by the common ways owners here sell.

What is East Hempfield like as a place to sell?

The township's municipal building stands beside Amos Herr House and Park, where a farmhouse dating to 1852 remains. Kellogg's and Y&S Candies are listed among its manufacturers, and Census figures put 2022 retail sales above $1.1 billion.

East Hempfield had 23,522 residents in 2010, 26,304 in 2020 and an estimated 27,287 on July 1, 2025. Growth has been steady, not explosive, and the age mix is older than in many suburbs, with 27.0 percent of residents 65 or over.

  • Households: 11,427 in 2020 through 2024
  • Persons per household: 2.32
  • Average commute: 20.0 minutes

What do East Hempfield housing figures look like?

About 72 percent of East Hempfield households own their homes. The table below uses the Census Bureau's QuickFacts page.

East Hempfield Township housing and income, Census Bureau QuickFacts

How do school and county property tax bills work in East Hempfield?

The Lancaster County Treasurer collects county and township real estate taxes for East Hempfield, according to the county's tax collector list, while the Hempfield School District issues the school bill. The district's published rate for 2026-27 is 19.8786 mills, up 4.1 percent from the year before. The district's 2026 school bills were mailed June 30, with a 2 percent discount for payments postmarked by August 31, the base amount due by October 31, and a 10 percent penalty after that, with all payments due by December 31.

If a bill is not paid by year-end, the balance goes to the Lancaster County Tax Claim Bureau. That is also the office to call for questions on delinquent balances.

Tax certifications for closings have a new procedure. Starting July 1, 2026, the Lancaster County Tax Collection Bureau processes them for the school district. The request goes by email and must give the owner's name, the property address, the 13-digit parcel number, the settlement date and a return email or fax number. The fee is $25, and a check payable to LCTCB Real Estate Tax Group goes by mail with the request. Missing information sends the request back and delays closing.

How much transfer tax applies when selling in East Hempfield?

The township's realty transfer tax ordinance levies 1 percent of the value of the real estate, for general township purposes, on top of the 1 percent the Commonwealth charges. The ordinance was adopted in 1987 under the state Tax Reform Code and the Local Tax Enabling Act. It makes the tax payable when the deed is presented for recording, and no later than 30 days after acceptance of the document.

The state Department of Revenue treats the buyer and the seller as jointly liable. Several transfers are exempt in the township ordinance, including transfers to an heir from a decedent and certain transfers to the trustee of an ordinary trust, provided the Recorder of Deeds gets a copy of the trust instrument. Family transfers are also covered in the state's list of exemptions.

Ask the Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds for the total transfer tax on your deed, including the school district portion, before you set your asking price. On a sale at the $360,500 Census median, each 1 percent equals $3,605.

What does the 2027 countywide reassessment mean for a seller?

Lancaster County's Property Assessment Office assesses more than 195,000 parcels across 60 municipalities and 17 school districts. Its last countywide reassessment took effect January 1, 2018, when assessed values were set at market value as of that date with a 100 percent ratio. A new reassessment is underway for 2027, with assessors permitted to make outside-only inspections and photograph exteriors during 2025 and 2026.

The school district's reassessment page says the purpose is to keep taxes fair relative to value and that it does not raise revenue. Taxing bodies must adjust their rates to stay revenue neutral before making other changes, so a higher assessment on your house does not automatically mean a higher bill. A buyer will still compare your assessed value with similar houses.

  • Annual appeals are due August 1
  • In a reassessment year, an owner has 40 days from the date of the reassessment notice
  • The county's page says the next opportunity for an annual appeal after 2027 is 2028
  • Appeals go to a three-member Board of Assessment Appeals

The county warns that no form freezes or eliminates property taxes for seniors. Be cautious of any video or mailer that says otherwise, and contact the Assessment Office at 717-299-8381 for the real programs.

How do township permits and inspections affect a sale?

East Hempfield employs a Building Code Official who reviews permits and carries out inspections, and an inspector who handles property maintenance. Inspections are performed by Code Administrators Inc., which requires 24 hours' notice to schedule. The township's page also lists code enforcement services, a code enforcement complaint form and records research requests.

If you built a deck, finished a basement or replaced a furnace, locate the permit and the final inspection record before you list. Missing paperwork is easier to resolve with the township while you still own the house. The township uses a single generic form for residential building and zoning and another for commercial work, and its zoning map is online.

When a buyer asks about an old addition, the records research request is the route for pulling what the township has on file.

What are the common ways to sell an East Hempfield house?

A listing works well for a house in good shape in a strong school district. An as-is sale suits an estate, a house that needs major repairs, a rental with a difficult tenant or a move that cannot wait for showings and a buyer's financing. Compare offers on net proceeds after the transfer tax, any tax balance, the prorated school and county taxes, and repairs you agree to credit.

Get any offer in writing, ask who pays for title work and recording, and ask when the buyer wants to close.

More questions about East Hempfield, PA

Is East Hempfield part of the City of Lancaster?

No. East Hempfield is a separate township in Lancaster County, though it shares the Lancaster mailing designation with five other suburbs. Permits and zoning come from the township.

Who collects school taxes on an East Hempfield house?

The Hempfield School District handles its own bills, with its 2026-27 rate set at 19.8786 mills. The Lancaster County Treasurer collects county and township taxes.

How do I get a tax certification for an East Hempfield closing?

Email the Lancaster County Tax Collection Bureau with the owner name, address, 13-digit parcel number and settlement date, and mail a $25 check payable to LCTCB Real Estate Tax Group.

When can I appeal my East Hempfield assessment?

Annual appeals are due by August 1. In a reassessment year, you have 40 days from the notice date. The county says the next annual appeal opportunity after the 2027 reassessment is 2028.

Does the township require an inspection before I sell?

The township's page lists permit review, inspections through Code Administrators Inc. and code enforcement. Ask the township's code office whether anything further applies to your address before you list.

What is Upper Dublin Township like for a home seller?

Upper Dublin is a first-class township in Montgomery County, covering 13.3 square miles north of Philadelphia, with 26,665 residents at the 2020 census. It was farmland and limestone country until the 1950s, then filled in with postwar subdivisions: the population went from 6,637 in 1950 to 19,562 in 1970. Wikipedia ranks its median income fourth highest in the county.

The township's name goes back to a land grant that created Upper and Lower Dublin. Lower Dublin was folded into Philadelphia in 1854, and Upper Dublin kept going on its own, taking first-class township status on January 1, 1946. Limekiln Pike, a legacy of the township's limestone past, is still an important travel route.

Many addresses use a mailing name other than Upper Dublin. Those community areas include Ambler, Dresher, Fort Washington, Jarrettown and Maple Glen, with small slices of Abington, Ardsley, North Hills, Oreland and Willow Grove. They use ZIP codes 19001, 19002, 19025, 19034, 19038, 19075 and 19090, and none of them is a separate municipality. Property records and tax bills go through the township and county, regardless of the postal name.

How does the Fort Washington Office Park affect housing in Upper Dublin?

The office park is the township's economic engine. Wikipedia says it opened in 1955 as the first modern suburban business park on the East Coast, sits at a Pennsylvania Turnpike interchange, covers 566 acres and holds more than 80 buildings with over six million square feet of space. It is described as home to about 230 businesses and more than 12,000 workers.

The township has been planning for a change in mix, from light industrial toward offices, and has formed a municipal authority to finance public improvements there. A proposed mixed-use zoning change would allow more multifamily housing, retail and dining. For a seller in Maple Glen or Fort Washington, an employment hub a short drive away is an easy point to make in a listing.

  • Describe the commute to the office park and the turnpike interchange.
  • Note the Upper Dublin Public Library, which moved into a township-owned building in the park and opened in 2020.
  • Mention the township's seven wards if buyers ask who represents the street.

Did the 2021 tornado and flooding change anything for Upper Dublin sellers?

It left a record you may be asked about. An EF2 tornado spawned by the remnants of Hurricane Ida struck Upper Dublin on September 1, 2021, hitting the Fort Washington and Maple Glen areas. Nearly all of the township drains through Wissahickon Creek into the Schuylkill River, with only small corners draining to Neshaminy Creek and Pennypack Creek, so low lots near those streams deserve a closer look.

If your house had storm repairs, keep the permits, invoices and final inspection records together. Under the township's transfer process, every open permit must be closed out before the sale, so storm-era work that never received a final inspection is the kind of thing that stops a closing. The township's Code Enforcement department can tell you which permits on your address are still open.

Ask for a copy of the property file before you list. It also shows past zoning hearings tied to the address, which the township reviews at transfer.

What does Upper Dublin require before a property can be sold?

Upper Dublin has a point-of-sale process, and the township's Property Transfers page says every property being sold must submit a Property Transfer Application under Ordinance 10-1228. The steps run alongside your sale, so start early.

  • A township official inspects the exterior for sidewalk compliance and correct house numbering. Anything found must be fixed before the sale.
  • The property file is checked for open permits. Every open permit must be finalized before the sale.
  • The file is also reviewed for zoning hearings tied to the property.
  • You sign an affidavit that smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps are present.
  • Open Notices of Violation must be resolved before the sale.
  • Curbs and aprons are inspected and documented. The page says this is not required for the sale to proceed, but a failed curb or apron is marked for replacement under the property maintenance code.

Permits and applications go through the township's online OpenGov portal at upperdublin.net/permits. Paper applications are no longer available, so file everything there. Leave time for both the inspection and any sidewalk repair it turns up.

What does the Montgomery County transfer tax cost on an Upper Dublin sale?

Montgomery County's Recorder of Deeds states that the realty transfer tax is 2 percent. Pennsylvania's share is 1 percent, and the rest is local. The state says both parties to a deed are jointly responsible, so decide in the contract who pays. On a $500,000 sale, 2 percent comes to $10,000.

Upper Dublin transfer and appeal facts. Sources: Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds and Board of Assessment Appeals, Upper Dublin Township

Ask the Recorder how the ratio applies if your deed shows no price, as with some family transfers. Transfers claiming an exemption record with a REV-183 form from the Department of Revenue.

How do assessment appeals and delinquent taxes work in Upper Dublin?

Assessments are county business. The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals sets August 1 as the filing deadline for annual appeals, and the same date applies to exemption applications under 53 Pa.C.S. § 8844(c)(2). The county explains that annual appeals must be decided by October 31 so that new values reach taxing districts by November 15. Appeals are mailed to the Board at P.O. Box 311, Norristown, or hand-delivered during office hours.

Postmarks can lag. The county tells filers to ask for a hand cancellation, a certificate of mailing, registered or certified mail, or postage purchased at the counter. The Board's page also lists homestead forms, an exemption application and a "Taxing Authorities" document that names the school district and other taxing bodies for each address.

If you are behind on taxes, the Tax Claim Bureau holds an upset sale each September and December of parcels whose taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid. Buyers at an upset sale take on all liens, and the Bureau advertises each property beforehand. Paying the delinquent bill first, or selling before your parcel is listed, keeps the house out of that sale.

What are my options if I need to sell an Upper Dublin house fast?

You can list, sell privately, or take a cash offer from a buyer who buys houses as-is. The township's transfer requirements apply to each route, so the real question is who finishes the paperwork and how soon.

  • List when open permits are closed, the sidewalk is sound and the house shows well.
  • Choose a cash sale when you inherited the house, face repairs, or have a closing date to meet. Confirm the buyer will handle the sidewalk, permit and affidavit steps with you.

Whichever route you choose, call Code Enforcement first, get the property file, and make sure the 2 percent transfer tax is set out in writing.

More questions about Upper Dublin, PA

Does Upper Dublin require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes. Every property sold must file a Property Transfer Application, and a township official inspects the exterior for sidewalks and house numbers. Open permits and open violations must be cleared before the sale, and you sign an affidavit about smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps.

What is the transfer tax in Upper Dublin?

The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds lists the realty transfer tax at 2 percent, which includes the state's 1 percent. Both buyer and seller are liable under state law, so the sales contract should say who pays.

When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Montgomery County?

August 1 each year for annual appeals. The same deadline applies to exemption applications, and the Board advises hand delivery or a post office counter postmark.

Can I sell an Upper Dublin house that has open permits?

Not until the permits are finalized. The township's transfer review checks the property file, and every open permit must be closed before the sale, so schedule the missing inspections first.

What happens if I do not pay my property taxes before selling?

Unpaid taxes become a lien and can lead to a Tax Claim Bureau sale. The Bureau runs an upset sale each September and December for parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier, and buyers there take on the liens.

How do I sell my house fast in Shaler, PA?

The quickest way to sell a Shaler house is a direct cash sale, because it avoids the lender and appraisal steps that stretch out a listing. Shaler Township, in Allegheny County, also has its own pre-closing checklist that every seller has to clear, and that checklist is the real schedule driver whichever route you choose.

The township publishes a Selling Your Home guide that lists what the seller does, what the closing company orders, and what the buyer sets up afterward. Knowing it in advance keeps a fast sale from stalling at the last week. Below is how that guide works, along with the township's layout, housing profile and flood and mine issues that can come up in an inspection.

What is Shaler Township, and where is it?

Shaler Township is a first class township in Allegheny County about 11.2 square miles in size, covering much of Glenshaw and part of Allison Park in the North Hills suburbs of Pittsburgh. The 2020 census counted 28,132 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 26,833, a 4.6 percent decline from the 2020 base.

It was decreed in 1847 as Marion Township and renamed Shaler the same day, after a Pittsburgh-area judge. In 1900 it became a township of the first class, and the boundaries have changed little since. After World War II it filled in as a residential suburb, which is why most of its housing is mid-century. Several Pittsburgh mailing addresses fall inside the township, and the area is served by the Shaler Area School District.

The terrain is hilly and cut by three stream valleys that drain north to the Allegheny River: Pine Creek, Little Pine Creek and Girtys Run. Neighbors include Hampton, Ross, O'Hara, Indiana and Reserve townships and the boroughs of Etna, Millvale and Sharpsburg.

What does the Shaler housing market look like on paper?

Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 describe a stable owner-occupied township. 87.0 percent of units are owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied home value is $245,500, and median household income is $95,654 across 12,314 households. Median gross rent is $1,226 a month.

Residents age 65 and over make up 24.6 percent of the population, and 95.8 percent of people lived in the same house a year earlier. With so many long-time residents, a cash buyer who takes the house as it stands suits owners who are downsizing or settling an estate.

What does the township require before I can close?

Shaler requires a dye test, a backflow preventer check and a final water reading from the seller, plus four township letters the closing company orders. The township says every document on its list is required for closing.

  • Dye test. The home must be tested to confirm that downspouts and rain leaders are not tied into the sanitary sewer. Results stay valid for three years. The township asks sellers to request the test at least 14 days before closing.
  • Backflow preventer. At least two weeks before closing, the seller contacts the Hampton Shaler Water Authority at (412) 486-4867 for a visit to confirm a dual check valve and thermal expansion tank are in place.
  • Final meter reading. Sellers and landlords schedule a final reading and send a copy to the closing company so escrowed funds can be released.
  • Trash account. Close the account with the hauler and leave the recycling cart for the new owner.

If the dye test fails, the plumber notifies the township and the owner. Repairs can go to any contractor, but the township's building inspector must be told at least 24 hours before work starts so the work can be inspected.

What do the closing documents cost in Shaler?

The dye test itself is paid separately. Three plumbers under contract with the township charge $30, $35 and $40 per test, and you may hire your own registered plumber if the dye test form and waiver go back to the township office.

How does the tax certification work for a Shaler sale?

For a sale or refinance, the seller gives the closing company three years of township and school district real estate tax receipts. The closing company may use those receipts or order a tax certification letter from the township for $50.

Property tax in Shaler involves the county, the township and the school district, so a bill can come from more than one place. If you have lost old receipts, call the township tax office at 412-486-9700 and ask for copies before the closing company needs them.

What are the transfer tax and recording steps?

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the property's value, and local governments add their own share, all collected by the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds when the deed is recorded. Both buyer and seller are legally liable for the tax, though the sales agreement normally says who pays it.

Some transfers are exempt, including certain moves between family members and property passed by will or intestate succession. If the house is part of an estate, ask the Recorder or the closing company which exemption, if any, fits your deed. Ask the Recorder for the current local rate for Shaler before you work out your net proceeds.

Does flooding or mine subsidence affect Shaler houses?

Both can, depending on the street. The township keeps FEMA flood maps on file and publishes zone maps for Girtys Run, Little Pine Creek and Pine Creek, which the township says flood periodically. The building and zoning office at 300 Wetzel Road will review the maps with you and help work out which flood zone a property is in.

Part of the township sits over land that was mined in the past. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection sells mine subsidence insurance because homeowner policies usually leave it out. Coverage of $150,000 costs $41.25 a year, and a buyer needs a new policy of their own because the seller's does not carry over. Sellers who cancel at closing can get unused premium back if they notify DEP within 30 days of the sale.

What does the buyer handle after closing?

Shaler buyers register for the 1 percent earned income tax with Keystone Collections Group and open a water and sewer account with the Hampton Shaler Water Authority, since both charges share one bill. They also set up trash service, which is mandatory under the township code and handled by the township's contracted hauler.

If the property will sit empty for longer than three weeks, the owner can apply for a trash waiver good for up to six months and renewable. A seller who knows the house will be vacant before closing should ask about it.

Is a cash offer a good fit for a Shaler seller?

It is worth pricing when the house needs work, the dye test or backflow check looks like a problem, or the family wants a closing date it can plan around. A cash buyer is usually willing to take on the township checklist, but ask who pays for the dye test, the $50 letters and any repairs before you sign.

Compare the offer against a listing net of commission and the transfer tax. If the gap is small, the speed may be worth it. If it is large and the house is in good shape, a traditional listing may still make sense.

More questions about Shaler, PA

Does Shaler Township require an occupancy permit to sell a house?

No. The township's Selling Your Home page states that occupancy permits are not required for the sale or refinance of a property. A dye test, backflow check and several township letters are required instead.

How long is a Shaler dye test valid?

Three years from the test date, and the township keeps the result on file. Request the test at least 14 days before closing so a failed result can be fixed in time.

Who orders the Shaler no lien letter?

The closing company orders it from the township for $50. It confirms that no municipal liens are unfiled against the property, and the water authority issues its own separate lien letter.

What is the Shaler Township population?

The Census Bureau estimates 26,833 residents as of July 1, 2025, down from 28,132 counted in the 2020 census. The township covers about 11 square miles of land.

Can I sell a vacant or inherited house in Shaler as-is?

Yes, as long as the township's closing requirements are met, because they apply to every sale. Notify the water authority if the house is empty so service can be shut off, and ask about the trash waiver while it sits.

Bethlehem Township at a glance

Selling in Bethlehem Township?
We buy Bethlehem Township houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

How does selling a house in Bethlehem Township work?

A sale in Bethlehem Township goes through an agreement of sale, a township resale inspection that produces a certificate of use and occupancy, settlement and a recorded deed. The township sits entirely in Northampton County, so the county recorder of deeds and assessment office are the same for every parcel. The township office at 4225 Easton Avenue handles the resale paperwork through its Community Development Department.

Do not confuse the township with the neighboring City of Bethlehem. The two have separate governments and separate sale rules, and this page covers only the township.

What is Bethlehem Township like?

Bethlehem Township is a suburban municipality of 14.43 square miles of land northeast of the City of Bethlehem, home to an estimated 26,769 people in July 2025. The Lehigh River separates it from Lower Saucon Township to the south, and it borders Palmer, Hanover and Lower Nazareth townships along with Easton, Freemansburg and the city.

Its villages include Brodhead, Butztown, Farmersville, Middletown, Prospect Park and Wagnerville. The township was formed in 1746 as part of Bucks County and took its name from the Moravian settlement founded on Christmas Eve 1741. Students in grades nine to twelve attend Freedom High School inside the township as part of the Bethlehem Area School District, and Northampton Community College has its campus here. The climate is humid continental, with Farmersville averaging 28.8 degrees in January and 73.8 in July, so roofs, gutters and heating systems see real seasonal wear.

Which roads and commutes matter to buyers here?

Buyers in the township reach the rest of the Lehigh Valley mainly by US 22, PA 33 and PA 191. US 22 crosses the northern part along the Lehigh Valley Thruway, PA 33 runs north and south through the eastern part, and PA 191 begins at US 22 and heads north along Nazareth Pike.

  • Other major roads: William Penn Highway, Freemansburg Road, Butztown and Hecktown Roads, Farmersville Road and the Main Street Extension.
  • Road mileage: 140.29 miles of public roads in 2021, of which 113.09 miles belong to the township and 27.20 miles to PennDOT.
  • Average commute for workers: 26.1 minutes, per the Census Bureau.

What do Census figures show for Bethlehem Township housing?

The township is mostly owner occupied and carries higher values and incomes than the city next door. The table compares the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates for the township.

MeasureBethlehem Township
Owner-occupied housing rate81.7%
Median value, owner-occupied homes$376,500
Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage$2,217
Median gross rent$1,794
Median household income$119,050
Residents aged 65 and over21.5%

Source: U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, Bethlehem township, Northampton County. The township grew from 23,730 people in 2010 to 25,868 in 2020 and an estimate of 26,769 in 2025.

What is the township resale inspection?

It is a Certificate of Use and Occupancy inspection that the Code Enforcement Officer performs for the resale of residential property and whenever a rental changes tenants. The application lives in the township's Forms and Documents list under the Property Resale/Lease Inspection Program.

  • The form asks for the premises address, the reason (residential resale or change of tenant) and the type of building, such as single-family dwelling, townhouse or condo.
  • It records the settlement date and whether the agreement of sale is attached.
  • It names a contact for scheduling: seller, buyer, or the agent or attorney.
  • The owner signs permission for the inspection.

The township says the inspection checks general compliance with its property maintenance, building and zoning rules under Ordinance Nos. 6-78 and 06-23. It is not a home inspection, the electrical portion looks only at GFCI protection, and the certificate carries no township liability for the condition of the house. Call the Code Enforcement Officer at (610) 814-6467 with questions.

Which projects at a Bethlehem Township house need a permit?

Zoning permits cover small outdoor projects, while construction permits cover structural, mechanical and interior work, and the township says the lists are not all-inclusive. The township enforces the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code and the 2018 International Codes. Call the Permit Department at (610) 814-6435 if you are unsure.

  • Zoning permit only: detached garages and sheds under 1,000 square feet, decks under 30 inches above grade, patios, fences, driveway expansions and retaining walls of 48 inches or less.
  • Construction permit: structural changes, plumbing, electrical, HVAC and replacement water heaters, replacement windows, decks 30 inches or higher, pools, hot tubs, finished basements, living space conversions and patio roofs.

Finished basements and replacement water heaters appear on the permit list, and both are common in houses that are decades old. If a previous owner did that work, ask the Community Development Department whether a permit was closed out before the resale inspector arrives.

Where can I check zoning and parcel facts for my property?

The township's Interactive Mapping System shows parcel number, lot dimensions and zoning for any address. Tax values, sales data and ownership records come from Northampton County, whose public records site is ncpub.org, and the township notes that the land use code there is a tax code, not the township's zoning.

Zoning matters at resale because the township sorts every land use into permitted by right, special exception or conditional use. A use that predates the ordinance may be grandfathered as nonconforming, and variances go to the Zoning Hearing Board. Boundary and survey questions go to the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds.

What if the Bethlehem Township house is vacant or in foreclosure?

The township requires vacant properties and properties in foreclosure to be registered, and it administers the program through Hera Property Registry. Owners, mortgagees and trustees register online and pay a registration fee.

The program exists because neglected, unsecured houses draw complaints and sometimes crime, and out-of-state owners are hard to notify of violations. If you inherited an empty house or fell behind on a mortgage, register it first and then deal with the resale inspection. Most code enforcement actions start with a concern raised by a resident or owner, and the township does not accept anonymous complaints.

What permits and taxes affect a Bethlehem Township sale?

Open permits are the usual snag. After a complete building permit application, the township has fifteen business days to respond, and the work needs a Certificate of Occupancy or Compliance after final inspections. If past work was done without a permit, ask the Community Development Department how to close it out before you list.

Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent realty transfer tax on the value transferred, with seller and buyer jointly liable, and the county recorder of deeds collects it along with any local share. Ask the Northampton County Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on your deed. For assessment appeals and the annual filing date, contact the Northampton County Assessment Division, since that office sets the deadline.

More questions about Bethlehem Township, PA

Do I need a township inspection to sell in Bethlehem Township?

Yes. The Code Enforcement Officer performs required inspections for the resale of residential property, and the buyer receives a Certificate of Use and Occupancy. Submit the Property Resale/Lease Inspection application once you have an agreement of sale and a settlement date.

Is the Bethlehem Township inspection the same as a home inspection?

No. The township form says its purpose is general compliance with property maintenance, building and zoning rules. Electrical review covers only GFCI items, and the township takes no responsibility for the home's condition.

Does the City of Bethlehem sale inspection apply to my township house?

No. The city's rule covers property inside city limits. A house in Bethlehem Township uses the township's resale program, even though the mailing address says Bethlehem.

Register it. The township runs a vacant and foreclosure property registry through Hera Property Registry, and owners, mortgagees and trustees must register online and pay the fee.

Where is Moon Township, Pennsylvania?

Moon Township lies on the south bank of the Ohio River in western Allegheny County, at an elevation of about 1,175 feet. The 2020 census found 27,261 residents across 24.1 square miles, and the ZIP code is 15108.

Six municipalities touch its borders, and across the river it faces three more:

  • Crescent Township to the north-northwest and the borough of Coraopolis to the north-northeast
  • Hopewell Township in Beaver County to the northwest
  • Findlay Township to the west and southwest, and North Fayette Township to the south
  • Robinson Township to the southeast, east and northeast
  • Edgeworth, Sewickley and Glen Osborne on the opposite bank, linked by the Sewickley Bridge

How did Moon Township get its start?

Moon was created in 1788 as one of the original townships of Allegheny County, and in 1789 it absorbed part of Washington County south of the Ohio River. At that point it covered roughly 145 square miles, and legend says a rider needed two days to cross it. Settlers kept asking for smaller units, so Fayette Township was cut away in 1790, followed by Findlay and Crescent townships. Beaver County later took the land north of the river.

The township stayed rural for almost two centuries. Population was 1,383 in 1850 and still only 2,900 in 1930. Then it jumped to 7,096 in 1950, 10,642 in 1960 and 18,317 in 1970, driven first by defense work and then by the airport.

The Mooncrest housing plan was built in 1943 for defense workers who made armor plate, munitions and ships at the nearby Dravo yard, and its homes were sold to private investors in the mid-1950s. A Cold War missile battery known as Nike Site PI-71 once stood here and is now a nature preserve.

How do the airport and the university shape Moon's housing market?

Pittsburgh International Airport opened in Moon in 1951 and turned the farm country of the western hills into a transportation crossroads, with Parkway West, I-376 and I-79 exits nearby. The passenger terminal later moved to neighboring Findlay Township in 1991, which cost Moon tax revenue, but a large share of the runways and the airport cargo area remain inside the township.

Military and public-sector tenants include the 911th Airlift Wing of the Air Force Reserve Command, the 171st Air Refueling Wing of the Pennsylvania Air National Guard and the National Weather Service office that forecasts for Pittsburgh. Robert Morris University has its main campus here, and the stretch renamed University Boulevard in 2003 is the township's business corridor. Walmart opened a supercenter on the former West Hills Shopping Center site in 2016.

Houses close to University Boulevard or the airport face different noise and traffic conditions than those on quiet interior streets.

How do Moon housing and income figures look?

Owners occupy 78.1 percent of Moon's homes, and median household income is $113,170. The rows below come from the Census Bureau's profile for Moon.

Population slipped 1.8 percent from the 2020 base to the 2025 estimate, after growing 12.7 percent in the 2010s, and workers spend 28.2 minutes getting to their jobs on average.

What is the weather like, and how does it affect a Moon house?

NOAA normals for 1991 to 2020 put Moon's average January high at 35.6 degrees and low at 19.4, against 83.0 and 62.2 in July. Precipitation totals 41.80 inches a year, between 2.6 and 4.4 inches in every month.

Winter temperatures hover around the freezing line and moisture arrives in every season. Features worth checking before you list include:

  • Roof condition and gutters, since water has to move off a hillside lot
  • Basement dampness and sump pump history
  • Retaining walls, steps and driveway surfaces that heave in winter
  • Furnace age and the efficiency of the heating system

Receipts for roof or drainage work give a hillside seller something concrete to show.

Does Moon Township regulate rental properties and historic homes?

Yes on both counts. Moon requires a rental inspection before each change of occupants. The township's rental packet asks for an inspection request form, an affidavit, an inspection agreement and a rental registration, with a $20 fee per unit. The Fire Marshal's office then schedules the appointment, and owners must report the names of all occupants within 30 days of move-in. An investor buying to rent would go through the same steps.

The Mooncrest Historic District adds another layer. A property there needs a Certificate of Appropriateness before the township will issue a building permit, and the township's Mooncrest Historic Overlay Advisory Committee advises the Board of Supervisors on those certificates. Building permits are required for alterations, additions, porch roofs and sheds, and rules cover windows and doors along building fronts, dryer vents, coal chutes and roofing materials. Ask the township office at 412-262-1700 whether an address falls inside the district.

How much is the transfer tax on a Moon sale?

Moon's county-listed rates are one-half percent for the township and one-half percent for the Moon Area School District, so with the state's 1 percent a sale carries 2 percent in transfer tax. It is paid at recording by its own check, apart from recording fees.

As a worked case, a $300,000 sale in Moon produces $6,000, split $3,000 to the state and $1,500 each to the township and the school district. Allegheny County's own example, a $40,000 house in Shaler Township, is taxed $800 at the same 2 percent. Family transfers can be exempt, and deeds that show no price need a Statement of Value.

An owner who disputes an assessment can go to the county's BPAAR board, whose hearings are held by phone.

What are the options for a quick sale in Moon Township?

Speed comes down to inspection readiness and whether the buyer needs a lender. Moon owners usually compare three routes:

  • List on the open market and wait for a buyer who will live there, the route that can bring the top price for a house in good shape.
  • Sell as is to a cash buyer, a fit for estates, tenant-occupied houses and properties needing repairs.
  • Sell to a neighbor, a relative or an investor you already know.

A house in the Mooncrest district or with a rental history should come with its permits and inspection records, since buyers will ask.

More questions about Moon, PA

Is Moon Township the same as Moon, Pennsylvania?

Yes. Moon Township is in Allegheny County and is the place most people mean. A separate Moon Township exists in Beaver County, so confirm the county when you search property records.

What is the transfer tax on a house sale in Moon Township?

Two percent altogether: 1 percent to the state, one-half percent to Moon Township and one-half percent to the Moon Area School District.

Do I need a rental inspection to sell a Moon house with a tenant?

Moon inspects a rental before each new occupant, charging $20 a unit, and wants a rental registration within 30 days of move-in. A buyer keeping the tenant should check that the paperwork is on file.

What is the Mooncrest Historic District?

It is a historic overlay area built in 1943 as defense worker housing. A Certificate of Appropriateness must come before any building permit there, with an advisory committee making recommendations to the supervisors.

Which school district serves Moon Township?

The Moon Area School District appears in the Allegheny County transfer tax table for Moon Township. Crescent Township also sits in that district, which helps when comparing nearby addresses.

What does a Lebanon seller need to understand first?

Lebanon packs about 26,500 people into a small grid of older homes, many of them rented, with a typical owner's home valued at $156,500. That price level means repairs, taxes and closing costs take a large share of any sale, so the details below are worth reading before you set a price.

The city is also Lebanon County's seat of government, 26 miles east of Harrisburg and 88 miles northwest of Philadelphia. It covers just 4.17 square miles, which works out to about 6,435 people per square mile. The Census Bureau's mid-2025 figure is 26,479, a 1.1 percent drop from 2020. The city had gained 5.2 percent in the previous decade.

A Lebanon owner can use a broker, post the sign personally or take a cash bid for the house. In every case the deed is filed at the courthouse on South 8th Street, and the county treasurer keeps the tax payment records.

How did Lebanon become the city it is?

George Steitz founded the town in 1740 under the name Steitztown. Settlers arrived about 1720, streets were laid out in 1753, a borough charter came in 1821, and city status followed on November 25, 1885. Population passed 14,000 by 1890 and peaked at 30,045 in 1960 before sliding to 24,461 in 2000.

Manufacturing built much of the housing. The Union Canal ran along the north side from 1828 to 1885, San Giorgio pasta has been made here since 1914, and a large Bethlehem Steel mill once operated in the city. Lebanon bologna, first made here before the 1780s, still carries the city's name. The Quittapahilla Creek drains the city westward toward the Susquehanna.

  • Neighboring municipalities: North Lebanon, South Lebanon, West Lebanon and North Cornwall townships.
  • Schools: the Lebanon School District, which serves the city and West Lebanon Township, plus a Harrisburg Area Community College campus and the Lebanon County Career and Technology Center.
  • Weather: about 46 inches of precipitation and 24 inches of snow in a typical year, with January averaging about 30 degrees and July about 74. Gutters, roofs and basements on older homes get tested every winter.

How do Lebanon homes show up in Census data?

Lebanon has more renters than owners, lower incomes than the state's suburbs and a younger, more diverse population. Most homes here are rented, so landlords make up a big part of both the selling and the buying side.

With rent near $992 against a $156,500 home value, the rental market is a major buyer of Lebanon houses. A seller of a tenant-occupied property should expect investors to ask for the rent roll, the license and the last inspection results.

What are the City of Lebanon's rental license rules?

Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the city must be licensed, and each parcel with rental units needs its own application. The rules matter to a seller because a buyer inherits the license history.

  • A $25 penalty is added every 60 days a fee stays unpaid after billing.
  • Renewal is delayed or denied if money is owed to the city or code violations are open.
  • The owner must keep a contract with a licensed trash hauler on file, and a property manager must be within 20 miles of the city limit.
  • Grass and weeds cannot exceed 12 inches, snow and ice must come off sidewalks within 24 hours after a snowfall ends, and inoperable or unlicensed vehicles cannot sit on a premises more than 5 days.
  • Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors are required, and a license revoked for unsafe conditions costs $100 to reinstate.

Questions go to the city's code enforcement office at 717-639-2800, option 2, at 735 Cumberland Street. For a rental, get copies of the current license and any violation notice into your file before you answer a buyer.

What permits and zoning rules can slow a Lebanon sale?

The city's Building and Zoning Division, part of Public Works, runs permits and zoning. A zoning permit is required for building or altering a structure, adding an addition, demolishing or moving one, and putting up fences, decks, sheds and garages. It is also required for a change of use, a swimming pool or hot tub deeper than 18 inches, and a sign.

Construction inspections are done by outside code inspection firms under contract, and the city asks for at least 24 hours' notice. A deck or shed that an earlier owner added without a permit is something an inspector may catch. Settle that question before listing, or ask the zoning office what the city would require.

The city zoning ordinance defines 10 districts. A Zoning Hearing Board hears variance and special exception requests.

How do county taxes and the Tax Claim Bureau affect a Lebanon sale?

The Lebanon County Treasurer collects the county real estate tax, the city tax and, now, the Lebanon City School District bill, so one office can tell you whether anything is owed on a city parcel. The Tax Claim Bureau charges $15 per parcel for a tax certification, and a mailed request must include a stamped return envelope.

Delinquent taxes pass to the Tax Claim Bureau each January. The owner is sent a certified letter showing the balance, interest and costs, along with the date to pay in order to avoid a sale. About 17 months after that first notice the bureau mails a notice of sale. Buyers at the upset sale take the property subject to judgments, liens and mortgages, and bidders must pre-register for a $25 fee. The 2026 upset sale list set the sale date for October 12, 2026, and that date has passed.

A seller behind on taxes should pay or arrange the balance before closing. Once a property is on the sale list, the process follows a fixed bureau and court calendar.

How are assessments appealed and the deed recorded in Lebanon County?

The county's rules set September 1 as the yearly filing date for assessment appeals, with a 4:30 closing time at the Board of Assessment Revision. A notice that arrives late waits for the following year. The filing fee for a residential property of one to four units is $50 and is not refunded. You or an authorized representative must attend the hearing, and the board can raise, lower or keep the assessment.

Filings go to the Assessment Office at 400 South 8th Street, Room 118. The county also lets owners view their records free on DataScout, using the control number and web password printed on the tax bill.

The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 107 of the same courthouse, open on weekdays, and accepts cash or check only. Most documents come back the following business day, and the Assessment Office must certify the parcel identifier before a deed records. The state transfer tax is 1 percent, and the recorder's office adds any local share when it collects.

Which Lebanon houses suit a cash offer?

A cash sale suits a house with heavy repairs, a rental carrying open code items, a vacant building or an estate. It is also useful when tax delinquency puts the house on a calendar you cannot move.

Price comparison matters here because the median value is modest. Add up the commission, repairs, transfer tax and months of ownership on a listing, and compare that net with a cash figure. To ask for an offer on a Lebanon house in its present state, contact Cash Home Buyers.

More questions about Lebanon, PA

Does Lebanon require a rental license?

Yes. Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the City of Lebanon must be licensed, with a separate application for each parcel that has rental units.

When are Lebanon County assessment appeals due?

September 1 each year, filed with the Board of Assessment Revision at the Assessment Office on South 8th Street. A residential appeal costs $50.

How long can Lebanon County delinquent taxes sit before a sale?

Unpaid taxes move to the Tax Claim Bureau every January, and owners have until the last working day of the next June. A notice of sale follows about 17 months after the first notice.

Where is a Lebanon deed recorded?

At the Lebanon County Recorder of Deeds, Room 107 of the courthouse at 400 South 8th Street. The office takes cash or check and can also accept electronic recording.

Which school district serves the City of Lebanon?

The Lebanon School District, which covers the city and West Lebanon Township. The county treasurer now collects its tax bill for city parcels.

What do I need to do to sell a house in Warrington, PA?

In Warrington Township the seller must obtain an Occupancy Certificate before settlement, which means applying at least 30 days ahead, paying $140 per residential unit and passing an inspection. The township puts this duty on the seller or landlord, and a real estate agent or other representative may file on the seller's behalf. After that, the sale follows the usual Pennsylvania disclosure, tax and deed-recording sequence.

Warrington is a Bucks County township of 13.7 square miles with an estimated 26,261 residents. Its motto calls it the Gateway to Historic Bucks County, and the township was founded in October 1734 and named for Warrington, England. Its population grew from 2,336 in 1950 to 25,639 in 2020, so a large share of its houses date from the 1980s through the 2000s, the years when the count rose from 10,704 to 23,418.

How does the Warrington occupancy certificate work?

The certificate is a township inspection that confirms a home meets safety and property maintenance requirements before it changes hands. The Permits Office takes applications online or by mail or drop-off at the township building, and the applicant is responsible for making sure the fee is paid and the inspection is scheduled.

The township's program page sets out these terms:

  • Apply at least 30 days before settlement so there is time to fix problems the inspection finds.
  • The residential fee is $140 per unit. Confirm commercial fees before you submit.
  • A certificate is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued, so do not schedule the inspection months before closing.
  • Homes with fire sprinkler systems need a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency, and that sprinkler certification is valid for six months.
  • The township publishes a residential inspection checklist, so you can walk the house before the inspector does.

If a sale falls through and the certificate expires, you would have to apply again for the next buyer. Build that risk into your timeline if your buyer needs financing.

What do Census figures show for Warrington housing?

What is the Warrington area like for buyers?

Warrington is a suburb of winding creeks and commuter roads, and buyers compare it on schools, drive time and storm drainage. Natural features include the Little Neshaminy Creek, Mill Creek, Park Creek, Fretz Valley, Griers Hill and Prospect Hill. Villages within the township are Warrington, Neshaminy, Tradesville, Eureka, Frog Hollow and Palomino Farms.

Public schools are part of the Central Bucks School District: Barclay, Mill Creek and Titus elementary schools, Tamanend Middle School and Central Bucks High School South. Neighbors include New Britain, Doylestown, Warwick, Warminster, Horsham and Montgomery townships.

  • US 202 runs through the western part of the township as a parkway, and PA 611 (Easton Road) crosses the eastern side.
  • PA 152 (Limekiln Pike), PA 132 (Street Road), Lower State Road and County Line Road connect the neighborhoods.
  • The township maintains 83.51 of its 102.37 miles of public roads.
  • SEPTA City Bus Route 55 follows PA 611, and the DART South bus runs weekdays along the same corridor to Doylestown.

Warrington has also had a local fight over land use. In 2010 a pharmaceutical company proposed the largest warehouse facility in Pennsylvania near residential neighborhoods in the township, residents objected loudly, and the company chose a site in Northeast Philadelphia instead. Buyers who care about open land and traffic remember that history, and the township's zoning rules decide what can be built near your street. If a buyer asks about nearby development, point them to the township's Planning and Zoning staff, who work with the Bucks County Planning Commission on zoning updates, and keep a copy of your own survey and any permit records for the closing file.

The humid continental climate brings about 47 inches of precipitation a year, with July the wettest month and seasonal snowfall of 30 to 36 inches. Wet basements and roof wear are therefore the questions inspectors ask most.

What taxes and disclosures apply when I sell in Warrington?

Bucks County's recorder says the transfer tax on a Pennsylvania sale is 2 percent, 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid when the deed is recorded. The recorder no longer accepts personal checks for it; cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card will do. Sellers and buyers usually divide the tax by agreement, and a family transfer may be exempt with a Statement of Value form where the deed does not state the exemption.

The disclosure rule is in 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. Before the agreement of sale is signed, you deliver a signed property disclosure statement covering the roof, basement, drainage, plumbing, wiring and similar items. Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information, which matters in a township with several creeks.

For assessment, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, and that date has passed. Annual appeal changes apply to the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead exclusion filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year that starts July 1. A new owner must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of buying, so remind your buyer.

Should I fix the house, list it or sell as-is in Warrington?

Warrington's high median values reward a well-presented house, but the 30-day occupancy lead time and a sprinkler certification, if you have one, can slow a quick listing. A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is still has to see the township certificate handled before settlement, so ask how that works before you agree to a date.

  • Apply for the occupancy certificate as soon as you have a contract, not at the closing table.
  • Walk the township checklist yourself and fix cheap items first.
  • Compare a listing net sheet with a cash offer that states who pays for repairs the inspector requires.

More questions about Warrington, PA

The township charges $140 per unit for residential properties. Commercial fees differ, and the township asks you to confirm the amount before submitting.

How long does a Warrington occupancy certificate last?

It is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued. If settlement slips past that window, you will need a new certificate.

Who applies for the certificate when a house is sold?

The seller or landlord is responsible, and an agent or authorized representative can file for the seller. The certificate has to be in hand before settlement.

What is the median home value in Warrington?

Owners in Warrington report a midpoint value of $553,100 for 2020 to 2024, the highest of the four townships in the same QuickFacts table.

Does my sprinkler system change anything?

Yes. Houses with fire sprinklers need a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency before the occupancy certificate can be issued, and the sprinkler certification lasts six months. The township posts a list of registered agencies.

What should I know before selling a house in Lower Providence Township?

Lower Providence Township is a Montgomery County suburb of about 25,600 residents where a sale runs through a township resale certificate, three account certifications and a 1 percent local transfer tax. Those three items set the timeline more than anything else, so sellers who line them up early close faster.

The township covers roughly 15.5 square miles along the Perkiomen Creek valley and includes the Audubon and Evansburg census-designated places. It shares borders with Upper Providence, Skippack, Worcester, West Norriton and Upper Merion townships, plus the borough of Collegeville. The 2020 census count was 25,625 people.

Whether the house goes on the market with an agent, sells by owner or goes to an as-is cash buyer, the same township paperwork applies, and the sections below walk through it.

How did Lower Providence Township develop?

The township was created in 1805, when the old Providence Township was split into Upper and Lower halves along the Perkiomen Creek. The land sits in the historic homeland of the Lenape and was once part of the tract granted to William Penn.

Growth came late and fast. The 1930 census counted 3,189 residents, and the count passed 15,000 by 1970 and 22,000 by 2000. Since 2010 the pace has flattened, with 25,436 residents that year and 25,625 in 2020. The biggest gains came between 1940 and 1980, when the township grew from 3,822 to 18,945 residents.

A few landmarks anchor the township's character and help a listing description:

  • Skippack Bridge, built in 1792 and added to the federal register of historic places in 1970.
  • Evansburg State Park, with trails, fishing and horseback riding.
  • Mill Grove, the first American home of the painter John James Audubon, run by the county as a museum and wildlife sanctuary.
  • A portion of Valley Forge National Historical Park.

Which schools and roads matter to buyers in Lower Providence?

The Methacton School District serves the township, and school boundaries are a common question from out-of-area buyers. Arrowhead, Eagleville and Woodland elementary schools take students from different sections, while Skyview Upper Elementary and Arcola Intermediate sit inside the township. Methacton High School is across the line in Worcester Township. Visitation B.V.M. School, a Catholic school in West Norriton, is nearby for families who want a parish option.

Commuters look first at U.S. Route 422, the Pottstown Expressway, which crosses the southern part of the township. Route 363 handles local trips along Trooper Road, Ridge Pike and Park Avenue. The township reports 113.66 miles of public road, with 90.11 miles maintained by the township itself and 23.55 miles by PennDOT. SEPTA suburban buses 91, 93, 99 and 131 connect to the Norristown Transportation Center.

What does the township require before a Lower Providence house changes hands?

Sellers need a residential resale use and occupancy certificate, and the township charges $100 for it, which covers the first inspection and one follow-up visit. Re-inspections cost $50 each, starting with the third. The application goes through the township's online permit portal, and residential resale fees are due when the application is filed.

The township finance office also expects tax, sewer and trash accounts to be certified before settlement. The real estate tax certification costs $25 and comes from the elected tax collector. Sewer fees are handled by the sewer authority on Parklane Drive in Eagleville, and trash service is billed by J. P. Mascaro and Sons.

For questions on the inspection, call the Community Development Department at 610-635-3512. The office takes calls on weekdays and returns voicemail left after hours the next business day.

What taxes and closing costs apply to a sale in Lower Providence?

The realty transfer tax on a Lower Providence sale is 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the Commonwealth and 1 percent local. The township's fee schedule splits the local share evenly, one half of a percent to the township and one half to the Methacton School District. The state describes its piece as a 1 percent tax on the value transferred, and both buyer and seller are liable for it. Contracts usually say who pays, and splitting it is common.

Several recurring tax facts matter at the closing table:

  • The township's 2026 real estate levies are 2.1298 mills for the general fund, 0.3727 for the library, 0.7485 for debt service, 0.7614 for emergency services and 0.241 for parks, which together equal 4.2534 mills. County and Methacton school taxes are billed in addition.
  • Tax bills go out on March 1. Payment before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies after July 1.
  • If a mortgage servicer pays your taxes from escrow, forward the bill to the servicer.

Some transfers, such as certain deeds between family members and property passed by inheritance, are exempt from the state tax. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds how an exemption is documented before you sign.

Can I appeal my Montgomery County assessment before I sell?

Yes. The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals takes annual appeals up to an August 1 deadline, and a postmark on or before that date counts. Fax and email filings are rejected.

A single-family appeal carries a $50 processing fee payable to the county treasurer, and the filing needs three copies of supporting documents such as an appraisal, comparable sales or photographs. All appeals must be heard by October 31, and the board grants rescheduling only in extraordinary circumstances. A homestead or farmstead appeal costs nothing. The board's office phone is 610-278-3761.

A lower assessment helps the next owner more than the seller, but a documented appeal can still support a price discussion with a buyer.

What if I am behind on property taxes in Lower Providence?

Unpaid township, school and county taxes are turned over to the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau, which can sell a parcel when taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid. Its upset sales are held each September and December, and the 2026 sale dates have already passed. A buyer at an upset sale takes the property subject to all liens, while a judicial sale presents parcels free and clear.

The practical lesson for a seller is to settle a delinquency before it reaches that stage. Selling before the bureau acts lets the closing pay the arrears from proceeds. Call the bureau at the Norristown office to confirm the payoff figure before you accept an offer.

Is a cash offer or a listing the better route in Lower Providence?

Three things decide it: how fast you must move, what repairs the house needs and how much certainty you want. Marketing the house widens the buyer pool, yet it adds showings, post-inspection repair requests and loan contingencies. A cash buyer usually has no lender to satisfy, so the closing date can follow your schedule.

  • Ask each buyer who orders and pays for the township resale inspection, and put the answer in the contract.
  • Compare net proceeds after the 2 percent transfer tax, any payoff, and your share of the township certifications.
  • Confirm that the buyer will accept the house with its current sewer, trash and tax accounts settled at closing.

Get the township certificates started as soon as you decide to sell. They are the part of a Lower Providence sale that you control.

More questions about Lower Providence, PA

Does Lower Providence Township require an inspection when I sell?

Yes. Residential sales need a resale use and occupancy certificate, which costs $100 and includes an initial inspection and one follow-up. Apply through the township's online permit portal.

How much is the transfer tax on a Lower Providence home sale?

The total is 2 percent of the value transferred. The state collects 1 percent, and the local 1 percent is split between the township and the Methacton School District. The county recorder collects it at deed recording.

Which school district serves Lower Providence?

Methacton School District. Arrowhead, Eagleville and Woodland elementary schools serve parts of the township, and Methacton High School is in neighboring Worcester Township.

When are Lower Providence property tax bills due?

Bills are mailed March 1. Paying before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies to payments made after July 1.

When is the Montgomery County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 each year. The appeal form, three copies of supporting papers and a $50 check for a single-family home must be postmarked or delivered by then.

What steps are required to sell a house in Plum Borough?

Plum requires a Residential Occupancy Permit whenever the occupancy of a home changes, which includes a sale. The owner files a Residential Occupancy Transfer Application with the Community Development office, pays $100 and then schedules an inspection. Once the house passes, the borough issues the permit.

Timing is the part to plan. The application has to be signed by the owner and submitted at least five business days before the inspection date you request. After it arrives, a building inspector contacts you to set a day and time. The borough posts a list of what inspectors look for, so read it and fix small items before the visit.

  • Fee: $100, payable by check to the Borough of Plum.
  • Lead time: five business days before the requested inspection.
  • Limit: the borough requires the permit for a change in ownership or residents, but no more than once every two years regardless of how many changes occur.
  • Result: a passing inspection produces the Occupancy Permit.

How much transfer tax does a seller pay in Plum Borough?

The total realty transfer tax on a Plum sale is 2%: one half of one percent to the borough, one half of one percent to the Plum School District and 1% to the Commonwealth. That is lower than neighboring Penn Hills, where the municipal share alone is 1.5%. Allegheny County collects the tax at the time the deed is recorded and takes it on a separate check from the recording fees.

On a $250,000 sale the total comes to $5,000. The sales agreement says who pays it. A transfer between close family members may need only a sentence on the deed describing the relationship, and other exemptions use the state's Statement of Value.
