What is Plum Borough like for a home seller?

Plum was organized as Plum Township on December 18, 1788, as one of the original seven townships of Allegheny County, and it became a borough in 1956. At 28.57 square miles of land it is the second-largest borough in the state by area. The borough sits northeast of Pittsburgh, with the Allegheny River on its northern edge, and it borders Monroeville, Penn Hills, Oakmont and, across the river, Cheswick, Springdale and Lower Burrell.

The Census Bureau estimates 26,225 residents for July 2025, about 3.4% below the 2020 base of 27,147. The 2020 census counted 27,144 people and 11,869 housing units, 4.7% of them vacant. Postal mail may carry a Pittsburgh address, even though the borough is outside the city limits.

  • Owners report a middle home value of $227,600 in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates, and 80.7% of households own.
  • Median household income: $98,705, well above Pittsburgh's $65,742.
  • Persons per household: 2.45, and 22.8% of residents are 65 or older.
  • Median gross rent: $1,177.
  • Commutes average 31.1 minutes.

The Pennsylvania Turnpike crosses Plum between mile markers 49 and 55. Oakmont Country Club lies mostly within the borough and has hosted ten U.S. Opens. The Plum Borough School District operates five school buildings: O'Block and Pivik elementary schools, Holiday Park Intermediate School, Plum Middle School and Plum Senior High School.

Do Plum Borough zoning and permits matter for a sale?

They can, because a buyer or inspector may notice work that was done without a permit. The Community Development department issues residential building permits for new dwellings, additions, decks, porches and porch roofs, pools deeper than 24 inches, structural alterations and demolitions. Zoning certificates cover front yard fences, sheds, detached garages, carports, gazebos and similar structures under 200 square feet.

If you added a deck or shed yourself, ask Community Development whether a permit or certificate is on file before the inspection. Fixing a paperwork gap before the occupancy visit is simpler than doing it after a buyer raises the question. The department also administers subdivision, conditional use and variance requests, which matter if the lot is large enough to split.

How do Allegheny County taxes and appeals affect a Plum sale?

Plum parcels are assessed by the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments on a base year of 2012, and the county notes that these figures are not current market values. Appeals go to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. The annual window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026, so it has closed, and the county says a parcel taxed by the county for the first time in 2027 will not appear on its portal until values are certified in January 2027.

Ask the county treasurer and the Plum tax collectors for a paid-to-date statement before closing. Any balance owed gets paid from the sale proceeds, and a title search will show open amounts. The county also runs a homestead exclusion under Act 50 for owner-occupied homes, and a buyer who will live in the house applies through the county.

What does Pennsylvania require a Plum seller to disclose?

Under 68 Pa.C.S. Chapter 73, the seller must deliver a signed, dated property disclosure statement before the buyer and seller sign the agreement of transfer. The statement covers the roof, basement, structure, plumbing, electrical systems, heating and cooling, water and sewage service, land and drainage, hazardous substances and title issues. It also asks about the condition and location of storm water facilities and whether the owner or someone else maintains them.

The seller does not need to carry out special testing but may not say anything known to be false or leave out a known material defect. The method of delivery can be in person, by first class mail, by certified mail or by fax. A disclosure can be amended in writing before the agreement is signed.

  • Condominium sellers disclose only about their own unit.
  • Estate fiduciaries are outside the chapter.
  • A buyer's damages suit must begin within two years after final settlement.

How can a Plum homeowner sell quickly?

Choose the route first, then line up the permit. A listing gives the widest audience, a sale by owner keeps the commission, and a cash sale usually shortens the schedule. All three still need the Plum occupancy inspection before the deed transfers, so book it as soon as you have a target closing date.

  • Submit the occupancy application at least five business days ahead of the inspection date.
  • Check the borough's inspector checklist and fix small items beforehand.
  • Confirm permits for any deck, porch or shed you built.
  • Ask the settlement agent for the 2% transfer tax figure and the payoff before you accept terms.

More questions about Plum, PA

Does Plum Borough require an occupancy permit to sell a house?

Yes. A Residential Occupancy Permit is required when the occupancy of a home changes. The owner files the application with a $100 fee, an inspector schedules a visit, and a passing inspection gets the permit.

How far ahead must I apply for the Plum occupancy inspection?

Apply at least five business days before the inspection date you want. The application must be signed by the owner and paid by check to the Borough of Plum. An inspector then contacts you to set the day and time.

How much is the transfer tax in Plum Borough?

It is 2% in total: 0.5% to the borough, 0.5% to the Plum School District and 1% to the state. On a $250,000 sale that is $5,000. Allegheny County collects it when the deed is recorded.

Can Plum require a new occupancy permit every time ownership changes?

Not more than once every two years. The borough requires the permit for a change in ownership or residents, but caps it at one every two years regardless of how many changes happen. Ask Community Development how that rule applies if the home changed hands recently.

Is the appeal window for my Allegheny County assessment still open?

No. The window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026 and is closed. Watch the county's real estate portal for the next window if you think your value is off.

Where is Montgomery Township, Pennsylvania?

Montgomery Township is the largest municipality in the North Penn area of Montgomery County, along PA 309 near the Bucks County line. It covers 10.63 square miles of land, largely built out with suburban neighborhoods, and the 2020 census counted 25,862 residents. A July 2025 estimate puts it at 26,210.

Its downtown is Montgomery Square on PA 309, and the township's ZIP code is 19454. The township also includes parts of villages shared with neighbors: Colmar and Fortuna with Hatfield Township, and Christy and Eureka with Bucks County and Horsham Township. Little Neshaminy Creek drains most of the area, which puts it in the Delaware watershed. Neighbors include Horsham, Lower Gwynedd and Upper Gwynedd townships, the borough of Lansdale and Hatfield Township, plus New Britain and Warrington townships across the line in Bucks County.

How did Montgomery Township begin?

The township was incorporated on May 17, 1714. Alexander Edwards, one of the first settlers, was born in Wales and wrote "of Montgomery" in his will before his death in 1712. Many Welsh families settled in this part of old Philadelphia County, and the county that formed on September 10, 1784 was probably named for Montgomeryshire in Wales. The Knapp Farm earned a National Register listing in 1976.

The population curve explains the housing stock. The township had 850 residents in 1930 and 2,700 in 1960, then 5,718 in 1980 and 12,179 in 1990. It reached 22,025 in 2000. The count more than doubled during the 1980s, a 113 percent jump, and rose another 81 percent by 2000, so many houses here come from those two building waves.

How do Montgomery Township housing and income figures look?

Owners live in 89.4 percent of the township's homes, and median household income is $134,074. Each row is from the Census Bureau's profile of the township.

What roads and transit connect Montgomery Township?

Several major routes cross the township:

  • U.S. 202 runs southwest to northeast through the center on a parkway-style road.
  • PA 309 runs north to south on Bethlehem Pike through Montgomery Square.
  • PA 63 follows Welsh Road along the southwestern edge, and PA 152 passes through the eastern corner on Limekiln Pike.
  • PA 463 crosses on Cowpath Road and Horsham Road, and County Line Road marks part of the Bucks County boundary.

SEPTA runs Suburban Bus routes 94, 96 and 132 to Montgomery Mall. Workers spend an average 29.0 minutes getting to their jobs. A plant hardiness line between zones 6b and 7a follows a ridge near Stump Road, and Montgomeryville averages 29.9 degrees in January and 74.3 in July.

Does Montgomery Township require an inspection when a house is sold?

The township's fee schedule lists a Use and Occupancy permit for residential property only for new construction, at $150, with other occupancy permits aimed at manufactured homes and non-residential space. The schedule does not list a resale permit for an existing house. Call the township at (215) 393-6920 to confirm for your address, since a homeowner association or your buyer's lender can add their own steps.

Any work you did on the house is a separate question. Montgomery Township publishes residential requirements and a list of projects that need permits, so collect your permit history before listing. The Codes and Permits office is at 1001 Stump Road, with posted weekday hours of 8:30 to 4:30.

How do taxes, homestead and appeals work for a Montgomery Township seller?

Assessed values for county, municipal and school bills come from the county Board of Assessment Appeals. A yearly appeal is due August 1 ahead of the tax year at issue, and exemption applications share that date. The early date lets the board finish hearings by October 31 and notify owners and taxing districts by November 15.

A homestead exclusion trims the taxable value of a primary residence. A March 1 filing reaches school taxes starting the next July 1, and a December 15 filing reaches municipal taxes in participating municipalities starting the next January 1. The rule that concerns sellers is that a sale clears the exclusion automatically, so the seller files nothing and the buyer applies fresh. A denial may be appealed within 40 days.

The county also warns that mailed filings can be postmarked late. Ask the post office for a hand-cancelled postmark or deliver the paper to the Norristown office.

What is the transfer tax and what disclosures apply in Montgomery Township?

Transfer tax on a Montgomery Township deed runs 2 percent of the price, according to the county Recorder of Deeds. A deed claiming an exemption must carry the Department of Revenue's REV-183 Statement of Value. For deeds dated July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027, Montgomery County's common level ratio factor is 3.36.

Pennsylvania's Seller Disclosure Law has a seller complete a disclosure statement and get a signed, dated copy to the buyer ahead of the agreement. No investigation is required, but a known defect may not be left out or misdescribed. Anything that turns inaccurate before settlement must be corrected, and a buyer has two years after settlement to bring a damages claim.

What happens if taxes are unpaid, and what are the ways to sell?

Back taxes can lead to a county upset sale, held each September and December for parcels whose taxes from two years earlier are still unpaid. Parcels that fail to sell move to judicial and repository sales. A buyer at an upset sale takes on every lien, and judicial sale parcels are offered free and clear.

For a Montgomery Township house with back taxes, the usual choices are:

  • Pay the balance, then list as usual.
  • Sell to an owner-occupant and pay the taxes off at settlement.
  • Take an as-is cash offer from a buyer who handles the condition.

Get a payoff figure from the bureau first, since penalties and interest change the comparison.

More questions about Montgomery, PA

How much transfer tax applies to a Montgomery Township sale?

Two percent of the price, per the county Recorder of Deeds, collected as the deed is recorded. Claiming an exemption takes a Statement of Value.

Does a buyer keep my homestead exclusion?

No. Montgomery County removes it automatically once the deed changes hands, and the new owner files a fresh application.

What is the last day to appeal a Montgomery County assessment?

August 1, one year ahead of the tax year at issue. Exemption applications share the date.

Is a township resale certificate needed in Montgomery Township?

On the township's fee schedule, the residential Use and Occupancy permit is for new construction. Call the township at (215) 393-6920 to confirm, since your buyer's lender or an association may want other paperwork.

What must a Pennsylvania seller tell a buyer about the house?

Known material defects, listed on a property disclosure statement that is signed, dated and delivered before an agreement of transfer. Subjects include the roof, basement, plumbing, heating, wiring and drainage.

Where does Exeter Township sit, and how did it grow?

Growth followed trolley lines and then post-war suburban building, and the US 422 expressway toward King of Prussia opened in the 1980s.

  • Village names: addresses and maps use Reiffton, Jacksonwald, Stonersville, Lorane, Neversink, Limekiln, Baumstown and Stonetown, none of which is a separate municipality.
  • Roads: US 422 (Perkiomen Avenue) and PA 562 (St. Lawrence Avenue and Boyertown Pike) cross it east and west, while PA 345 runs from Baumstown over the river to Birdsboro. Of 137.33 public road miles, the township itself maintains 115.88.
  • Transit: BARTA routes 7 and 8 connect the township to the BARTA Transportation Center in Reading.
  • Weather: a hot-summer humid continental climate in zone 6b, with Jacksonwald averaging 29.9 degrees in January and 74.7 in July.
  • History: the Daniel Boone Homestead lies inside the township, and the Exeter Friends Meeting House, a Quaker meetinghouse, is on the National Register of Historic Places.
  • Schools: the district operates Lorane, Owatin Creek and Jacksonwald for kindergarten through grade 4, Reiffton Elementary for grades 5 and 6, then a junior high and a senior high. St. Lawrence borough also sends students there.
  • Government: five elected supervisors run the township, and its Parks and Recreation department looks after the parks.

Early residents were mostly Quakers living near the meetinghouse and the Monocacy and Limekiln creeks, and the Boone family is credited with the Exeter name, after the English town. Besides the meetinghouse, the Mordecai Lincoln House, Boonecroft, Levan Farm, Mill Tract Farm, Snyder Mill and the John Bishop House are on the National Register, which is useful context if your property sits near one of them.

How do incomes and home values look in Exeter Township?

Exeter households earn a median $100,083, and an owner's home is typically valued at $281,800 (2020 to 2024). Nearly one resident in five, 19.3%, is 65 or older, and 93.6% lived in the same house a year earlier.

Exeter Township in numbers, Census QuickFacts

Rented houses are a small slice of the market here, since owners occupy 87.1% of homes.

Which township rules could affect my Exeter sale?

Look at the zoning code, the historic resources rules and the short-term lodging license before signing anything. The township's code is posted online, and its Building, Zoning and Engineering department publishes forms for building, plumbing, zoning and sign permits, plus a complaint form and a flood plains map.

  • Historic resources: the zoning code sorts historic properties into Classes I to IV and routes changes to them through the Planning Commission and the Board of Supervisors. Class I status requires the owner's written consent and binds heirs and later owners. After a historic resource is demolished through neglect, the township may withhold building and occupancy permits for a year.
  • Short-term lodging: a license from the Zoning Officer lets a property serve as short-term lodging, but never for more than 90 days in a calendar year. A buyer planning nightly rentals has to apply.
  • Floodplain: a flood plains map sits in the township's document center, so check whether your parcel falls on it.

If your house is a listed historic resource or sits in a mapped flood area, say so early.

How do Berks County assessments and appeals affect an Exeter sale?

The last countywide reassessment in Berks County took effect for the 1994 tax year, so assessments can sit far from sale prices. The Assessment Office at 400 E. Wyomissing Avenue in Mohnton holds the records but sends no bills and collects nothing. Ask the municipal tax collector what is owed.

Annual appeals open June 15 and close August 1, and a changed assessment has to be contested within 40 days of its notice. New filing fees took effect January 1, 2026, and the board has met in person since April 2026. A reduction requires proof that the assessment exceeds current market value, because the law presumes it correct, and high taxes or trouble paying do not count. School districts and municipalities can appeal too, often to raise a value.

The county warns that no age-based or special form freezes or removes property taxes for seniors. Homestead and farmstead exclusions do exist, and the school district supplies the forms.

What does recording a deed involve in Berks County?

A document conveying real estate in Berks County has an $88 base fee, after the Pennsylvania Judicial Fee rose by $1 in December 2025. The Recorder of Deeds sits on the third floor of the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, Reading. It refuses personal checks for transfer tax, and a Statement of Value adds one page to the fee count.

The state tax is 1% of the property's value, with both parties to the deed liable. The recorder sends the state share to the Department of Revenue and the local share on to the municipality or school district. Certain family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt. Call the Recorder of Deeds to learn the total rate for your price.

What does Pennsylvania require of an Exeter seller?

68 Pa.C.S. section 7308 does not make a seller investigate the property, yet the seller may not state anything known to be false or omit a known material defect. Under section 7306, items the seller cannot know can be answered from the best information available. Delivery can be personal, by first-class or certified mail, or by fax, and a buyer paying cash gets the same form.

When does a cash sale fit an Exeter Township house?

Cash appeals to owners who want no showings, repair lists or long wait. Exeter examples include an estate house that needs clearing, deferred upkeep on a home held for decades, a relocation near family, or a short-term lodging license problem. Set the offer next to what a listing would net after repairs and transfer tax, then pick the route you prefer.

More questions about Exeter, PA

What sets the closing date for an Exeter Township cash sale?

Title work and your preferred date set it, since no lender's schedule applies. The deed is then recorded with the Berks County Recorder of Deeds.

Is Exeter Township part of Reading?

No. Exeter Township is its own municipality in Berks County and borders St. Lawrence borough and Birdsboro. Confirm your municipality on the tax bill, since the township, not the city, sets your zoning.

May I still contest my Exeter assessment while the house is for sale?

Yes, during the June 15 to August 1 annual window or within 40 days of a change notice. You must show the assessment exceeds market value.

What school district covers Exeter Township?

Exeter Township School District, which also takes in the borough of St. Lawrence. Its buildings are Lorane, Owatin Creek and Jacksonwald elementary schools, Reiffton Elementary School, Exeter Junior High and Exeter Township Senior High.

Can an Exeter house be used for short-term rentals?

Only with a short-term lodging license from the Zoning Officer, and the code caps use at 90 days in a calendar year. A buyer should confirm the license before counting on rental income.

How does selling a house in Upper Moreland, PA work?

Selling in Upper Moreland follows the usual Pennsylvania path, with one local advantage: the township's code enforcement department does not require a use and occupancy certificate or any inspection when a residential or commercial property is resold. You sign an agreement of sale, deliver your disclosure statement first, pay transfer tax at recording and settle through a title company or attorney.

Upper Moreland Township is in Montgomery County, about 13 to 15 miles north of Center City Philadelphia, with an estimated 25,880 residents. Most of it is Willow Grove-area housing built during the post-war growth that took the township from 5,103 people in 1940 to 21,032 in 1960. That growth curve points to a stock of mid-century houses, so expect buyers to ask about roof age and original systems.

What is Upper Moreland like for home buyers?

Upper Moreland is a compact, mostly residential township of just under 8 square miles, so almost every house is a short drive from the turnpike, a rail station or a shopping strip. It borders Hatboro, Horsham, Upper Dublin, Abington, Bryn Athyn and Lower Moreland in Montgomery County, and Bucks County lies to the north.

The land has a documented past. William Penn gave the tract to Nicholas More in 1682, when it was called the Manor of Mooreland. In 1916 a line drawn through Pennypack Creek created Upper and Lower Moreland, and in 1930 Upper Moreland was organized as a first-class township. A seven-member board of commissioners, one from each ward, governs it.

Buyers will compare your house on these local points:

  • The Willow Grove interchange of the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276) sits inside the township.
  • PA 611 (Easton Road), PA 263 (York Road) and PA 63 (Moreland Road) carry local traffic, with Davisville, Byberry, Fitzwatertown, Terwood and Blair Mill roads feeding neighborhoods.
  • SEPTA's Warminster Line stops at Willow Grove station, and bus routes 22, 55, 310 and 95 serve the township.
  • Of 85.02 miles of public road, 65.51 miles belong to the township, which also handles trash and recycling through its public works department.
  • PECO supplies power and gas, Aqua Pennsylvania supplies water, and the Upper Moreland-Hatboro Joint Sewer Authority handles sewage.

What do Census figures show for Upper Moreland housing?

Upper Moreland has the lowest home value among the four Montgomery and Bucks townships that share this Census table, which affects both pricing and who can buy without a large down payment. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts give these figures for the township.

Population has dipped 0.4 percent since the 2020 base, and 89.0 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Low turnover means fewer comparable sales, so a pricing opinion that uses recent sales on nearby streets matters more here than a township average.

Does Upper Moreland require an inspection or certificate before I sell?

No. The code enforcement department states that it does not require a Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of a residential or commercial property, and its FAQ says no inspections are required on resale. Businesses moving into the township do have to file a Zoning Use Registration Permit.

Work you did on the house is a different matter, and buyers' inspectors check it. The department answers permit questions at 117 Park Avenue, Willow Grove, and by phone at 267-607-1032 or 267-607-1033 on weekdays from 7:30 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon Its published rules for open projects are short:

  • Residential permit plans are normally reviewed in about 15 working days, and two sets of plans are required.
  • Only a registered master plumber may submit a plumbing permit. An owner may do electrical work but still needs the permit.
  • A fence needs a permit, with a maximum height of 6 feet in a rear yard and 4 feet in a front yard.
  • Installing a pool requires a building permit.

If you built a fence, deck or pool without a permit, ask the department how to close it out before you list.

Which schools serve Upper Moreland homes?

Upper Moreland Township is served by the Upper Moreland School District, which runs by grade band rather than by neighborhood elementary school. Upper Moreland Primary School takes kindergarten through grade 2, the Intermediate School covers grades 3 to 5, the Middle School covers grades 6 to 8, and Upper Moreland High School serves grades 9 to 12.

The area Catholic option is Queen of Angels Regional Catholic School in Willow Grove. For health care, Jefferson Health-Willow Grove offers outpatient services in the township. Buyers with children often ask about both, so mention them in your listing text.

What taxes and paperwork come with an Upper Moreland sale?

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the value of the property at the state level, and local governments add their own share. Bucks County's recorder describes the combined statewide tax as 2 percent and notes that sellers and buyers usually divide it. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds what applies to Upper Moreland and how it is collected.

Before the agreement of sale is signed, you deliver a completed property disclosure statement under 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. The form asks about roofs, basements, termites, structural problems, plumbing, wiring and storm water facilities. Act 74 of 2026 amended the form's land item and added a flood-insurance notice, so ask your agent or attorney for the current form. If property tax is in arrears, the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau runs upset sales each September and December for parcels unpaid from two years earlier. You contest an assessment through the Board of Assessment Appeals, whose page lists the annual appeal deadline document.

Is a cash sale a good fit for an Upper Moreland house?

A cash sale fits best when the house needs repairs you do not want to fund, when you are managing an estate, or when timing matters more than the last dollar. Older houses often carry aging roofs and mechanicals, and a buyer who purchases as-is removes the inspection-repair back and forth. A listing usually fetches more on the open market, with more showings and a financing window.

  • Get at least two written offers and compare closing dates.
  • Confirm who pays transfer tax and whether the buyer covers recording costs.
  • Check that the buyer can show proof of funds before you sign.

More questions about Upper Moreland, PA

Do I need a resale certificate in Upper Moreland?

No. The township's code enforcement department says it does not require a Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of residential or commercial property, and it requires no resale inspection. Contractor-built work still needs the permits listed on the township website.

What is the typical home value in Upper Moreland?

Upper Moreland owners report a typical value of $391,600 for 2020 to 2024. That is a township-wide midpoint, so use recent sales close to your house to set a price.

Which county records a deed in Upper Moreland?

Montgomery County records it, through the Recorder of Deeds office. Your title company or attorney handles the filing, so ask them what the recorder needs with the deed, including transfer tax paperwork.

How do I find out who handles trash and sewer for my house?

The township's public works department handles trash and recycling, and the Upper Moreland-Hatboro Joint Sewer Authority provides sewage service. Buyers ask for the latest bills, so gather them before listing.

Can I sell an inherited house in Upper Moreland as-is?

Yes. Pennsylvania's seller disclosure chapter does not apply to transfers by a fiduciary administering a decedent's estate, though the sale still needs proper authority to sign. Ask the estate's attorney to confirm who may sign the deed.

What shapes a house sale in Derry Township and Hershey?

Derry Township is the municipality that contains Hershey, and a sale there is shaped by two things: a very stable local economy built around chocolate, tourism and a major medical center, and a tax setup that runs through Dauphin County rather than a local collector. The township sits in southeastern Dauphin County, east of Harrisburg, with Lebanon County on its eastern edge and Swatara Creek forming most of its northwest border.

It covers about 27.4 square miles, almost all of it land. The unincorporated communities inside it include Hershey, Palmdale, Swatara, Hockersville, Oakmont, Waltonville and part of Stoverdale. When people say they live in Hershey, their deed usually says Derry Township.

This page walks through what a seller here should line up: who bills the taxes, what transfer tax applies, how assessments and appeals work in Dauphin County, and what the township's Community Development office handles.

How has Hershey shaped Derry Township?

The township was incorporated on August 1, 1729, by the sons of William Penn, back when it was much larger and part of Lancaster County. It joined Dauphin County when that county was created in 1785. In 2002, township supervisors proposed renaming it Hershey Township, and voters turned that down, with 54 percent opposed.

The township's own website describes Hershey as a model town that Milton S. Hershey set out to build for the needs of the factory workers. That planning still shows: the community has its own police department, public works department and public library, and the Hershey Medical Center and Children's Hospital stand on a large tract inside its borders.

  • Hersheypark and other attractions are run by Hershey Entertainment and Resorts
  • The township levies an amusement tax tied to those attractions
  • The climate is hot-summer humid continental, with monthly averages from about 30 degrees in January to about 75 in July

How do Derry Township homes and incomes measure up?

The Census Bureau estimates 25,179 residents for July 1, 2025, only slightly above the 2010 count of 24,679. This is a mature community that grows slowly. Nearly one in five residents is 65 or older.

Health care receipts of about $2.5 billion in 2022 and accommodation and food service sales of $354 million show how much of the local economy rests on the medical center and visitors.

Who bills property tax in Derry Township, and at what rates?

Since January 1, 2023, the Dauphin County Treasurer's Office collects both township and Derry Township School District real estate taxes. The township's Tax Association Office closed that day, and occupation and local services taxes moved to Keystone Collections Group. The county's tax collector list also shows the county treasurer handling Derry bills.

The township's tax page lists these real estate millage rates: 2.53810 mills for the township, 20.3387 mills for the school district and 9.193 mills for Dauphin County. Rates change when budgets pass, so confirm the current numbers with the county treasurer before you build a net sheet.

Other township taxes depend on the person, not the house. Earned income tax is 1 percent, split evenly between the township and the school district, and the township also receives $250 from each employed resident earning over $12,000. A buyer moving into Derry will pay those, but they do not affect your proceeds.

What does a Derry Township sale cost in transfer tax?

The total is 2 percent of the sale price. Dauphin County's Recorder of Deeds explains that the state's Department of Revenue receives 1 percent, and the municipality and the school district each receive half of one percent. The township's tax page confirms the township share: 0.5 percent of the purchase price.

On a $390,000 sale, which matches the Census median value, 2 percent comes to $7,800. The sales agreement determines which side pays, and the state holds both parties responsible. Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are generally exempt, though the Dauphin recorder suggests checking with an attorney or the Department of Revenue for other exemptions.

The Recorder of Deeds is at the Dauphin County Courthouse in Harrisburg, and its records begin in 1785. Fees for recording are set by the state legislature.

How do assessments, appeals and relief programs work in Dauphin County?

The Dauphin County Office of Tax Assessment values real property, keeps ownership records and runs the county's homestead and farmstead exclusion, its Clean and Green preferential assessment program and its tax deferral program. Its office is on the second floor of the County Administration Building at 2 South Second Street in Harrisburg, and its parcel data is online.

The office does not set tax rates. The county, the township and the school district do that after assessments are in. If you think your assessment is too high, ask the office for the appeal rules and the filing date that applies to your parcel.

A new state law matters for owners of rental houses. Act 29 of 2026 creates a county-kept contact registry for properties that are not owner-occupied, effective September 18, 2026. Owners, and lenders after a foreclosure, must give the county a name, address, phone and email for someone authorized to resolve code violations, within 30 days of taking ownership and within 30 days of any change. A failure to comply can bring a $500 fine, and owner-occupied principal residences are exempt.

What does the township's Community Development office handle?

The township municipal complex at 600 Clearwater Road in Hershey is where you ask about permits, zoning and any open code issue on an address. Do that before you list, because a buyer's lender or inspector may ask for the same paperwork.

  • Check whether any past work on the house, such as a finished basement, a deck or a pool, had a permit
  • Ask which zoning district the lot is in if your buyer plans a business, an addition or a rental
  • Confirm that street light assessments and other township charges on the account are current
  • Sign up for the township's eNews to follow notices that affect your street

A little time spent on these items before you list keeps surprises away from the closing table.

What are my choices for selling a Derry Township house?

With a median home value near $390,000 and strong local employers, a house in good order can sell through a normal listing. An as-is sale makes more sense when you are settling an estate, relocating, or facing repairs you would rather not finance.

Whichever path you choose, ask for the net figure in writing: price, less 2 percent transfer tax if you agree to pay it, payoffs, prorated county, township and school taxes, and any repair credit. Request the buyer's proof of funds and closing date before you take the house off the market.

More questions about Derry, PA

Is Hershey a separate town from Derry Township?

No. Hershey is an unincorporated community inside Derry Township, so deeds, permits and taxes for a Hershey address go through the township and Dauphin County.

What is the transfer tax on a house sale in Derry Township?

It totals 2 percent: 1 percent to the state, 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the school district, collected by the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

Who collects real estate taxes on a Derry Township house?

The Dauphin County Treasurer's Office collects both township and school district real estate taxes. Call the treasurer for balances before closing.

Do I need to register a rental house I am selling in Dauphin County?

Act 29 of 2026 requires owners of non-owner-occupied property to give the county contact details, effective September 18, 2026, with updates within 30 days of any change. Your buyer takes on that duty when they become the owner.

Are family transfers exempt from realty transfer tax in Dauphin County?

Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are generally exempt, though other exemptions exist. Confirm with an attorney or the Department of Revenue.

What does selling a house in Springfield, PA involve?

Springfield here means Springfield Township in Delaware County, a suburb of single-family homes southwest of Philadelphia with the 19064 ZIP code. Several Pennsylvania townships share the name, so note the neighbors: Haverford, Upper Darby, Ridley, Morton, Swarthmore, Nether Providence and Marple all touch this one. Whoever buys, the sale runs through a township resale inspection, settled tax bills and a deed recorded in Media.

The township was recognized as a governmental unit in 1686 after Quakers arrived with William Penn, and it grew from farmland into a residential community once developers bought up the fields. One of the largest developments, Stoney Creek, was built between 1949 and 1954 with stone-fronted houses that were each slightly different. That postwar housing explains why many Springfield sellers are dealing with older mechanical systems and original layouts.

What does the Census count in Springfield's homeowner base?

Census estimates put the 2025 population at 25,039, nearly level with the 25,070 of 2020 and above the 24,211 of 2010. Its 6.32 square miles of land hold about 3,966 people each.

Owner occupancy is 93.8 percent, a very high rate, and 92.3 percent of people kept the same address over the past year. The middle owned home was valued at $414,900, median household income is $138,205, and households average 2.87 people. Children under 18 make up 24.2 percent of the population, so the buyers most likely to want a Springfield house are families who need space close to the city.

With so few rentals, investor-owned houses are a small part of the market. Landlords file a Business Privilege Rental Tax Return with the township, so anyone who rented the house out should ask the tax office which filings to close.

How does the township's resale inspection affect a Springfield sale?

The township homepage carries a Resale Inspection Appointment Request, which signals that a sale triggers an inspection by the code office. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, and ask what the inspector will check and how long a certificate stays valid.

The code office posts the violations it sees most often, and they double as a checklist before you list:

  • Grass cannot grow higher than 8 inches.
  • Plantings at an intersection can be no taller than 18 inches, and shrubs cannot block signs or signals.
  • House numbers must be 4 inches high and visible from the street.
  • Vehicles may park only on paved surfaces, never on the lawn.
  • Owners must maintain the curbs and sidewalks in front of the property, and snow has to come off public sidewalks within 24 hours after it stops falling.
  • Trash containers stay behind the front building line and come off the street within 12 hours of pickup.

Apply for repair permits on the township's OpenGov portal and call the inspector with questions. Large repairs are easier to defend when the paperwork exists.

When are Springfield township and school taxes due, and who gets paid at closing?

Two bills arrive each year on separate calendars, and whatever is still owed gets paid from your proceeds at closing. The township publishes both schedules.

Springfield Township and Springfield School District billing windows
BillBilling date2% discount throughFace amount10% penalty after
Township tax, sewer, refuseFebruary 1March 31April 1 to May 31June 1
School tax (fiscal year July 1 to June 30)July 1August 31September 1 to October 31November 1

Refuse and sewer rent ride on the township bill, with sewer rent figured from last year's water use. A sewer or refuse balance that stays unpaid becomes a lien, and real estate tax still unpaid is returned to the Tax Claim Bureau in Media by the next January. The township tax office is at 610-544-1300.

Homestead-approved properties may pay school tax in three installments, and the township's collection books close on December 31. Get the exact balance on your parcel from the tax office before settlement.

How much does Delaware County charge in transfer tax at recording?

Delaware County charges 2 percent on a transfer: one point for the state and one for the municipality. The county names four higher-rate exceptions, Radnor, Upper Darby, Upper Providence and Chester City, and Springfield is absent from that list.

Using the township's $414,900 middle value, 2 percent comes to $8,298. The contract decides who pays it, though the state holds buyer and seller jointly liable, so a title company normally collects it at the table.

Recording happens at Government Center, Room 108, 201 W. Front Street, Media; call 610-891-4152. Staff there cannot draft a deed or run a title search, and mortgages are the only liens on file with them. After a payoff the lender files a mortgage satisfaction, and the county's public access site lets you confirm your own records.

What shapes buyer interest in Springfield beyond the house itself?

Buyers look at the schools, the commute and the parks. Springfield School District serves the township with the Springfield Literacy Center for kindergarten and first grade, Scenic Hills and Harvey C. Sabold for grades 2 through 5, E. T. Richardson Middle School for grades 6 through 8, and Springfield High School, whose new building opened in 2021.

  • Roads: I-476 touches the western edge, U.S. 1 follows State Road through the north, and Pennsylvania routes 320 and 420 cross the township. The township counts 84.34 miles of public roads.
  • Transit: SEPTA's Media-Sharon Hill light rail line serves the township, SEPTA suburban buses run routes 107, 109, 110 and 111, and Regional Rail stops at nearby Swarthmore and Morton. Commutes average 27.7 minutes.
  • Retail: Baltimore Pike, nicknamed the Golden Mile, was once known for car dealerships, and Springfield Mall has about 590,000 square feet. Census figures show 2022 retail sales of $1,289,004,000.
  • Parks: there are 24 parks, including Veterans Memorial Park and Williams Park.

Darby Creek forms the northeast border and Crum Creek the west. Winters average about 33 degrees in January and July averages near 78, a humid subtropical pattern. Expect buyers to ask about water in the basement.

What are the practical choices if you need to sell a Springfield house quickly?

Listing with an agent works for a house in good shape, and clearing the violations above before it goes live keeps the resale inspection from delaying closing.

When the house needs work or the calendar is tight, selling straight to an investor or cash buyer drops lender approval and most repair haggling. Whatever you choose, get the price, closing date and transfer tax responsibility in writing, then weigh it against the net a listing would leave after fees and repairs.

More questions about Springfield, PA

Which county records a Springfield, PA deed?

Delaware County. The Recorder of Deeds is in the Government Center in Media. It records deeds and mortgages and returns the originals according to the filer's instructions, usually through the closing agent.

What transfer tax would a Springfield sale carry?

Two percent, split evenly between the state and the municipality. Springfield is not on the county's higher-rate list, so a $414,900 sale would carry $8,298.

Do I need a resale inspection to sell in Springfield Township?

The township offers a Resale Inspection Appointment Request on its homepage, so plan on one. Call the Code Department at 610-544-1300, extension 125, to learn the current checklist and fees before you list.

When is the Springfield school tax discount?

School bills go out July 1. A 2 percent discount applies through August 31, the face amount is due from September 1 to October 31, and a 10 percent penalty starts November 1.

What happens to unpaid sewer and refuse charges when I sell?

They are filed as liens against the property, so they must be cleared. Ask the township tax office for the balance owed so the title company can pay it from your proceeds.
